International

International | What backlash? Oct 22nd 2026 AS A BOY growing up in the aftermath of the Korean war, Bae Oh-do would venture out into the forest to gather firewood to heat his family’s home. “The manual era is completely ingrained in me,” says the 70-year-old violin salesman, sitting under a tre...
item.content:encoded:
The surprising popularity of AI

International | What backlash?

Oct 22nd 2026

AS A BOY growing up in the aftermath of the Korean war, Bae Oh-do would venture out into the forest to gather firewood to heat his family’s home. “The manual era is completely ingrained in me,” says the 70-year-old violin salesman, sitting under a tree in a park in Seoul’s Jong-no district. He recalls having to use a foot-operated “treadle pump” to get water, as well as his delight when the first tractors rolled into the South Korean countryside.

In recent decades he has seen things “develop so conveniently”, with the internet and smartphones. And what about artificial intelligence? “It’s nothing for humans to worry about. This kind of thing is good,” he says. “They should keep developing the technology. Humanity has advanced so much up to our generation. There’s no telling how the world will change.”

Read the headlines in Western media and it may seem as though a backlash to AI is spreading fast everywhere. But so far, it is not. Mr Bae’s sunny disposition about AI is shared by almost two-thirds of South Koreans, according to a survey that GlobeScan, a polling firm, conducted for The Economist. Outside rich countries this good feeling is even more strongly shared: nearly nine in ten people in Nigeria and Vietnam, for example, said that AI will improve not only their own lives, but the lot of humanity (see chart 1).

The polling across 34 countries was carried out online, which could tilt attitudes in favour of AI. Yet in the same survey sentiment in rich Western countries was much gloomier. In America, Canada and France more people felt negatively than positively about AI’s future impact on humanity. In other Western countries sentiment was net-positive, but far less so than in the poor world. Another recent survey of 37 countries, carried out by Gallup with Microsoft, returned similar results: AI is broadly popular, but less so in rich Western countries.

Why the gap between the West and the rest? Some of the optimism may cool as more people in poor countries come into direct contact with AI or data centres, and see the technology helping or hurting some more than others. Around 9% of working-age Kenyans used AI in the second quarter of 2026, according to a study by Microsoft. Yet 85% told GlobeScan that it would change their lives for the better.

But plenty of people, poor and rich alike, are already at least vaguely conscious of AI’s pitfalls. In a survey by Pew Research Centre, South Koreans were most likely (along with Australians) to say they expect AI to generate massive job losses and worsen inequality. For now, though, such fears appear to be outweighed by intrigue about the technology’s promise.

Part of the explanation is that many workers outside the richest countries have less to lose from AI than do their counterparts in the West. In much of the poor world work is often informal and, compared with jobs in the West, precarious. The notion of losing a secure office job to technology is more of a rich-world problem (though in India, say, information-technology and other back-office workers look vulnerable to disruption).

The poor world has much to gain from AI, too. In countries where institutions and formal education can be lacking, AI helps some people help themselves. “Pessimism is a privilege for those who can afford to despair,” argues Payal Arora, author of “From Pessimism to Promise”, a book about diverging attitudes to technology.

In India users have gained cheap or free access to apps like Gemini from Google or ChatGPT from OpenAI; nearly one in five working-age Indians used generative AI in the second quarter of 2026, compared with a third of Americans, according to a recent Microsoft study. DeepSeek, a free Chinese alternative, is popular in Africa, where Microsoft estimates that in many countries about one in ten working-age people used generative AI in the second quarter.

A narrow street in a busy suburb of Mumbai illustrates the benefits. Many shops on it use ChatGPT to generate advertisements. Dinesh Chandra, an optician, asked the chatbot to produce a “gravity-defying” photo for his brand. It duly created an image, now printed on brochures, of glasses floating above clouds while riding a feather. Next door Omkar Sapre, who sells dried fruit, masalas and pickles, posts “beautiful pictures” from ChatGPT on Instagram and WhatsApp, and has noticed his sales pick up. Ashlesha, who works at a dry cleaner on the same street, says, “We work hard and AI is extra support for us. Everyone is on Instagram.”

All of them love the convenience of using AI; none worry about safety, privacy or data leaks, much less “AI slop”. The shaming of AI content seems less common outside America and Europe. Westerners “have historically monopolised knowledge and ideational production, but AI challenges that,” says Yuen Yuen Ang of Johns Hopkins University. “Is it a crisis only for those who lose from disruption?”

As Mr Bae illustrates, even in some rich and middle-income countries where there seems more to lose from disruption, AI is surprisingly popular. Singaporeans are among the world’s top AI users, says Microsoft; nearly two-thirds told GlobeScan they thought the technology would have a positive effect on their lives. In Malaysia, which is experiencing a big data-centre boom, minor protests against the sites have not yet turned into a wider backlash.

Some countries where AI-optimism runs high share common factors that seem to cut across socioeconomic lines. One is a looming shortage of workers. Parts of the world that have long had low fertility rates, like East Asia, are ageing rapidly. Many hope that AI (and AI-powered robots) can fill in for workers who do not exist, helping countries to care for greying populations.

Another feature of some AI-optimist countries is a living memory of technology radically transforming societies in the span of a lifetime. Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan went from poor to rich partly by rapidly adopting new technologies that originated abroad.

In China and India technological leaps, including through digital payment and delivery apps, have brought extraordinary convenience and autonomy. “At our age, we’ve lived through countless changes,” says Ms Meng, who works in advertising in Beijing and who, at 40, feels ancient. “Things haven’t even settled in China before another huge shift comes two or three years later.” In India smartphones have offered hundreds of millions of people a “God in their hand” over the course of just a few years, says Ms Arora.

In Western countries, by contrast, pessimism towards AI may reflect people’s perception that their lives are not getting much better, that AI could make their lives worse—and that politicians cannot be relied upon to protect their interests. Daniel Dobrygowski, author of the book “Technology Governance”, argues that this attitude is coloured by people’s experience of social media and Big Tech, which Western governments have struggled to rein in.

The ways in which politicians and firms talk about AI may also make a difference. Bosses of American labs warn of job losses and human extinction as they race towards “artificial general intelligence”. Asian politicians and tech bosses rarely talk like that, perhaps in part because they are not developing frontier capabilities of their own. Instead they tend to focus on the practical uses of AI—what they will do with the technology, rather than what it will do to them. You are unlikely to hear the boss of Samsung talking publicly about AI doom.

In China, where big advances in AI are being made, officials do worry about risks, from cyber-security threats to economic dislocation. But the general tenor of state media is boosterish.

It would be wrong to conclude, though, that people in more AI-positive countries have no worries at all. Some are more resigned to the advance of technology as a fate that cannot be avoided. “AI’s impact might be different from every previous shift. But the Earth has its own rhythms,” says Ms Meng in Beijing. “When it’s not meant for you to survive, you won’t. You can’t live every day worrying, right?”

Cho Kyu-jin of Seoul National University reckons that South Koreans are embracing AI despite their concerns because the “fear of being left behind is higher than that of losing stability”. Kim Ah-ran, a 40-year-old labour lawyer, says, “When changes came in the Industrial Revolution, there were positive and negative effects. We’ll find a way to live.” Her young son, standing next to her at the Galaxy Robot Park outside Seoul, is mimicking a humanoid that is practising Muay Thai moves, while clutching a workbook that explains how to use AI to code such robots.

Such pragmatic acceptance suggests that positive attitudes like Mr Bae’s could yet be fragile. Kim Jeong-nam of KAIST, a tech-focused university, serves on South Korea’s Presidential Council on National Artificial Intelligence Strategy. He thinks that South Koreans’ tolerance is conditional on “competently built” policy. If AI starts to “produce visible losers”, such as in exam fairness or jobs, he worries that leeway could vanish. The same could hold true elsewhere. “How are you going to invent an AI that can drive a motorbike?” asks Anderson Santos, a delivery driver in São Paulo, Brazil, who is later dismayed at a mention of driverless cars.

There are some nascent signs of data-centre backlash in other parts of the world, too, if nothing like the outright rebellion seen in many parts of America. In the Philippines people are marching against “Pax Silica”, an American-led initiative to develop AI and semiconductor supply chains. In Thane, a city near Mumbai, hundreds have protested against an Amazon hyperscale data centre that is planned for their neighbourhood. Rage is not yet all-consuming, though. “It’s just like any other factory,” says one resident. “AI is the future.”■

item.title: MAGA foreign policy is a mess
item.description:
International

International | The Telegram Oct 22nd 2026 “INEVER MEANT to start a war…I just closed my eyes and swung,” sings Miley Cyrus in “Wrecking Ball”, a break-up ballad that seemed to play on every American radio in 2013. Though melodically a bit relentless, the pop song deserves a revival as a guide t...
item.content:encoded:
MAGA foreign policy is a mess

International | The Telegram

Oct 22nd 2026

“INEVER MEANT to start a war…I just closed my eyes and swung,” sings Miley Cyrus in “Wrecking Ball”, a break-up ballad that seemed to play on every American radio in 2013. Though melodically a bit relentless, the pop song deserves a revival as a guide to the second-term statecraft of President Donald Trump.

It is clear that traditional foreign-policy theories are a poor guide to Mr Trump. That offers both risks and opportunities to anyone running to be America’s next president.

This newspaper has noted Mr Trump’s wrecking-ball tendencies before, but in the two years before the next presidential election his yen for demolition has a specific impact. It has broken the “pendulum theory”, a once-reliable tool for predicting American foreign policy. Going back to Richard Nixon and his successor Jimmy Carter, most presidents have (over-)corrected for the biggest flaws of the guy who came before. In reaction to Tricky Dick’s devious realpolitik, the Carter presidency offered hairshirt moralising. Before long, voters felt that America was disrespected and chose can-do Reaganite optimism. When Americans wearied of George H.W. Bush, a wise but stiff statesman, they elected feel-your-pain Bill Clinton. After shoot-from-the-hip George W. Bush, Americans fell for cool, cerebral Barack Obama, before souring on haughty brainiacs and betting the country on Mr Trump.

Today the theory is less use, because Mr Trump swings every which way. When bullying Ukraine to settle with Russia, he is a might-makes-right realist. In Venezuela his rule-by-proxy would impress a 19th-century imperialist. In the Middle East he scorned regime change right up until his bungled war to bend Iran to his will. He declares that communism menaces America, but calls China’s party boss, Xi Jinping, his friend. The one constant is an impulse to smash the status quo. Cue mental images of Mr Trump atop a demolition ball (hopefully, unlike Ms Cyrus’s music video, the 80-year-old is wearing more than Dr. Martens boots).

It is quite plausible that this president will be hooted from office after wrecking America’s good name (though AI dominance could create riches and clout). Successors wishing to do the opposite will be spoiled for choice. For the foreign-policy pendulum to swing through a full arc, the 48th president could put the national interest ahead of personal profit. Alternatively his successor could avoid reckless wars and shun regime change. The next administration could work to rebuild alliances, pledging to help Europe confront Russia and friends in Asia deter China. All these options would break with some version of Trumpism.

The range of options is especially wide for Democrats. Whether Mr Trump’s vice-president, J.D. Vance, clears the field or faces a contested primary, Republicans will be wary of angering the MAGA faithful by repudiating Mr Trump.

Because Democrats are a self-indulgent bunch and—for a political party—surprisingly bad at politics, they are responding to this moment of opportunity with a navel-gazing argument. Conversations with foreign-policy heavy-hitters in Washington describe two broad camps, one centrist and one on the progressive left. These agree that voters care most about domestic and economic issues: there is much talk of heeding the kitchen-table concerns of working families. Yet each camp knows, too, that the outside world has a habit of intruding.

Responding to demand, delegations of Democratic thinkers and former officials have begun meeting foreign governments and politicians. One such group, involving both moderate and leftish Democrats, visited Brussels, London and Paris this month. A consistent message from these envoys is that the old post-1945 order is not coming back, and that some pillars of Trumpism—rhetoric about putting Americans first, and a focus on industrial production—will remain, whoever wins.

Trump-era tariffs are divisive. Polls suggest that voters blame them for high prices. Centrist Democrats cannot decide, though, whether it is better to juice the economy by scrapping most import taxes on taking office, or keep them temporarily as leverage over trade partners. The left believes in protected favoured industries (which will lobby to keep trade barriers) and likes tariff revenues.

A loud group would bar from future service those Biden-era officials who worked on Israel policy, deeming them steeped in Gazan blood. A cross-party consensus exists to deny Israel uncritical support. Some on the left would pull America out of the Middle East and offer only cautious support for Ukraine.

China sparks sharp disputes. Centrists believe that America is in an epochal contest with China for global leadership in technology and the world order. Prominent leftists call that overblown and hope to work with China on climate change and other global challenges. Some, ludicrously, imagine China will permit its workers to ally with America’s to agree on global minimum wages. Unfortunately for such China dreamers, their growing anxiety about AI safety and the power of big tech leads in another direction. Politically no Democrat can safely call for the slowing of American AI firms without calling for their Chinese rivals to be held back, too. That would involve imposing export controls on high-end computer chips and tools to make them, which would enrage China.

In some fields Democrats can break with Mr Trump while offering elements of continuity. Shrewd Democrats can keep tough border controls, which voters like, but promise less cruel enforcement of immigration laws inside America and a warmer welcome for legal migrants. His proposed defence budgets are so large that hawkish Democrats can spend less without much fear of seeming weak. Disruptive, unknowable change is coming: the thing to know about wrecking balls is that they are erratic. ■

item.title: A genocidal militia was coming for his city. He was one of the last doctors left

item.content:encoded:
A genocidal militia was coming for his city. He was one of the last doctors left

1843 | Sudan

Oct 22nd 2026

The woman spoke in a whisper. “You’re the doctor. I know you.” Adam could barely hear her over the babble of the other captives. Militiamen had seized them as they fled the slaughter; now they were trapped in a disused school on the edge of the Sudanese desert. The woman was one of the locals let in to sell peanuts.

Until she spoke, Adam had been in a kind of trance. When the city fell in October 2025, he was already weak from the months-long siege. All he’d been given to eat in the two weeks since were a few mouthfuls of flatbread a day. As his body shut down, the past and present blurred. He day-dreamed about the last days of el-Fasher: joking with friends at the hospital; his dog, Bulldoze, padding behind him as he walked through the wards; the screams when the militia finally overran the city’s defences.

The woman leaned closer, her headscarf slipping forwards. “You’re the doctor,” she repeated. “From Saudi hospital.”

Suddenly Adam was alert. Fighters from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the militia that had captured him, were hunting down doctors. Hospital staff had evidence of the atrocities they had committed since they began fighting the Sudanese army in 2023; some doctors, like Adam, had spoken publicly about them.

When Adam was first taken captive on the road out of el-Fasher, he’d been held under the scorching sun with thousands of others, and had watched RSF fighters search the crowds for people they considered enemies. They grabbed prisoners at random and shouted, “Where are the soldiers? Where are the doctors?” as they punched and kicked.

The gunmen offered to let people go free if they informed on wanted men. Sometimes they snatched captives’ phones and searched them for incriminating material. Adam, who had left his phone at the hospital and shaved off his beard, managed to avoid discovery. Others weren’t so lucky. Several times he saw a fighter pull a man from the crowd and drag him behind the nearby trees. After a burst of shots, the fighter would come back alone.

For all he knew the woman before him could be an RSF informant. “Sorry, you’re mistaken,” he told her politely. She moved on.

A few days later she was back. She asked him again if he was the doctor, and he denied it a second time. He wasn’t sure he should have. He needed a friend. The only way out seemed to be to get a family member to pay a ransom to the RSF, but Adam had no way of contacting anyone.

In theory he could have escaped, as the school wasn’t heavily guarded. But the desert sands stretched all around him; he’d die of thirst without help. Someone might have mercy on him if he ran into the nearby village. But they might also report him to the RSF.

Later, the woman tried a third time. “I know you,” she insisted. “You helped my sister.”

Adam thought about his parents, who had escaped to safety, and his friends. He longed to see them again. With a deep sigh, he commended his life to God and leaned in close.

“Yes,” he admitted. “I’m the doctor.”

RSF forces stormed el-Fasher on October 26th 2025, briefly putting Sudan’s civil war on front pages. Humanitarians and diplomats had been warning for months that the RSF’s capture of the city, the last stronghold of the Sudanese army in the Darfur region, would lead to a bloodbath.

The events that followed were only sparsely documented. Internet and phone signals were down, and those who survived often had their phones stolen. Researchers relied on satellite imagery to quantify the scale of the killing. The UN later concluded that it bore the “hallmarks of a genocide”. A year after its fall to the RSF, investigators are still working out how a city that once housed a million people was emptied. El-Fasher has yet to gain the name recognition of other sites of modern-day massacres, such as Srebrenica.

Adam had a happy childhood there, even during the previous civil war. A rebellion in Darfur broke out in 2003 when Adam was six, the result of decades of neglect by the corrupt, authoritarian government in Khartoum. When armed rebels, drawn from the region’s African ethnic groups, attacked military bases, the Arab-dominated regime in the capital retaliated against the rebels’ communities. Warplanes bombed villages, burning families alive. The Janjaweed, a feared Arab militia, were sent in. They looted, gang-raped women, and bludgeoned children to death.

But these horrors impinged only tangentially on Adam’s life in el-Fasher. For centuries, the city had been a hub on trans-Saharan caravan routes linking north, central and east Africa, and it retained its cosmopolitan roots. Children from different African ethnic groups as well as pupils with Arab roots studied together at Adam’s primary school. His classmates sometimes relayed gossip they’d overheard about bands of marauders in the countryside, but Adam was more interested in talking about football and anime series, like “Detective Conan”.

Eventually a series of truces, together with the deployment of an armed peacekeeping force, tamped down the violence in Darfur. As Adam got older, he noticed things he’d overlooked as a young child: the refugee camp on the edge of the city; the portraits of the president, Omar al-Bashir, looking down from the walls of shops; the fact that no one would talk about politics in public.

For him and his family at least, life was good. His parents both had decent jobs, and he and his two sisters grew up in a spacious house with a garden. Even as a child, Adam knew that he wanted to help people, so he studied hard in science in the hope of one day becoming a doctor.

On special occasions, the family went out for dinner at shisha bars illuminated by lights strung between the trees like glowing cobwebs. Sometimes Adam’s father took him for coffee in el-Fasher’s main market, where the shops glittered with bangles made from gold mined in south Darfur.

By the time Adam started studying medicine at el-Fasher university in 2014, the economy was crumbling. The Bashir regime’s dysfunction had helped create a surge in food and fuel prices. Critics were disappearing. Protesters around the country began demanding Bashir’s resignation; Adam helped organise demonstrations at the university. He and his fellow students were teargassed, beaten and sometimes jailed. In April 2019, after months of popular revolt, Bashir’s security chiefs forced him to step down.

A fledgling transitional government took charge with the backing of the two main powerbrokers in the country: the Sudanese army and the RSF, the official paramilitary organisation that had emerged from the Janjaweed. For the first time in Adam’s life, peace and democracy seemed within reach. Adam and his fellow students would stay up late chatting about their dreams for a new country.

Then in 2021, the army and the RSF overthrew the civilian government in a coup. Adam was deep in his studies by then, and struggled to juggle exam preparation with participating in pro-democracy protests. Classes were often cancThe aftermath of an attack on the World Food Programme’s offices. Saudi hospital’s obstetrics clinic (clockwise from top left)elled owing to the tumult. But eventually, towards the end of 2022, he graduated.

His proud father hosted a barbeque for their family and friends; guests sipped sweet, sticky glasses of ruby-red hibiscus juice while frankincense smoke curled through the evening air. Afterwards Adam and the other graduates zoomed around town, cheering loudly and hooting their car horns.

The next week he started work at el-Fasher’s teaching hospital. Later, he’d marvel at how cosseted he was there. One of the hospital’s 30 consultants was always there to give him advice. When he had to tell a young woman she had cancer, older staff counselled him on how to break the news gently.

On the morning of April 15th 2023 Adam was at home getting ready for a shift when his phone buzzed and he looked down. He didn’t know it at the time, but it was the moment his old life ended.

Wassim, a 25-year-old laboratory technician who would later become one of Adam’s closest friends, was at the teaching hospital when the news broke. He had recently graduated, and had brought his CV to the hospital seeking an internship. As he waited he heard the crack of gunshots outside, but assumed it was just another protest being dispersed. Within half an hour, bloodied civilians began stumbling in. Hospital staff triaged them while shouting out the updates flashing on their phones. Gunmen were fighting near the military barracks a few streets away. The RSF and the army were at war.

Staff and patients fled the building. Two other hospitals caught up in the fighting also had to close. Along with other doctors, nurses and support staff, Adam made his way to South hospital, then the only one operating.

The next few days were chaos, with casualties piling up and the hospital stretched beyond its limits. Fortunately, the Sudanese are used to handling crises without any help from the state. The network of volunteers that had helped organise pro-democracy demonstrations became an emergency-response force: mending, scrubbing and scrounging for supplies to keep the hospital working. Wassim, his internship application long forgotten, joined in.

One of the most prominent figures in the network was Abdullah, a graduate in management studies. Abdullah and Adam were university friends, and had sometimes marched in the same protests. Abdullah’s easy manner and confidence meant he was often called on to give speeches at community events, and he was well-known even before the war. Once it started, he got to work asking people for money and medicine on behalf of the hospital.

Sometimes there was a pretty young woman at the hospital, who caught Abdullah’s attention. Aisha, an economics graduate, had been visiting an ailing relative when the war broke out and then pitched in to assist with the volunteer effort. She helped Abdullah look after a mentally ill man who had been injured, and later they distributed medicines together. Abdullah was drawn to her spirit and grit.

Adam, too, threw himself into the collective effort, sometimes joining Wassim for night-time raids on abandoned hospitals in search of supplies. He decided he was most needed at the Saudi maternity hospital (or “Saudi”, as everyone called it), which had reopened two weeks after the start of the war. Other doctors and volunteers began splitting their time between Saudi and South.

For a few months it looked as though el-Fasher might be spared the worst of the conflict ravaging other parts of Sudan. The governor of Darfur, Minni Minnawi, was a former rebel leader. His fighters had been at war with both the Sudanese army and the RSF’s predecessor, the Janjaweed, for years, and trusted neither. Shortly after the fighting broke out, Minnawi declared his forces’ neutrality. Instead of becoming a battle site, el-Fasher was divided into zones of influence.

Minnawi’s men held a buffer zone in the centre. The RSF held the east. The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) held the west and parts of the south, where South and Saudi hospitals were located. Like most people, Adam and Wassim knew fighters in all three groups. The city was tense, but it functioned.

Then in November 2023, Minnawi announced that he was going to fight alongside the Sudanese armed forces, citing RSF atrocities. Panic gripped el-Fasher. Families strapped bulging suitcases onto cars and fled. One night Saudi’s senior medical director called Adam. They’d worked closely together, and he wanted to tell Adam himself that he was leaving.

Then came the kicker: he asked Adam to take over his responsibilities, alongside two other people. Saudi had a staff of 400, and was the only specialist maternity hospital in Darfur, a region of 12m people. Adam was ten months out of medical school.

That night he lay awake for hours, his mind churning. Would the older staff accept him? Where should he start? He began compiling lists of available staff in his head.

He awoke feeling calmer. There was no point trying to fake authority. He had to earn trust by being humble: cleaning the floors himself and leaning on his more experienced colleagues. Rather than make a big speech, he met staff individually. “You are the real leaders of the hospital,” he told them.

He was particularly reliant on the hospital’s middle-aged administrative director, Mahasin, who was a surrogate mother to the younger staff. She ticked them off over behaviour she considered risky, such as leaving the hospital for coffee or parties, and cooked up enormous vats of food for them.

The hospital was Adam’s home now. He moved in with some essential belongings, including Bulldoze. A few months later fighting reached the neighbourhood where his family lived. His parents and sisters decided to flee, packing only a few bags of clothes and Adam’s degree certificate. He escorted them to the city gates in the morning, hugged them, then went back to work. He found it hard to concentrate on anything until they called that evening to say they had made it out safely.

As the RSF seized town after town in Darfur, reports of atrocities mounted. Adam’s mother begged him to flee himself. In November the RSF captured el-Geneina, a city 300km west of el-Fasher. Civilians from the tribes fighting the RSF were executed; some were tortured to death. Those who tried to escape were shot. If they did that to el-Geneina, his mother said, what did he think the RSF would do in el-Fasher, the centre of resistance?

After several of these entreaties, Adam snapped. He told his mother he was already dead. “Consider that I have given my life to this city,” he said. “Consider me a martyr.”

They spoke most days, but she never brought up the subject of him leaving again.

The war sometimes got to Adam. He took care to hide black moods from his colleagues. Often the only place he could find solitude was in the operating room, where he’d lean against the walls and brood in the antiseptic dark.

Small victories buoyed him, such as the time his team was able to save a baby who had been shot in its mother’s womb. But the injuries were becoming worse as both sides’ weapons got more powerful. When the war first broke out, Adam and his colleagues had mainly treated people for bullet wounds. But then both sides obtained more sophisticated equipment, including drones. Though the RSF tried to keep their foreign benefactors a secret, an overwhelming body of evidence pointed to the UAE (the UAE denies the accusation). By the summer of 2024, people were arriving at Saudi eviscerated, or with limbs sliced off.

One day in June 2024 about 50 wounded people arrived at Saudi within half an hour. Many were women and children with gaping shrapnel wounds. Adam ran to help with triage when someone yelled: “South hospital has been overrun by the RSF!”

He refused to believe it at first. So many of his friends were working there. Then he froze as he noticed how dirty and tired the new arrivals looked: they had run the 5km distance between the two hospitals. The rumour was true.

Over the next few days, staff from South hospital limped in. Many had scaled the hospital walls under fire to escape. Among them was the director-general of the facility, who had been beaten, stabbed in the face and left for dead.

The staff didn’t know what happened after they fled, but they found out a few days later when a team was briefly able to re-enter. Some patients were shot in their beds; the bodies of their relatives lay sprawled in the lobby. A handful of survivors said the RSF had rounded up men of military age. Saudi was now the last functioning hospital in the city.

They got used to the sounds of drones overhead. The smaller ones whined; the bigger, military-grade ones sounded like small planes. Sometimes quadrocopters hovered for hours, blades whirring, before releasing a bomb.

Adam managed to get hold of some shipping containers, and the team buried them to use as bomb shelters. But there were no sirens to alert them to attacks, and often people didn’t make it to the shelter in time. Amna, a pharmacist with a penchant for romance novels who had joined them after escaping South hospital, was killed in a direct hit on Saudi’s pharmacy.

Soon Adam gave up trying to run to the shelter when the bombs fell. Ignoring Mahasin’s scolding, he would enjoy his coffee in the sunshine instead, with Bulldoze by his side.

“No one cared any more,” Adam recalled. “You would hear a bomb hit the hospital and just shrug.”

Once a ward was hit in the middle of the night. Adam ran into the darkness, guided by screams. Then he heard a drone loitering above. Second strikes were common if there was a sign of life, so Adam couldn’t switch on his torch. In the darkness, a young boy clutched his leg and begged him, “Uncle, save me!” But he couldn’t help anyone without light. For hours, the screaming continued, then slowly subsided. Around 70 people died.

The hospital was targeted so often that the staff set up operating theatres and emergency rooms in abandoned buildings. But it didn’t make them much safer: the drones just tracked the wounded to these secret outposts, and attacked them too.

In spite of the risks, hundreds of people—patients, doctors, staff from other hospitals and their families— moved into Saudi hospital. Nowhere in the city was safe; at least in Saudi they had each other. Room Three, where Adam and his friends lived, was the hospital’s beating heart. It had only four beds, but more than a dozen people would crash there at a time.

People didn’t come just to sleep. Room Three was where they went when they were feeling hopeless and alone. Room Three was life. “In Room Three someone was always dancing, someone was always singing,” one surgeon told me later. “Someone was farting.”

Room Three was also directly opposite Room Four, where some of the young female staff slept. Inhabitants of both rooms rolled out mats in the corridor between them, and chatted there over coffee and music. Sometimes they fell in love with each other: there was a spate of marriages between doctors, lab technicians, nurses and pharmacists.

The love story that gripped the hospital was that of the two volunteers: Abdullah and Aisha. Abdullah was a great favourite with the hospital staff, as was his mother, Zeinab, who cooked for them. When Aisha’s family home was overrun by RSF fighters in 2024, she moved in with Zeinab. In January 2025 a stray bullet hit Zeinab in the chest. Before she died, she made Abdullah promise to take care of Aisha.

Abdullah and Aisha married a few months later. At the ceremony Abdullah asked for a moment’s silence for his mother. Everyone wept.

Then they threw a party in one of the damaged emergency rooms. Blue and purple balloons dangled from the walls and people danced to Sudanese love songs. The men threw their hands in the air while women sang along. “It was like there was no war,” Adam said. “We were not living like rats underground.”

Two days after Abdullah’s and Aisha’s wedding in April 2025, the RSF overran ZamZam, a camp for families displaced during the last war, which lay on the main road out of el-Fasher. The UN says at least 1,000 people were killed; the real number is probably much higher.

The camp had a medical clinic run by Relief International, an aid agency. Though other charities pulled out as the RSF approached, Relief International staff stayed at their posts. One of the doctors, 26-year-old Mahmoud Babikir Idris Adam, also worked shifts at the Saudi hospital. He had been one of the guests at Abdullah’s and Aisha’s wedding celebration.

When RSF fighters overran ZamZam they shot Mahmoud dead in his clinic, together with eight of his colleagues. Adam found out shortly afterwards. It was one of the only times in the war that he cried.

After ZamZam, el-Fasher was the RSF’s last significant target in Darfur. RSF soldiers began bulldozing earth into piles to make a barrier round the city. Most exit roads were blocked by RSF checkpoints, and the soldiers manning them were much less inclined to let people pass through for a bribe than they had been in the past. Now travellers were frequently raped, held for ransom or executed. Men of military age were especially at risk. The Yale Humanitarian Lab, which monitored the RSF’s barrier construction from space, described it as a “kill box”.

There was hardly anything to eat. By then, the hospital’s windows had all been blown out and replaced by sandbags. The medical staff tried to distract themselves. Adam obtained a PlayStation 5; between shifts he and the other staff lost themselves in “Grand Theft Auto”, “fifa” and “Assassin’s Creed”.

The men pooled their remaining supplies of cologne and swapped bottles of Sauvage and Baccarat for novelty. Adam contributed a heady scent called Rose Tobacco. His friend Yasir, who was also a doctor, instituted a weekly fashion ritual called “smart Tuesdays”. He and one of the volunteers would put on their most colourful clothes and take pictures of each other pulling model poses. If they were going to die, they said, they might as well be dressed for it.

There were other small comforts. A black-and-white cat came to the hospital; Yasir adopted it and named it c5 after the incoming RSF rockets. When Bulldoze came home after going missing for three days in August, Adam was so happy he gave the dog some of his precious rice.

Music was another balm. A song by Abdullah Alawad, a Sudanese singer with a white streak in his beard, became their anthem. Once Yasir used flour to whiten his own beard, and they recorded a cover version on their phones, bawling out the chorus together: “A person can die but their memory lives on.”

No one wanted to acknowledge the fear they all lived with. Wassim, the lab technician, felt suicidal some days. “My family was in danger, everyone around me was in danger, every morning a lot of people died. Children died of starvation,” he said when I met him much later. “I felt like it was better for me to die.” At his lowest point he confided in Adam. The doctor talked him round, promising that God saw their work and would not forget them.

That summer, the staff’s resolve started to crumble. The bombardment was unrelenting, and roads out were getting more dangerous every day. Izzadin, one of the surgeons, watched as his operating team dwindled. A few asked him whether they should flee, but he refused to advise them. Some just stopped showing up; others came tearfully to say goodbye. Izzadin thanked them and gave them his blessing: “May Allah preserve you and help you reach a safe area.”

Wassim watched the other lab technicians leave. He was getting calls from a former classmate in the RSF, warning that the militia were about to seize the city and offering to get him out. The classmate spoke with contempt for those still in el-Fasher. He spat out a racist slur sometimes used to describe the dark-skinned people of Darfur: slaves.

“He called many times, saying ‘we are coming,’” said Wassim. Eventually, he blocked his old classmate’s number.

By the end of the summer, a kilo of rice, which fed a dozen medical staff for a day, cost more than $750. Sometimes surgeons would operate on an injured child and find his bowels full of leaves. Often all the staff had themselves was animal feed made out of crushed peanut waste. They re-used the same coffee grounds for weeks. Some doctors tied sheets around their stomachs to alleviate the stabs of starvation. Adam had weighed 88kg at the beginning of the war: now he was just 38kg.

Medical supplies were also scarce, and doctors were forced to use medicines that were several years out of date. The only remaining spinal anaesthesia had expired in 2021.

The RSF executed anyone caught smuggling medicine into the city, but some people did it anyway. One of them was an elderly man the Saudi team had operated on; he was frail but would walk three days across the desert to bring back supplies. After hearing the hospital was nearly out of anaesthetic, some women walked to a town 90km away to buy ketamine, which they smuggled back in their bras.

The doctors’ cheerfulness became their armour. When a new load of casualties arrived, Yasir would announce, “Life is beautiful!” before getting down to work.

But by September it had become hard to maintain. On September 19th a missile slammed into a mosque near the hospital. The imam was married to Mahasin, the hospital’s administrator, who rushed to the site. Her husband was badly injured and begged her to look for their two young sons in the rubble. By the time she found their bodies, her husband had died. She buried them all in their bedsheets and left the city with her teenage daughter.

The hospital was down to two surgeons. Adam and his friends still didn’t want to go. If Saudi went unstaffed, most of the remaining population would leave and the city would be easy to capture. In any case, leaving was now as dangerous as staying. Yasir’s brother was killed at a roadblock trying to escape. A volunteer had left and was never heard from again.

By October everything was breaking. A bomb blasted a hole in the wall of the maternity ward that was big enough to walk through. There was an outbreak of cholera. On October 25th Abdullah decided he had to get Aisha, who was now pregnant, to safety.

They left with a group of other civilians. Among them was a man who had written social-media posts supporting the Sudanese army. An RSF fighter recognised him at a roadblock, and pulled his family aside. The soldier grabbed the man’s six-year-old son and cut the boy’s throat as he struggled and screamed for his mother. Then he released the man, telling him: “You couldn’t save your son. Go live with this pain.”

One of the RSF soldiers beckoned to Aisha. Abdullah stepped forward instead, meekly explaining that his wife was pregnant. To his surprise, the RSF soldier waved them through. “Go with my best wishes,” he told them. Abdullah looked the man in the face, astonished. It was the first time he’d seen evidence of humanity in an RSF fighter. He never forgot it.

That evening Adam and the remaining crew talked about whether they should follow Abdullah and Aisha out of el-Fasher. They were determined to live or die together, so they held a vote.

Adam, like the majority of them, voted to stay. It felt appalling to leave the patients to the RSF. But he sensed it would all be over soon no matter what he did. That night, as explosions shook the building, he walked through the hospital in the dark, saying a silent goodbye. He patted Bulldoze.

Ali, one of the last pharmacists, lay awake listening to the RSF artillery. In the early hours he fetched the others and told them they should vote again on leaving. “It’s the end,” he said. Reluctantly, Adam agreed.

It was shortly before sunrise. They had no plan—they just ran outside. All Adam took with him was a bottle of water and his Rose Tobacco. Terrified families filled the streets; mothers carried crying children. A few were riding donkeys but most were on foot. They were heading west, towards the city’s last collapsing defence.

Behind them, giddy RSF fighters roared in from the south, east and north, looting and shooting. Crowds of people seeking refuge at the university were strafed and mortared. Families were forced to lie down at gunpoint and crushed with armoured vehicles.

Later, videos would emerge of an RSF commander gleefully murdering groups of unarmed people. He boasted that he had personally killed more than 2,000.

Adam and the rest of the hospital workers joined a flood of people heading west, but the RSF seized them on the road. In the chaos, Adam’s friends were put on trucks while he was marched to the abandoned school. For the first time since the siege began, he and his colleagues were separated.

Wassim, Ali and Yasir were imprisoned in the yard of the abandoned Children’s hospital, along with thousands of others. For three days, there was virtually no water. Some prisoners died of dehydration. When a commander eventually brought in a tank, dying men swarmed towards it, trampling each other. A fighter shot into the crowd, killing three people.

Maddened by thirst, the prisoners broke into the septic tank and began to scoop up the fetid water with their hands. There was another cholera outbreak and diarrhoea coated the ground. The RSF fighters, terrified the disease would spread, appealed for doctors to come forward from the crowd. An official said there had been orders from the top not to kill people with medical skills.

The Saudi team worried it was a trap. On the other hand, they were as good as dead anyway. Eventually, one by one, they pitched in, isolating cholera patients with a barricade of broken chairs and branches, and treating them as best they could with the medicines they were given. Over the course of the next ten days they managed to contain the outbreak, though not before 200 people had died.

Afterwards, the RSF took them back to Saudi. The militia’s leaders seemed to want the hospital working again. In the courtyard the team found a small boy crying. He whispered to them that his mother and father, both patients, had been killed by RSF gunmen just after the doctors had left. The UN later said around 460 people were shot dead when the hospital was taken—mostly patients in their beds.

A few weeks later Wassim, Ali and Yasir all managed to escape, reaching the border with Chad via a circuitous route of small villages. They worried all the time about what had happened to Adam.

Far away, in the darkened schoolroom on the edge of the desert, Adam was listening to the peanut-seller explain how she would help him escape. Tell the guards you need to relieve yourself, she said, then meet me at the back of the building. He did as she said, walking unsteadily into the glaring sun. The woman guided him surreptitiously to her home, where he hid for 20 days.

Adam moved from house to house, mostly at night. Each time a person hid him, he’d ask them to try to find someone on the path ahead who might help. Sometimes a friendly driver would give him a lift. It took him a month to reach Khartoum.

He was desperate to find out what had happened to his friends, but was still afraid that the RSF would track him down. In the end he made a fake Facebook account, and found one of the hospital volunteers online. It’s Adam, he wrote. I’m alive.

Today, el-Fasher is a ghost town. Satellite images show grass growing on its market. Several staff from the Saudi hospital are still missing. The surviving members of the team are scattered. Many cannot sleep or are plagued by nightmares. One woman can’t stop dreaming about scrambling over a ditch full of dead bodies.

This summer I met Adam in the town where he’s been hiding. He was still nervous about RSF reprisals, and asked me not to name it.

“Those who survived, some are bitter,” he said. “When we were working, the world said we were heroes. But now we are forgotten.”

Every time he connects his phone to the internet it is flooded with messages from desperate colleagues: asking for medicine, a job or money. It overwhelms him. But he can’t switch off. He is a helper. If he doesn’t help, who is he?

In a strange way, he said, he and the others felt nostalgia for the siege. Not for the suffering, but for the purpose and unity they had back then, and the family they became.

“Even now, I feel as though I never truly left el-Fasher. My soul is still there,” said Adam. “The city is not destroyed as long as some of its people are alive.” ■

Names have been changed

Katharine Houreld is a journalist based in Rome. Previously she was East Africa bureau chief for the Washington Post. Hafiz Haroun is a Sudanese journalist

Illustrations by Michelle Thompson

Source images: EL Fasher Medical staff, Getty, AFP, UN, OCHA

item.content:encoded:
AI行业巨额债务令投资者焦虑不安

商业 | 信贷责任所在 2026年10月22日

信贷市场正在对CoreWeave施压。这家“新云”公司出租数据中心容量以运行人工智能模型，其发行的五年期债券价格自7月以来已下跌16%。该债券的收益率目前为15%——这一水平通常与陷入财务困境的公司挂钩——高于7月份的10%。为CoreWeave违约提供保险的信用违约互换价格暗示，该公司未来五年无力偿还债务的概率已升至60%以上（见图表1）。投资者日益担心，处于AI繁荣核心的公司将无法产生偿还巨额债务所需的现金流。这些担忧已从信贷市场蔓延至股市，导致股市也出现震荡：科技股为主的纳斯达克指数大幅下跌后，目前又回到了5月中旬的水平。投资者正在对不断增大、更加不透明且风险日益上升的债务存量进行定价。

让投资者皱眉的不只是CoreWeave。包括Nebius和TeraWulf在内的其他新云公司，其债券收益率也在上升。10月19日，韩国竞争对手Elice的公开上市遭遇挫折，其股价单日暴跌三分之一。另有其他三家公司在过去一个月里推迟或取消了上市计划。这些企业靠债务生存。在十家上市的新云公司中，只有两家盈利。该群体合计借款达1000亿美元，是其年收入的九倍。其中570亿美元的债务是今年发行的。此外，这些数额只是快速增长的AI相关债务存量中的一小部分。由软件销售商转型为云服务提供商的甲骨文（Oracle）目前已累计借款1690亿美元，其中今年发行了250亿美元。日本企业集团软银（SoftBank）也有类似雄心，自1月初以来已借款约同等规模。埃隆·马斯克的SpaceX今年发行了650亿美元债务，其收入飙升主要得益于快速增长的云业务。还有领先的“超大规模云服务商”——Alphabet、亚马逊、微软和Meta——它们在2026年共借款2140亿美元，而去年全年仅为830亿美元。另有790亿美元的数据中心债务由特殊目的载体（SPV）发行，其中大部分是云服务商与金融机构的合资企业。此外，英伟达等芯片制造商及半导体供应链上的其他企业还借款840亿美元。再加上其他提供数据中心设备的公司和美国电力公司（它们也不得不投资以跟上AI繁荣）的借款，今年迄今的总借款额接近8500亿美元——大约是同一批公司在2023年发行金额的四倍（见图表2）。这些公司的资产负债表上合计携带超过3万亿美元的债务。

不久前，AI繁荣还依靠超大规模云服务商的现金流来融资。但投资规模已超出它们其他业务所能支付的范畴，也远远超出消费者和企业目前在AI上的支出。摩根大通银行预计，从现在到2030年，为支持该技术发展将需要约5.5万亿美元的资本支出，其中四分之三将由债务融资。借款人正转向富有想象力的融资策略，并利用各类贷款机构。债券——包括Alphabet在2月发行的320亿美元巨额债券——仍然是热门选择。然而，即使是这些常规工具，所需规模也意味着发行者必须发挥创意。外国信贷市场越来越受青睐。今年迄今，五大云服务商——即四大超大规模云服务商加甲骨文——发行的债券中约有30%以非美元货币计价，包括欧元、英镑和日元。与此同时，其他工具也越来越受欢迎。SPV现已司空见惯。一个例子是Meta策划的“Sopaipilla”项目（以一種糕點命名）。该项目由位于得克萨斯州埃尔帕索的十个数据中心组成，总计将提供约一千兆瓦的计算能力。该场址由一家名为Wurldwide的公司所有，而Wurldwide又由Meta（持股20%）和资产管理巨头贝莱德（持股80%）所有。Wurldwide于8月发行了130亿美元债务，用于该园区建设，Meta已同意租用该园区20年。这种结构满足了许多需求。贝莱德及其客户获得由Meta担保的稳定收入流，而Meta则增加了计算能力，同时将债务留在表外。信用评级机构给予该SPV的评级仅比Meta低一个档次。芯片支持融资——即以数据中心中部署的硅片作为抵押——也在兴起。据称，SpaceX正寻求通过这种方式获得400亿美元融资，以便从英伟达购买更多芯片。芯片支持融资通常通过SPV安排。甲骨文正在与私募市场巨头Apollo和投资银行高盛洽谈，为其一大笔半导体采购提供资金，这些芯片将由一个独立实体持有并租赁给甲骨文。前沿AI模型制造商Anthropic和OpenAI渴望对其计算能力获得更大控制权，据报道也在谈判类似安排，以直接采购大量芯片。惠誉评级公司的Roelof Steenkamp表示，芯片支持融资使风险评估变得“无比复杂”。此类安排的一个后果是，数据中心的基础设施、其中的芯片，甚至场址的电源（如果有自备电源）都可能分别由各自的债务层融资。除此之外，还有一些算不上债务但接近债务的义务。研究公司CreditSights的数据显示，五大云服务商的资产负债表上租赁负债总额超过2500亿美元。还有1.2万亿美元的租约已达成但尚未开始。此外还有价值1.5万亿美元的从供应商处采购产品的承诺。最后一个复杂性来自AI生态中资产负债表更大更健康的公司提供的“后盾”支持，为其他公司的债务提供担保。英伟达在这方面尤为积极，如果客户无力偿还债权人，它愿承担用于购买其芯片的至多3000亿美元债务。Alphabet和博通（开发面向云服务商和模型制造商的定制芯片）也为部分客户提供了后盾。此类交易使投资者更难确定风险所在，以及违约损失可能蔓延多远。

谁有风险敞口？简而言之，人人都有。所有类型的金融公司都在持有AI债务，部分原因是这类债务太多了。大型资产管理公司是最大买家。例如，全球最大的债券基金管理公司之一Pimco，在Meta位于路易斯安那州的Hyperion数据中心园区发行的270亿美元债券中买入了180亿美元。随后它将部分债务分层出售给养老基金和保险公司等机构投资者。Apollo和黑石等私人信贷提供者正在牵头许多更具创意的交易。有时这些贷款也会银团化给机构投资者——包括由私人信贷提供者自身控制的保险公司。据报道，Apollo在6月贷给博通的相当一部分债务最终记在其保险子公司Athena的账上。对冲基金也涌入AI债务市场，对新云公司表现出特别兴趣。

尽管近期市场波动，但总体而言投资者尚未对债务狂潮感到恐慌。今年发行的AI相关债券中只有约15%的规模属于垃圾级。此外，尽管现有的各种后盾使AI债务存量更难查究，但英伟达等公司现金充裕的资产负债表有助于吸收任何冲击。10月15日，英伟达CEO黄仁勳为CoreWeave的前景辩护，该公司部分债务由英伟达担保，他认为其“资本成本实际上在随着时间下降”。即便如此，前方仍有危险。一个威胁来自借贷成本上升。海湾战争、持续的通胀以及对公共债务增长的担忧，导致政府债券收益率近几个月迅速攀升，推高了企业借款人的利率。为支持AI繁荣而发行的债务规模本身也起了作用。对那些财力雄厚的超大规模云服务商来说，这只是痛苦之源；而对于CoreWeave这样根基不稳的借款人——其利息账单已占年收入的四分之一——这可能致命。更大的威胁则是AI需求停滞。企业支付卡提供商Ramp的数据显示，由于企业试图控制不断攀升的成本，其客户的AI支出自7月以来已趋于平稳。增长放缓反过来可能导致Anthropic或OpenAI无限期推迟备受期待的公开上市，这可能促使投资者重新审视自己对AI的风险敞口。AI债务之塔越高，就越脆弱——而一旦轰然倒塌，后果也将越严重。■

更正（2026年10月22日）：本文早期版本低估了上市新云公司债务相对于收入的规模。致歉。

商业 | 呼叫我的代理 2026年10月22日 硅谷长期以来一直梦想打造一款功能足够强大的数字助手，让用户摆脱许多耗费时间和精力的繁琐个人事务。《钢铁侠》系列电影中的J.A.R.V.I.S.（Just a Rather Very Intelligent System，只是一个相当智能的系统）等虚构形象，让人们对此期望甚高。2010年，iPhone制造商苹果收购了Siri这一助手应用，结果却令人失望地愚蠢。如今，在当下这波人工智能投资热潮中，个人AI代理的时代可能终于到来了。过去两个月里，社交媒体巨头Meta和初创公司Instinct各发布了一款此类机器人，并大张旗鼓地宣传。Instinct的...
item.content:encoded:
个人AI助手可能很快重塑数字经济

商业 | 呼叫我的代理 2026年10月22日 硅谷长期以来一直梦想打造一款功能足够强大的数字助手，让用户摆脱许多耗费时间和精力的繁琐个人事务。《钢铁侠》系列电影中的J.A.R.V.I.S.（Just a Rather Very Intelligent System，只是一个相当智能的系统）等虚构形象，让人们对此期望甚高。2010年，iPhone制造商苹果收购了Siri这一助手应用，结果却令人失望地愚蠢。如今，在当下这波人工智能投资热潮中，个人AI代理的时代可能终于到来了。过去两个月里，社交媒体巨头Meta和初创公司Instinct各发布了一款此类机器人，并大张旗鼓地宣传。Instinct的助手可通过苹果的iMessage服务或Meta的WhatsApp联系，它们已经在为用户办理航班值机、寻找售罄的演唱会门票、安排与朋友的晚餐等等。Meta推出的Muse也有类似功能，但可通过WhatsApp、网页浏览器、移动应用——或者从今年晚些时候起，通过Meta的智能眼镜——来访问。投资者兼博主M.G.西格勒解释说，与早期几代数字助手的重大区别在于，这些新机器人可以主动行动，而不仅仅是对用户明确提出的要求作出反应。Instinct“确实以我相信我们都希望AI运作的方式在工作”，这家初创公司24岁的创始人诺亚·欣恩表示。采用率正在飙升，以至于欣恩先生认为“几年之内，世界上每个能上网的用户都将能使用像Instinct这样的产品。”然而，在此之前，开发个人代理的公司在更广泛采用方面还必须克服各种障碍，包括对安全性和可靠性的担忧，以及一些大企业不愿让这些工具与其系统交互的问题。Instinct和Meta在吸引用户方面采取了截然不同的方式，但两者都取得了巨大成功。就Instinct而言，用户必须由朋友邀请，或从候补名单中精选出来。即便如此，用户数量仍以每天约10%的速度增长。简洁性让用户持续回归：据这家初创公司称，大约一半注册Instinct的用户在一个月后仍会每周至少使用一次。给Instinct的代理下达指令就像写一段简短文字一样简单；它们随后会回复进度更新。如果Instinct是幕后的私人派对，那么Muse就是任何人都能参加的开放邀请狂欢（只要他们居住在美国或加拿大）。各方反馈显示，这场派对热闹非凡——人们也在流连忘返。根据数据提供商Sensor Tower的数据，自一个多月前首次亮相以来，Muse应用的下载量已超过1000万次。引发AI热潮的OpenAI热门聊天机器人ChatGPT，在其移动应用发布后的同期内仅有370万次下载，而该应用是在网页版首次亮相约六个月后才发布的。Muse的用户留存率也与ChatGPT大致相当。然而，说服派对参与者暴露他们的数据并不总是那么容易。个人代理需要私人信息才能发挥其潜力：如果无法访问日历或信用卡，它们不过是美化版的聊天机器人。一些科技界人士担心，这些机器人会让用户容易受到新威胁的攻击，例如提示注入——攻击者通过网站的计算机代码将文本偷偷传给AI，诱使其做出不当行为。这些公司似乎正在认真对待这些担忧。Meta为每位Muse用户分配一台专用服务器来存储他们的数据并运行他们的助手。它还教Muse多种抵御提示注入的方法，尽管一些安全研究人员认为它仍然容易受到恶意指令的攻击。Instinct对其网络安全措施向公众披露较少，但欣恩先生表示，该服务的设计原则是用户“应该始终控制自己的数据”。除此之外，还有人担心个人代理可能因纯粹愚蠢而造成严重破坏。Meta已承认Muse会犯错，并设置了大量防护措施以在出错时尽量减少潜在损害。即便如此，一些用户可能仍会犹豫是否交出信用卡信息，直到他们确信自己的代理能够明智地处理这些信息。长期接触似乎能建立这种信任。约40%的Instinct用户会在三周内关联信用卡。Instinct和Meta还与支付公司Stripe合作，提供数字钱包，让用户无需直接交出银行详细信息即可购物，这或许能让一些人放心。机器人开发商面临的另一个重大挑战是说服其他企业欢迎他们的代理。有些企业似乎乐于这样做。电子商务软件平台Shopify正在努力让Instinct和Muse更容易从其后端供应商网络中购买商品。Meta还与美国最大零售商沃尔玛、杂货配送服务Instacart以及旅行预订网站Expedia合作。但其他公司仍持怀疑态度。例如，亚马逊目前对Instinct和Muse都设置了限制。这家电商巨头很大一部分利润来自向用户展示广告，目前并不需要通过个人代理带来的额外流量。亚马逊还抱怨Meta在发布Muse时没有提前通知。一些硅谷高管表示，他们正在观望这项技术如何发展，然后再向个人代理开放他们的系统。与此同时，机器人开发商正在忙着争取他们。欣恩先生举了餐厅预订平台的例子，Instinct通过同意防止其代理预订大量预订座位、然后只保留一个而取消其余所有预订，从而赢得了其中一些平台的支持。就连亚马逊老板安迪·贾西似乎也在对未来保持开放态度，他此前曾表示，他“非常希望”最终能达成一项公平协议，允许代理使用其市场。如果个人代理要成为一项可行的业务，这类协议将是必要的。扎克伯格先生曾表示，他设想Muse将靠订阅收入和促成交易的抽成相结合来维持运营。欣恩先生认为，大多数在线支出最终将通过个人代理流动。哪家机器人开发商能赢得最大份额的业务仍悬而未决。Instinct迄今已筹集14亿美元。对于一家成立一年的初创公司来说，这是一笔可观的资金，但与Meta可支配的资源相比不过是九牛一毛。OpenAI和Gemini模型的制造商Google都提供自己的个人代理。尽管这些目前更多面向商业而非消费者使用，但它们可能会扩大重点。Airbnb这个短期租赁平台希望将自己打造成各种体验的一站式商店，也宣布计划明年推出个人代理。还有苹果，它在六月份对Siri进行了大改造。新机器人不再那么笨拙，但它缺乏目前赢得消费者青睐的代理的大部分自主能力。也许这家iPhone制造商应该考虑给Instinct发个信息。■

item.title: 奈飞是否已迷失方向？
item.description:
Business

商业 | 被抢风头 2026年10月22日 上周，奈飞在好莱坞掀起了一场让人想起昆汀·塔伦蒂诺电影的血洗。这家流媒体巨头解雇了约6%的员工，这是自2022年以来最大规模的裁员，并清除了部分最高级别的创意高管。毫无疑问，其目的是缓解投资者对热门剧集匮乏影响其收入的担忧。但可惜的是，就像塔伦蒂诺的电影一样，剧情变得更加复杂。其10月20日公布的季度业绩显示出奈飞目前的低迷状态。该公司报告称，截至9月的季度营收同比增长11.8%，并预测今年最后三个月的增幅将降至11.5%，低于2025年同期的17.6%（见图表）。这一消息导致奈飞股价下跌。其市值在过去一年中几乎腰斩。 一家曾经看起来势不可挡、以...
item.content:encoded:
奈飞是否已迷失方向？

商业 | 被抢风头 2026年10月22日 上周，奈飞在好莱坞掀起了一场让人想起昆汀·塔伦蒂诺电影的血洗。这家流媒体巨头解雇了约6%的员工，这是自2022年以来最大规模的裁员，并清除了部分最高级别的创意高管。毫无疑问，其目的是缓解投资者对热门剧集匮乏影响其收入的担忧。但可惜的是，就像塔伦蒂诺的电影一样，剧情变得更加复杂。其10月20日公布的季度业绩显示出奈飞目前的低迷状态。该公司报告称，截至9月的季度营收同比增长11.8%，并预测今年最后三个月的增幅将降至11.5%，低于2025年同期的17.6%（见图表）。这一消息导致奈飞股价下跌。其市值在过去一年中几乎腰斩。 一家曾经看起来势不可挡、以至于被当作科技公司估值的公司，如今却像一家沉闷的媒体公司一样，定期让股东失望。一些人怀疑，它接下来是否会打破其到2027年保持营收两位数增长的承诺。更大的问题是，其联席首席执行官泰德·萨兰多斯和格雷格·彼得斯是否有能力改写剧本。面对一年来收视率疲软、缺乏引爆话题的节目以及在美国电视艾美奖上表现不佳，他们的做法是归咎于下属。奈飞内容主管贝拉·巴贾里亚以及另外两位高管被解雇。巴贾里亚在奈飞工作了近十年，接替她的是来自福克斯和迪士尼的新人彼得·赖斯。奈飞希望赖斯能够提高其节目在美国观众中的低迷命中率。然而，问题在于，萨兰多斯仍然对公司的内容战略负总责。“为什么解雇贝拉而不是泰德？”分析公司LightShed Partners问道。内容乏善可陈并不是投资者不满的唯一原因。在过去一年中，奈飞试图收购好莱坞巨头华纳兄弟探索公司的电影和电视制片厂，但未能成功，输给了规模较小的对手派拉蒙天舞。一些人认为，这一努力是一个误导性的分心之举，表明对奈飞的前景缺乏信心。“他们从来没有真正给出一个好的理由，”媒体研究公司Enders Analysis的汤姆·哈林顿表示。“如果你想要更多电影，那就拍更多电影。你不需要买下这个巨大的东西。”萨兰多斯在财报电话会议上尽力说服投资者，尽管增长放缓且奈飞试图进行大规模收购，但“没有必要进行根本性的战略转变”。然而，娱乐业正处于剧变之中。作为流媒体的先驱，奈飞曾经定下节奏让他人跟随。现在，YouTube做到了。根据市场研究公司尼尔森的数据，过去四年中，在电视上观看YouTube的人数超过了观看奈飞的人数。随着这个视频分享平台上最成功的创作者向高端市场迈进，他们越来越多地入侵奈飞的领地。而在移动端，YouTube、TikTok和Instagram各自吸引的关注度都远超奈飞。与迪士尼+等其他流媒体服务一样，奈飞正在做出反应。它推出了适合智能手机竖屏格式的短视频，吸引了一些YouTube创作者，并正在扩大其在包括体育在内的现场娱乐方面的努力。但奈飞越来越难脱颖而出，其对新竞争的反应也显得越来越随意。“这是对YouTube的恐慌，”Enders的哈林顿说。尽管如此，奈飞最大的优势在于其从流媒体中赚钱的能力。正如另一家研究公司Omdia的玛丽亚·鲁阿·阿戈蒂所说：“人们看YouTube，但他们为奈飞付费。”目前，YouTube的订阅业务仍然相对较小。奈飞对其广告销售努力也仍寄予厚望，这一努力是在2022年上一次低迷期间启动的。然而，这一副业——由彼得斯负责——最近令人失望。在财报电话会议上，彼得斯表示，由于新广告产品的采用延迟，他预计今年的广告收入为27亿美元，低于此前预测的30亿美元。如果YouTube和其他平台继续夺走观众的注意力，实现这些目标只会变得更加困难。彼得斯与他的联席首席执行官一样，没有表示要改变策略。最终，投资者可能会要求另一种形式的“血洗”。■

Business

item.content:encoded:
如果AI取代人类工人，他们失去的将不仅仅是薪水

商业 | 巴特比 2026年10月22日

有时候你开始一个项目，然后意识到自己误判了形势。令你恐惧的是，你发现回头已经太迟。于是你继续埋头苦干，希望避免灾难。但关于马克·扎克伯格喝健力士啤酒的话题就到此为止吧。其他人工智能巨头心中还怀有另一种深深的忧虑——关于他们正在开发的技术可能带来的影响。10月18日，人工智能实验室Anthropic表示，计划将其5%的股份投入一个公共利益基金，该基金最终可能会向受经济动荡影响的人们发放现金。一天后，埃隆·马斯克承诺给美国每个儿童一股SpaceX股票。目前还没有迹象表明会出现人工智能导致的就业末日。但如果这项技术摧毁的就业岗位远多于它创造的，那么有偿就业的重要性——不仅对人们的收入，而且对他们的幸福和尊严——将确实变得突出。

对于这个问题，有乐观的回答。有人指出，历史上充满了不以有偿工作为中心的社会。调查数据显示，大多数退休的美国人表示对自己的生活感到满意。换句话说，解决了如何为不需要工作的生活提供资金这个小问题，每个人都可以快乐地整天种植获奖番茄或乘船游览河流。但事实不可避免地要复杂得多。上个月，谷歌DeepMind（另一家AI实验室）的Stephanie Chan及其他研究人员发表了一篇关于福祉与工作的学术文献综述，它提醒我们，有偿就业带来的好处远不止收入，而在真正的经济动荡中通往良好结果的道路将是狭窄的。

想想工作提供了什么。有影响力的学者Marie Jahoda指出了就业的五个潜在好处：它为人们的日子提供的结构；它带来的社交接触；集体目标感；就业所带来的地位；以及它推动人们远离懒散、走向积极行动的作用。（还有其他好处：加州大学欧文分校的Noah Kouchekinia及其合著者最近发表的一篇论文发现，在达到退休年龄之前离开劳动力市场的成年人，其认知能力下降会加速。）即使是拥有很多选择的人似乎也对悠闲的生活心存警惕。没有多少硅谷亿万富翁会放弃一切去专注于自己的爱好。类似地，哥德堡大学的Bengt Furaker和Anna Davidsson撰写的一篇论文研究了瑞典彩票中奖者如何应对他们的好运。更大的意外之财确实会让中奖者更有可能休一段较长的无薪假并减少工作时间，但只有一小部分人完全辞职。

当然，有些工作远不如其他工作令人愉快。而且也有可能从其他地方获得潜在的益处，比如照护他人，或者做全职父母。墨尔本大学的Michelle Jongenelis及其合著者的一篇论文研究了志愿服务对澳大利亚退休人员福祉的影响。即使是非常少量的志愿服务——每周仅一小时——也能在生活满意度和目标感评分上带来显著改善。但这对于那些想要并期望工作的人来说，只是苍白无力的安慰。在另一篇论文中，利兹大学的Clemens Hetschko及其合著者追踪了德国成年人进入退休状态时自我报告的福祉。在职人员在离开劳动力市场后，其生活满意度没有太大变化。但那些在达到退休年龄时已长期失业的人，其福祉出现了大幅跃升。乍一看，这似乎很奇怪。那些一直在工作的人几乎肯定会在日常生活和收入方面经历更大的动荡。作者的理论是，失业者切换了社会类别，从处于工作年龄时不受欢迎的类别，转变为达到退休年龄时受人尊敬的类别。换句话说，任何轻率地声称人们可以用其他活动替代有偿就业的人，都是在无视证据。有些工作令人沮丧。但眼下，没有其他东西能以如此为社会所接受的形式，带来同样一揽子的心理和金钱益处。确保如果人工智能夺走人们的工作，他们仍有足够的钱维持生活，这是一个大问题。而给他们一种自我价值感，同样困难。■

item.title: Multinational businesses are losing confidence in Indonesia
item.description:
Business

item.content:encoded:
Multinational businesses are losing confidence in Indonesia

Business | The archipelago of broken dreams

Oct 22nd 2026

Ukraine and Palestine are no one’s idea of attractive markets. Yet that is the company Indonesia may soon keep. On October 15th MSCI, an index provider, threatened to reclassify it as a “standalone” market, two notches below its current status as an ”emerging” one. MSCI blamed a stock market plagued by opaque listings and suspected pump-and-dump schemes. Investors have been fleeing. In dollar terms Indonesian stocks have lost half their value in 2026, rendering it the world’s worst-performing market (see chart).

The sorry state of the bourse is emblematic of the deeper decay in Indonesia’s business environment during the presidency of Prabowo Subianto, under whom cronyism has grown rampant and the government has become increasingly meddlesome. His reign has unsettled multinational businesses, many of which covet Indonesia’s bountiful natural resources and vast population of consumers.

Earlier this year the China Chamber of Commerce in Indonesia, a business association, circulated a letter complaining that its members faced “excessively stringent regulation, over-enforcement, and even corruption and extortion” by authorities. Their plight is not unique. “If you swapped out the letterhead, it could have been written by us,” says someone from a similar Western association in Indonesia. If Indonesia’s president is not careful, the ranks of multinationals scaling back their presence in his country will grow.

Part of the problem is Mr Prabowo’s economic nationalism. It represents a reversal of the progress that has slowly been made in Indonesia since the Asian financial crisis of 1997-98. Mr Prabowo’s predecessor, Joko Widodo, elevated a business-minded coterie of fixers, including Luhut Pandjaitan, a coal baron. They let foreign businesses cut through Indonesia’s disorganised, corrupt bureaucracy, luring in firms such as Tsingshan, a Chinese miner, and LG Energy Solution (LGES), a South Korean battery-maker. Few doubted that Mr Widodo’s inner circle enriched themselves. But for foreign businesses, they made Indonesia a simpler place to operate.

Mr Prabowo, by contrast, rails against “irresponsible powers” that are “stealing” Indonesia’s resources, and has installed a new cohort of cronies with little interest in economic strategy. “No single person is playing the Luhut role in the Prabowo administration,” says Brasukra Sudjana of Vriens & Partners, a consultancy.

That has damaged confidence among multinationals. In the final quarter of 2024, during which Mr Prabowo took power, inflows of new foreign direct investment hit $16bn, more than double the level of four years earlier. They have since stagnated. A $12bn scheme backed by Xinyi, a Chinese solar-panel producer, to build an “eco-city” has lost momentum. LGES has dropped plans for an $8bn battery project.

The biggest deterioration in conditions has come in the commodities sector. Rules for miners, such as stringent quotas on production, are in constant flux. Businesses complain of shakedowns. After floods devastated the western island of Sumatra last year, the government blamed miners’ abuse of forest land. It then attempted to nationalise Martabe, a gold mine controlled by Jardine Matheson, a conglomerate operating from Hong Kong, though it later backed down.

Freeport-McMoRan, an American miner, was bullied into divesting a 12% share of its Indonesian arm last year, which had already been 51% owned by the state (it received next to nothing in return). Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin, Indonesia’s defence minister and one of Mr Prabowo’s closest confidants, has overseen a sweeping crackdown on forestry. A third of all palm-oil plantation land has been expropriated.

In May Mr Prabowo announced abruptly that a new state agency, Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia (DSI), would centralise exports of palm oil, coal and ferro-nickel. Officials claim it will act merely as a monitoring agency, but Mr Prabowo continues to muddy the waters. “Imagine in future how much we will save when all our export commodities will be monitored and controlled by DSI,” he said in August.

The regulatory leash is also tightening elsewhere. Take salt and sugar, where a push for self-sufficiency has curbed import licences. Indonesia has limited raw-sugar production, and food-makers complain that the quality of local salt is too low for them. Troubles with import licences have led to supply-chain snarls for Coca-Cola and PepsiCo, two drinks giants. In the past, stymied firms might have cut deals with officials or hired politically connected lawyers. “Now [my contacts] say companies are simply being squeezed with no clarity whatsoever,” says Tom Lembong, a trade minister under Mr Widodo (who faced jail in a dubious graft case related to illegal sugar-import permits, until Mr Prabowo pardoned him last year). Further burdens are being added: on October 18th new Halal-certification rules were put in place on various consumer goods sold in Indonesia, including cosmetics and supplements, though the government subsequently delayed the implementation for some categories to 2028.

Multinationals targeting Indonesia’s consumers have also encountered stagnant spending. Although official GDP growth is rarely lower than 5%, the share of workers in Indonesia’s middle class (as defined by authorities) has fallen from 16% a decade ago to 7% last year. The problem predates Mr Prabowo, but on his watch more Indonesians are slipping into low-paying informal jobs. Real wages have fallen for skilled workers, too. A recent survey by NielsenIQ, a data provider, found that only 9% of consumers felt financially better off than a year ago, down from 54% in 2024.

The pain has been felt across a wide range of industries. Domestic car sales remain shy of 2019 levels, hurting multinationals such as Toyota, the top auto brand in Indonesia. Foreign pedlars of packaged consumer goods have had to cut prices to attract shoppers—though even that is “not necessarily translating into proportional growth” in volumes, notes Krisetiadi Purwanto of NielsenIQ. At the Indonesian arm of Unilever sales have fallen by a fifth since 2019, while operating profit has more than halved. (A Gaza-related boycott, another risk in the Muslim-majority country, hasn’t helped.) In January the British conglomerate sold its struggling tea business in Indonesia to a local competitor. In a country where two-thirds of men puff, big tobacco has faced falling sales as consumers turn to cheaper sticks, including black-market ones that avoid taxes. Foreign firms’ dreams for Indonesia are at risk of going up in smoke. ■

item.title: 2010年代如何重塑商业
item.description:
Business

商业 | 熊彼特 2026年10月22日 按年代标准来看，2010年代令人难堪。如今专注于人工智能模型和火箭的科技老板们，谈起当年打造的消费类应用时满是不屑。银行家们则在那十年里烂醉如泥。在高管们漫长而狂热的夏天之后，2010年代在许多企业高管的办公室里成了一个纪律严明的冬天：这种纪律来自政府、公众、维权投资者和董事会。然而，这个“灾难十年”对当今商业的启示，远比投资者自我安慰时所津津乐道的1870年代、1920年代或1990年代的故事要多得多。 2010年代是一个令人尴尬的十年吗？当然。但它 nonetheless 也是一个革命性的十年。 硅谷最宜进行对2010年代的重新审视。美国何以能够...
item.content:encoded:
2010年代如何重塑商业

商业 | 熊彼特 2026年10月22日

按年代标准来看，2010年代令人难堪。如今专注于人工智能模型和火箭的科技老板们，谈起当年打造的消费类应用时满是不屑。银行家们则在那十年里烂醉如泥。在高管们漫长而狂热的夏天之后，2010年代在许多企业高管的办公室里成了一个纪律严明的冬天：这种纪律来自政府、公众、维权投资者和董事会。然而，这个“灾难十年”对当今商业的启示，远比投资者自我安慰时所津津乐道的1870年代、1920年代或1990年代的故事要多得多。

2010年代是一个令人尴尬的十年吗？当然。但它 nonetheless 也是一个革命性的十年。

硅谷最宜进行对2010年代的重新审视。美国何以能够开展一场规模空前、耗能巨大的建设热潮，而丝毫不受中东战争困扰？这要感谢2010年代。得益于页岩革命，美国在本十年结束时成为半个多世纪以来首次的能源净出口国。而现在为数据中心建设提供资金的取之不尽的资本之井又来自何处？金融危机后，银行被施加了速度限制，全球信贷体系被重塑。当今使用的许多资本市场技巧——从特殊目的载体到离岸保险资本——都是在2010年代经过试验和检验的。

如果这场豪赌成功，那将是因为人工智能彻底改变了白领工作。不理解2010年代，就不可能理解办公室生活。那时，政客们忧心忡忡地关注着Uber（2010年）或DoorDash（2013年）的零工工人。但办公室生活的变化要大得多。员工们被“挂绳秘密警察”命令将完整的自我带入工作。当他们抵达那布满软装家具的“圆形监狱”——也就是现代办公室——时，他们用Datadog（2012年）或Snowflake（2014年）搭建“仪表盘”，在“热办公桌”上接听Zoom（2013年）电话，也许是在WeWork（2010年）里，耳边响起Slack（2013年）消息如远处机枪般的连珠炮响。

当2010年代正在发生之时，它给人的感觉是一个缺乏新商业思想的时代。事实被证明是大错特错。有效利他主义是一种哲学，其严苛的伦理计算试图把握普遍性，但它只可能诞生于2010年代初牛津和斯坦福的学院深宅之中。其思想内容在在线留言板LessWrong（2009年）上阐述，并由80000 Hours（2011年）等慈善机构付诸实践。如今它已成为硅谷人工智能实验室的主导哲学，这使其轻松成为当下最具影响力的管理思想。

政客们同样从这个革命性十年留下的架子上找到了许多思想。全民基本收入在痴迷平等的2010年代曾是一个边缘想法，但在痴迷人工智能的2020年代已被当作严肃政策来讨论。左右两翼均 embraced 的“大即恶”反垄断学派，源自2010年代中期美国著名法学院的创造。在整个富裕世界，财富税已成为左翼的最爱政策。其核心思想由两位法国经济学家托马斯·皮凯蒂和加布里埃尔·祖克曼在2010年代提出。

2010年代的攻击最好由2010年代的防御来抵挡。Anthropic和OpenAI都采用公益公司（public-benefit corporation）结构，这种形式理论上更容易平衡社会与股东的利益。两家实验室都在特拉华州注册——依据的是2013年的规则。2019年，强大的CEO游说团体商业圆桌会议宣布，公司的股东从此应让位于利益相关者。如今，这读起来像是企业高尚情怀巅峰时期的一件文物。然而其影响力依然存在。本周，Anthropic承诺将5%的股份用于非营利事业。SpaceX也在向公众赠送股权。套用马克思的话说，商人并非随心所欲地创造历史，而是在2010年代传给他们的条件下创造的。

2010年代并非每一个大思想都完整存续。央行将利率维持在零附近的政策于2022年终结。热衷企业社会正义运动的现象比以前少了。尽管如此，商业的某些角落仍保留着未经改造的2010年代风貌。私募股权基金正在设计各种办法避免向出资人返还资金，以免面对后2010年代的世界。欧洲仍紧抱ESG不放。咨询公司也是如此。麦肯锡关于职场女性和少数族裔的研究是那个时代的圣典。本月，这家咨询公司因一名合伙人公开质疑类似观点而将其降职。竞争对手贝恩最近写道：“77%的美国客户表示他们担忧环境可持续性，高于去年的69%。”你说是就是吧。

就像无视二战结束的日本士兵一样，B型企业阵营中的一些强硬派仍在战斗。很难想象会出现像对1990年代和2000年代那样的对2010年代的怀旧潮。有什么值得怀念的呢？天然气的黄金时代算不上。流媒体的黄金时代，也许可以。音乐界的巨兽——泰勒·斯威夫特、德雷克等——拥有与漫威超级英雄系列一样永不过时的商业魅力。但对2010年代的关注肯定会增长。在2010年代大部分时间处于危机中的欧元区，如今再次站在另一场危机的边缘。理解硅谷意味着理解2010年代。关于Facebook的新电影《社交清算》不过是众多回望2010年代的作品之一。一部关于山姆·班克曼-弗里德——2010年代末的加密货币诈骗犯（本周他在狱中接受了《经济学人》旗下“Money Talks”播客的采访）——的剧集即将发布。另一位2010年代诈骗犯伊丽莎白·霍姆斯也成为一部新电影的主角。还有埃隆·马斯克，世界首富，如今又成为全球最长纪录片之一的拍摄对象。他的飞行汽车是对2010年代那句“我们最终只得到140个字符”的咒语的一剂解药。但马斯克同时也是一位电动汽车大亨，其权力源自一个无法无天的社交网络。一个属于他时代的人？绝对是：一个属于2010年代的人。■

item.title: AI compute is the new oil—and needs a new market
item.description:
Finance & economics

Finance & economics | The new market-makers Oct 22nd 2026 ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE is changing many things about the modern world. Language is no exception. The word “compute”, for instance, used to be regarded as a verb. Today even grammar pedants grudgingly accept it as a noun, referring to t...
item.content:encoded:
AI compute is the new oil—and needs a new market

Finance & economics | The new market-makers

Oct 22nd 2026

ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE is changing many things about the modern world. Language is no exception. The word “compute”, for instance, used to be regarded as a verb. Today even grammar pedants grudgingly accept it as a noun, referring to the processing power generated by advanced chips. This new, non-verbal compute is the fuel of a technological revolution.

Demand for processing oomph has surged, and it is in short supply. About $360bn was spent on AI compute last year around the world, according to Boston Consulting Group, about 50% more than on copper. By 2030 BCG expects $2.3trn in transactions, roughly the size of the global trade in crude oil today.

For all its impressive size, however, the compute market lacks sophistication. The “hyperscalers” (a still somewhat arcane piece of IT jargon for a handful of giant cloud-computing providers including Amazon, Google and Microsoft) and frontier AI labs (such as Anthropic and OpenAI) make deals for tens or even hundreds of billions of dollars of compute. But such arrangements are unavailable to thousands of smaller firms. Buyers and sellers also have few of the derivatives that in established markets allow them to hedge their exposures and speculate.

The compute supply chain, then, looks ripe for marketisation. In the most simple form, chipmakers (like Nvidia and AMD) sell advanced AI semiconductors to equipment manufacturers (such as Dell and Hewlett Packard Enterprises), which package the silicon into racks and servers to sell to data-centre operators. Besides the hyperscalers, these include a few large “neoclouds” (one more linguistic innovation, denoting independent providers like CoreWeave and Nebius) and hundreds of smaller, less well-known firms.

The operators, in turn, rent out access to compute to customers for a fixed period, often several years. Customers range from the hyperscalers (which supplement their in-house compute with rentals) to startups running open-source AI models.

So far, so simple—in theory. In practice, things quickly get complicated. That is because compute is heterogeneous: different chips are sold in different servers, at different locations, for different time periods. Matching buyers and sellers is finicky. Every business that needs processing power has a “compute guy” (or several) buying second-hand capacity through an opaque network of middlemen. Many of these informal brokers, some shadier than others, tout their offerings through messaging apps like WhatsApp and Telegram. The whole thing looks less like trading a high-tech commodity and more like peddling illegal drugs.

In a market that is so fractured and immature, providers and purchasers alike prefer the safety of long-term contracts. On paper, these guarantee capacity to users and revenues for themselves. In reality, given how fast the technology and the market of AI are evolving, it is hard to tell how much such deals are worth: today’s buyers and sellers may not be around in a few years to honour their commitments. The surging yields on CoreWeave’s bonds highlight the uncertainty. Who will make a killing? And who may not make it at all? With lenders struggling to price risk, many smaller operators buying and renting compute face double-digit interest rates.

Fortunately for everyone involved, proper markets are being built around the compute supply chain. Some budding bourses, such as Compute Exchange, list GPUs (the increasingly familiar shorthand for graphics-processing units, AI’s silicon workhorse) by location, rental duration, price and availability. Titans of global derivatives trading, including CME Group and the Intercontinental Exchange, hope to launch their own compute futures. They have teamed up with startups pioneering compute indices, pegged to the rental price of popular AI chips. They await regulatory approval.

Rather than wait for exchange-traded derivatives to be approved, some compute-market pioneers are creating over-the-counter instruments of the sort common in credit and foreign-exchange markets. In March a startup called Anera Labs arranged a six-figure pilot trade for June with FalconX, a cryptocurrency broker, based on the future rental price of Nvidia’s popular H100 GPUs.

Luxor, another startup, offers operators swap-like contracts that guarantee fixed cashflow per server, per hour. If the spot price for compute is below the price agreed in the swap, the operator is paid the difference. If the spot price is higher, it is the operator that pays. This payment, explains Ethan Vera, one of the firm’s co-founders, may for example be made through a revenue-sharing arrangement. Luxor’s bespoke derivatives are modest for now, in the tens of millions of dollars, but the potential is vast.

As American exchanges await the thumbs-up from regulators, upstarts are getting off the ground elsewhere. From its exchange in Bermuda, Architect Financial Technologies, founded in 2023, offers futures in compute linked to the value of chips in America. The firm has also recently launched a platform where model-makers bid to provide “inference”—the useful output produced by an AI model in response to a prompt—rather than the underlying compute capacity. Brett Harrison, the company’s founder and boss, believes that inference may prove easier to standardise than compute.

Given the uncertainty surrounding the all-new market, it is attracting risk-takers. Many, including Mr Harrison, spent time in crypto, once the most compute-intensive enterprise out there, which attracted financial engineers trying to turn processing power into a tradable asset. Mr Harrison was president of FTX US, the American arm of the crypto exchange founded by Sam Bankman Fried, resigning two months before the parent firm’s bankruptcy amid fraud in November 2022. Luxor once primarily served bitcoin miners. One of Anera’s co-founders, Vishwa Naik, was a crypto entrepreneur. (CoreWeave and some other neoclouds also began life as crypto-mining businesses.)

As opportunities grow, established financial companies are taking more of an interest. DRW and Jump Trading, two large market-makers, have both invested in Silicon Data, the compute-focused research firm with which CME hopes to launch its futures. Each market-maker has also assembled its own team to trade the new commodity. This month Jump Trading acquired Ito Markets, a compute-trading startup, whose founders will lead its efforts to break into the new industry.

David Olsen, Jump’s investment chief, points out that the market will grow more rapidly with the right institutions, such as clearing houses that limit the risk of blow-ups by ensuring that contracts are honoured by both sides of a trade. “We’re a long way from that,” he acknowledges, echoing many in this industry who think it may take years or even decades for the market to mature. “But”, he adds, “we want to be part of that discussion.”

His desire is unsurprising. After all, with surging demand for what remains a scarce commodity, and with so many businesses around the world exposed to it, the prize is enormous.

Mr Naik of Anera, who in his pre-crypto days was an oil trader at Reliance Industries, an Indian conglomerate, likens today’s moment in the compute market to the last days of the “seven sisters”, a cartel of Western giants that ruled the global petroleum trade between the late 1920s and the 1970s. Their chokehold was broken by nationalisation (in many exporting countries) and the rise of the open oil market (just about everywhere). As governments covetously eye the AI labs and ventures like Anera attempt to create a market from scratch, you do not need to squint too hard to see a similar future for compute. ■

item.title: 巴西怪异的经济需要认真改革
item.description:
Finance & economics

财经版块 | 一个真正的问题 2026年10月22日 巴西总统选举第一轮结束后，全世界的民主党人都为之颤抖。策划政变的前总统之子弗拉维奥·博尔索纳罗出人意料地击败了现任总统路易斯·伊纳西奥·卢拉·达席尔瓦。他看起来有望在10月25日的决选中击败这位80岁的左翼偶像卢拉。资本家们也同样颤抖——但却是兴奋。第二天圣保罗股指大涨近8%，雷亚尔走强，政府债券收益率下降。这是对卢拉经济管理的残酷裁决。GDP增长超过了（悲观的）预期，失业率低，通胀率保持在巴西中央银行（BCB）设定的1.5%-4.5%目标区间附近。但他的财政放纵和反商业言论吓坏了市场。他继承的“基本”预算盈余（即扣除利息支付前）如今变成...
item.content:encoded:
巴西怪异的经济需要认真改革

财经版块 | 一个真正的问题 2026年10月22日 巴西总统选举第一轮结束后，全世界的民主党人都为之颤抖。策划政变的前总统之子弗拉维奥·博尔索纳罗出人意料地击败了现任总统路易斯·伊纳西奥·卢拉·达席尔瓦。他看起来有望在10月25日的决选中击败这位80岁的左翼偶像卢拉。资本家们也同样颤抖——但却是兴奋。第二天圣保罗股指大涨近8%，雷亚尔走强，政府债券收益率下降。这是对卢拉经济管理的残酷裁决。GDP增长超过了（悲观的）预期，失业率低，通胀率保持在巴西中央银行（BCB）设定的1.5%-4.5%目标区间附近。但他的财政放纵和反商业言论吓坏了市场。他继承的“基本”预算盈余（即扣除利息支付前）如今变成了赤字，国际货币基金组织预计今年公共债务将达到GDP的97%，高于2022年的84%。“我们需要终结所有这些关于维持盈余和财政纪律的无稽之谈，”他最近断言。相比之下，博尔索纳罗以阿根廷手持电锯的总统哈维尔·米莱为榜样，后者的自由市场改革取得了一定成功（也带来了许多痛苦）。他也使用一种切割工具——一把巨大的剪刀——作为选举道具，誓言要大幅削减税收、繁文缛节和腐败。然而他的经济理念十分模糊。为了抵消他提议的减税以及四年内9000亿雷亚尔（1790亿美元，占GDP的6.6%）的基础设施支出，他想减少部委数量、实现公共行政数字化并出售联邦大楼。这不可信——他能从这种修修补补中兑现一半承诺的节省就算走运了。这也不足以胜任使命。要切开巴西的经济困境，需要真正米莱式的热情。这些困境源于高公共支出、顽固通胀和低储蓄三者纠缠不清的组合。结果是资本成本高得惊人。一些分析师认为巴西的实际利率——即央行政策利率经明年预期通胀调整后——高达9%或更高。这高于俄罗斯，是智利、菲律宾或南非等和平同侪的四倍。一切都要从公共财政说起。巴西那份长达6.5万字的宪法“巨著”禁止削减名义公共部门工资，并将养老金、残疾和失业救济金与最低工资挂钩，而最低工资每年根据近期通胀和GDP增长进行调整。这种棘轮效应将强制性支出推高至联邦预算的90%。它还使通胀压力长期存在。再加上慷慨的福利国家，巴西人因此不愿储蓄。国民储蓄率占GDP的14%，比世界平均水平低12个百分点。如果过去价格上涨经常侵蚀你的银行存款，而国家又为你的医疗、学校和养老金买单，那你不如立刻把赚到的所有钱都花掉——尤其是如果你像这个不平等国家的大多数人一样，本来赚得就不多。近年记忆中，没有哪届政府认真尝试过紧缩。而卢拉同样宽松。他多次允许最低工资（以及所有与之挂钩的东西）涨幅超过通胀。他还挥霍了近2600亿美元，为军火商、芯片制造商和制药商等提供廉价信贷，却几乎没什么成果——2022年至2025年间，工业占GDP的比重有所萎缩。当他在任期早期仍在试图平衡账目时，他提高了税收，给本已惨淡的企业雪上加霜。卢拉的刺激措施也意味着央行别无选择，只能加息。由于巴西近一半的贷款都受补贴——包括大多数抵押贷款、农业贷款和基础设施信贷——加息幅度必须高于其他国家，才能对价格产生同样的降温效果。2024年年中至2025年年中，政策利率七次上调，达到15%。尽管目前已回落至13.8%，但仍与疫情后物价飙升后的高点持平。 高实际利率推高了公共债务的偿还成本，并推高了债务与GDP之比（见图表）。而面对如此丰厚的回报，投资者更倾向于借钱给政府——尽管政府有这样那样的缺陷，但似乎比大多数公司更安全。这提高了其他所有人的资本成本。华盛顿智库彼得森国际经济研究所的莫妮卡·德博勒解释说，这还在金融体系中造成了不正当激励。大约一半的政府债务由浮动利率国库券（称为LFT）组成，其每日回报基于央行政策利率。商业银行的资产负债表上满是这种轻松得来的钱。因此，央行降息的幅度可能低于原本应有的水平，因为担心更深度的降息会损害贷款机构的利润并引发银行业危机。LFT还在另一方面削弱了货币政策。持有这些债券的银行和富有的巴西人获得的票息支付，削弱了紧缩政策旨在实现的消费降温效果。“我加息越多，持有者获得的收入就越多，”央行行长加布里埃尔·加利波洛今年早些时候抱怨道。摆脱这一乱局的唯一出路是紧缩。这将降低通胀、压低实际利率，并为生产性用途释放资本。博尔索纳罗的团队私下谈论改革，但候选人本人拒绝改变养老金或指数化规则。如果卢拉在决选中出人意料地翻盘，他也不太可能发现自己内心深处的财政鹰派倾向。而任何总统都很难说服国会两院五分之三的议员来拆除宪法棘轮。市场可能更喜欢博尔索纳罗而非卢拉。但无论他们得到谁，最终都会令人失望。■
