item.content:encoded:
Mark Carney shows middle powers how to handle a dangerous world

Leaders | Turning over a new leaf

Oct 15th 2026

ENTITLED CANADA has been feeding off America for decades. Like a parasitic bug, it enjoys the benefits of being America’s cherished 51st state without giving anything back. Canadians know they couldn’t live without America’s protection, yet their ungrateful prime minister, Mark Carney, refuses to defer to the great and beautiful country over the border.

That is how Donald Trump sees Canada, and it leaves no room for mutual benefit between the two allies. The bullying president is ratcheting up tariffs. He has renamed the southern side of Lake Ontario Lake America. Canadian consumers, in response, are spitting out their Kentucky bourbon and leaving Las Vegas. Mr Carney, in office for 18 months, remains defiant, the star of an extended, dramatic and riveting stand-off.

By now you might have expected Mr Carney to have caved in. Canada is only a mid-size power with a so-so economy and puny armed forces. It has vulnerabilities aplenty. One will be evident on October 19th, when the province of Alberta holds a referendum asking if it may one day secede, taking with it more oil in the ground than in the entire United States.

In fact Mr Carney is riding high. Polls suggest that those Albertans will probably vote to stay. And under him, Canada is doing better than you might expect. In January it was Mr Carney, at the annual jamboree in Davos, who argued that what he called the “middle powers” must find ways to take on threatening ones. Nine months on, his country offers lessons for what these middle powers should do when the hegemonic giant pulls the mat from under them.

Those lessons start with a bracing dose of realism. As we set out, middle powers will never replace the hegemons as the force that sustains powerful permanent institutions such as the UN. The world has grown more dangerous because both America and China are exploiting or undermining arrangements and norms in which power was shared. Emboldened, wreckers like Russia and Iran are becoming even more predatory. Co-ordinating the more herbivorous middle powers is often too hard to get much done—as you can see in even the most developed middle-power club, the European Union.

Yet middle powers can still mitigate some of the damage, as Canada and its allies show. Mr Carney has zipped around the world making new trade deals as well as drumming up symbolic agreements, such as talk of associate EU membership. In the same way, after the United States backed out of a big trans-Pacific trade deal known as TPP during Mr Trump’s first term, Japan stepped in to revive it. In the realm of defence, Canada is trimming its old reliance on America, and is considering placing an order for Swedish Gripen fighter jets—just as Norway is buying British frigates and the United Arab Emirates is purchasing Ukraine’s cutting-edge drones.

When middle powers face a particular threat, they can throw around some weight, as when Europe rebuffed Mr Trump’s designs on Greenland. The strengths and limits of this approach are clear in Ukraine. Financial and military support for Ukraine from Europe and Canada, stepping up after America pulled back, shows how middle powers can act in concert. Vladimir Putin’s army pays a dreadful blood price for its small gains in the Donbas. The limits are clear, too, as Mr Trump showed with this week’s diesel diplomacy.

Canada’s most important lesson, however, emerges from what the pragmatic Mr Carney is doing at home. A few years ago the country’s woeful politics and ailing government seemed broken. Income per person had drifted from 90% of America’s in the 1980s to just 71% in 2022, much of it following a recent burst of low-skilled immigration. Today Mr Carney is pushing through overdue measures to boost productivity, open the economy and lift defence spending from a pitifully low 1.3% of GDP to 2%.

Among his first steps, he scrapped an unpopular consumer carbon tax and vowed to build a pipeline to carry oil from Alberta to the west coast. He has started to cut internal barriers to trade, called off a hefty rise in capital-gains tax, cut the lowest rate of income tax and set out plans to trim federal spending. In that trade dispute with America, Canada has also shown that it can stand up for itself, targeting reciprocal tariffs on American imports from swing states in the run-up to the midterm elections and scrambling to cut its long-term dependence on its neighbour.

Mr Carney has so far managed to resist what is known as the “Juncker curse”, named after a president of the European Commission, Jean-Claude Juncker. Speaking of reform, Mr Juncker once said: “We all know what to do, we just don’t know how to get re-elected after we’ve done it.” Yet Mr Carney’s popularity has been surging even as he reforms. Two years ago, more than nine in ten Canadians could not recognise his photograph. Today a maple-leaf love-in is under way: polls show the prime minister’s approval rating nearing 70%. Internationally, he has replaced France’s beleaguered Emmanuel Macron as the centrists’ pin-up. The contrast with Mr Trump, unloved by his own voters, is stark.

True, Canada must go further and faster with its liberalising changes. There is every chance that relations with America will improve when Mr Trump leaves office in 2029, but it is not certain. It should therefore work on keeping its options open.

Other middle powers can learn from Canada. Naturally, it has some strengths they cannot copy, such as its vast energy and mineral reserves and its lucky geography, far from the nastiest geopolitical flashpoints. Yet there is room for them to co-operate on one-off projects with tangible and limited aims.

And they can fortify themselves abroad by harnessing the need for change at home. In a way, Mr Trump has done all democracies a favour, by giving them a reason to tackle long-standing problems that seemed too hard. The middle powers need to prepare for a dangerous world. They should look to Mr Carney and Canada for an answer on what to do. ■

item.title: Hardly his finest hour
item.description:
Leaders

Leaders | America and Ukraine Oct 15th 2026 NEVER in the field of human conflict was so much risked by one man for so little. Donald Trump is threatening to cripple Ukraine in its fight for survival—and to expose Europe to Russian aggression—seemingly for the pitiful prize of minimising his loss...
item.content:encoded:
Hardly his finest hour

Leaders | America and Ukraine

Oct 15th 2026

NEVER in the field of human conflict was so much risked by one man for so little. Donald Trump is threatening to cripple Ukraine in its fight for survival—and to expose Europe to Russian aggression—seemingly for the pitiful prize of minimising his losses in next month’s midterm elections. The hard question is what Ukraine and its allies should do.

On October 9th Mr Trump said he and Vladimir Putin had agreed that Russia will export 2.2m barrels of diesel, with the promise of more later. Mr Trump declared an energy ceasefire that Russia will not observe. His officials demanded that Ukraine should stop targeting Russian refineries, suggesting that America would withhold intelligence and weapons sales if it does not. On the night of October 13th a Pentagon-controlled part of the Starlink satellite system was degraded for fast-moving Ukrainian drones—stopping them hitting hard-to-spot targets in Russian-occupied territory.

All this is terrible for Ukraine, which must choose between losing crucial intelligence and weapons and carrying out the deep strikes on refineries that are its best answer to continuing Russian attacks on its cities. It also gives succour to Mr Putin. He can make some money and continue illicit oil sales to buyers such as India and China that America had been threatening with sanctions. If any deal holds, he also stands to gain Mr Trump’s help in protecting his battered refineries.

The deal is also shameful for America. Mr Putin terrorises his own people, kills Ukrainian civilians and is helping Iran fight America. Mr Trump’s repeated acts of indulgence towards him, supposedly in pursuit of peace, undermine deterrence, hastening further crimes.

And for what? Mr Putin may have promised to press Iran into a pre-election ceasefire, though his leverage is limited and it would be unlikely to last. And even if Russia actually has the diesel to export, which is in doubt, America burns 2.2m barrels every 13 hours. Presumably Mr Trump wants to take the credit if the price of diesel falls—and if it does not, he can always blame Ukraine. It’s a win-win!

What should Ukraine do? Defiantly hitting refineries would be self-defeating. American intel and Starlink’s satellites let Ukraine target Russia’s HQs, supply lines and radar, helping blunt its offensive power. Ukrainian jets need American ammunition to shoot down incoming drones and missiles.

But Ukraine does have options. The White House has suggested that Mr Trump’s energy truce covers only refineries—of which Ukraine has the grand total of one. Ukraine and its allies are rightly seeking to expand the ceasefire to all energy infrastructure. Even if they fail, highlighting this injustice bolsters efforts to seek help from the Senate in interceding with Mr Trump. They should remind him that losing Ukraine could brand him as a weak president. After the midterms, when Mr Putin’s diesel is worth less, Mr Trump may be prepared to move on, or simply become distracted.

Meanwhile, Ukraine should increase the tempo of attacks against other Russian infrastructure, including data centres and distribution hubs. Mr Putin needs to understand that Ukraine can threaten his rule and Russians need to be aware of the war being fought in their name. And such strikes demonstrate how Ukraine can still hit large, static targets without American help—including refineries if it is desperate.

Mr Putin appears to have concluded that he cannot win on the battlefield. His strategy now is to grind Ukraine down by making its cities uninhabitable in winter. How scandalous that Mr Trump has become his best weapon. ■

item.title: America makes waves in Cuba
item.description:
Leaders

Leaders | Havana go Oct 15th 2026 SINCE HIS return to power, President Donald Trump has made clear that he hopes to bring down Cuba’s repressive regime. This year he struck upon a cruel approach: blockading the impoverished island’s fuel supply. The idea was that growing hardship would spur Cuba...
item.content:encoded:
America makes waves in Cuba

Leaders | Havana go

Oct 15th 2026

SINCE HIS return to power, President Donald Trump has made clear that he hopes to bring down Cuba’s repressive regime. This year he struck upon a cruel approach: blockading the impoverished island’s fuel supply. The idea was that growing hardship would spur Cubans to protest, and then to topple their vile leaders. Misery duly followed, as Cubans suffered more blackouts, buses stopped running and food got more expensive. Political change did not come. Yet by accident or design, the blockade has still created an opportunity.

For decades Cuba got most of its imported fuel from Venezuela and, as with most of the economy, Cuba’s government had a monopoly over the trade. That arrangement collapsed in January when American forces captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela and threatened sanctions on anyone who sent oil to Cuba’s regime. Facing paralysis, the island’s government loosened its grip on private businesses, letting them import fuel for the first time since the revolution in 1959. America’s administration, in turn, authorised exporters to sell it to them.

American fuel exports to Cuba’s private sector are now rising swiftly. This, happily, is relieving a portion of the suffering that the sudden blockade has caused. The heavy fuel that is necessary to keep Cuba’s power stations running is not yet flowing. But cars are returning to the streets and you can hear the whirring of small generators.

As a result Mr Trump has gained leverage over a country that depends on America for food and remittances. Private business is growing, and not just in importing fuel. The state has leased some petrol stations to entrepreneurs. On October 12th it enacted a law to encourage private participation in the oil industry, from exploring and refining to selling. Cuba-watchers hope the government may next be forced to privatise power plants—and even the state’s oil-and-gas arm, Cupet.

A stronger private sector would in turn loosen the grip of Gaesa, a sprawling and corrupt military conglomerate. Marco Rubio, America’s secretary of state, says the deal on fuel is intended to put the private sector in a “privileged position”. Unfortunately, his boss has not got the memo. On September 30th, without explanation, Mr Trump’s administration reversed a 2024 rule that had let Cuban entrepreneurs bank with American institutions, forcing banks to freeze their accounts.

Mr Trump should backtrack and return to helping private firms grow. Many object that Cuba’s private businesses are a façade for the regime, or that America’s policies will create a new oligarchy. But the American administration can do much to weed out importers that are merely fronts for Cuba’s government. The announcement on October 7th that America had seized some 90 fuel shipments headed not for private buyers but for a state firm under sanctions is a welcome sign. On balance, it is better for Cubans if the children of the ruling class focus on getting rich rather than repressing them.

Another worry is that Mr Trump will settle for an America First arrangement, inspired by his deal with Venezuela’s interim government. That handed majority control of more than 65bn barrels of Venezuela’s oil reserves to a new American-backed company in which the Pentagon holds a 35% stake.

A new licence allows some Venezuelan oil to be resold to Cuba’s private sector. That could revive the Caracas-Havana route, only with the American government and American firms taking their cuts. Mr Trump would then be invested in keeping the oil flowing, whatever the situation in Cuba. Instead, private actors need the freedom to vie for business competitively.

A blockade with no end-game remains a recipe for humanitarian disaster. The Castro family and the ruling elite will be hard to dislodge. But America has found that strengthening the private sector in Cuba is the most effective tool available. Mr Trump should use it. ■

item.title: Millennials’ success deserves a toast (not the avocado sort)
item.description:
Leaders

Leaders | The comeback cohort Oct 15th 2026 Millennials, born between the early 1980s and mid-1990s, had a brutal coming of age. Many graduated in the wake of the global financial crisis. Youth unemployment rose above 50% in some parts of Europe, leading to talk of a “lost generation”. Living wi...
item.content:encoded:
Millennials’ success deserves a toast (not the avocado sort)

Leaders | The comeback cohort

Oct 15th 2026

Millennials, born between the early 1980s and mid-1990s, had a brutal coming of age. Many graduated in the wake of the global financial crisis. Youth unemployment rose above 50% in some parts of Europe, leading to talk of a “lost generation”. Living with their parents and deprived of the prospect of owning a home, they were lectured by unsympathetic elders not to spend so much money on brunch.

Today millennials, aged around 30-45, have dramatically turned their fortunes round. They earn more than any other recent generation did at the same age, and are catching up in terms of home-ownership. At the same time, millennial-era culture is enjoying a revival in television, music, gaming and even fashion, where their notoriously tight trousers are cool once again.

Some of this is simply the way of the world. As generations age, they get better jobs, earn more and buy homes. Millennials are not the first lot to reach middle age and revive the culture of their youth. The 1970s witnessed a 1950s revival, with a rock'n’roll renaissance, “Happy Days” and “Grease”. In the 1990s bell-bottoms and tie-dye emerged from the back of wardrobes. Nostalgia reliably runs on a two-decade timetable.

Yet the millennial comeback is different. True, part of it is luck. The generation’s early economic misfortune was later counterbalanced by serendipity, when the covid-19 pandemic triggered the early retirement of many older workers. The result was a senior-management vacuum—filled by millennials.

A bigger part of the story, however, is innovation and hard work. The leading lights of the tech industry, which has created enormous wealth, include many millennials. They account for more than twice the share of America’s billionaires that Gen X did at the same age. Tech’s next great leap, artificial intelligence, is likely only to strengthen their position. The bosses leading the revolution, such as Dario Amodei, Mark Zuckerberg and Sam Altman, are themselves millennials.

Tech has also boosted millennials’ cultural comeback. Online platforms encourage people to bathe in the content of their youth. YouTube and Spotify are nostalgia machines. Services like Netflix, with their vast libraries, introduce new generations to millennial hits like “The Big Bang Theory”, from 2007, which is the fifth-most streamed series in America this year. Meanwhile, social media have terrified Hollywood. Hence all those sequels and reboots—safer bets than original projects. “The Devil Wears Prada 2” is one of the world’s highest-grossing films this year.

Even those who dread the return of skinny jeans should cheer the millennial revival. The generation’s economic story shows that “lost” cohorts can find their way. Policymakers should note that millennials’ prospects improved thanks to markets and events, not the state-funded rescue that some once called for. As AI causes alarm about young people’s job opportunities, the millennial bounce offers a cautious cause for optimism.

Millennials’ cultural comeback has lessons, too. Many will look at the glut of 1990s reboots, such as a new “Baywatch” series, and feel that Hollywood’s creativity needs saving. But once more, technology is helping. The infinite breadth of online platforms means that you have plenty of alternatives if millennial favourites are not to your taste. And the vast back-catalogues stored on these platforms mean that the hits of every era are available to everyone. Twenty years ago, one generation bore the brunt of the financial crisis. Today, all generations should celebrate the millennials’ deserved rebound.■

item.content:encoded:
关于民粹主义的城市迷思

读者来信 | 精选通讯 2026年10月15日 欢迎通过电子邮件发送至letters@economist.com提交信件。了解更多关于我们如何处理您的来信。

亚历山大·赫夫纳认为，世界各地的市长是民主的捍卫者，而“威权主义者”在市政厅没有立足之地（《应邀撰文》，10月3日）。但他将民粹主义的概念局限于右翼类型。例如，他观察到“全球50个最大城市中没有一个由支持MAGA的市长管理”，这并不令人惊讶，因为其中只有7个城市由任何派别的共和党人管理。在这50位市长中，41位是民主党人，其中至少5位可归入民粹主义左翼阵营，包括纽约的佐赫兰·马姆达尼和芝加哥的布兰登·约翰逊。他举的德国例子也强化了这一点。柏林一直对德国选择党的民粹主义免疫，但在9月的选举中却屈服于民粹主义左翼，使左翼党成为最大政党。

赫夫纳对城市为何能坚守民主阵线的第一个解释是，城市拥有“更年轻、更多元、受教育程度更高的选民”。这只不过是用更冗长的方式说“以民主党为主”。他的第二个理由是，市长以更具体的政绩来评判，比如修复下水道，这似乎与他希望将市长职权扩展到住房、犯罪和气候等充满党派绊脚石的领域的愿望直接矛盾。最后，赫夫纳抨击那些“削弱”市长权力的州议会，并举了一个关键例子：得克萨斯州限制城市监管财产。我对此有疑问。如果休斯顿、奥斯汀、达拉斯和沃斯堡的市长可以自由复制旧金山或纽约的做法，今天的房地产市翅更有效吗？更重要的是，得克萨斯州的规则真的比许多市长珍视的“邻避主义”更少民粹色彩吗？

彼得·多纳霍

休斯顿

《经济学人》正确地指出，民主的力量在于通过选举而非暴力来疏导政治愤怒（10月3日）。只有当选民相信选举是合法的、对手有权执政、败者接受结果时，选票才胜过子弹。一旦这些假设被削弱，民主就可能不再是愤怒的出口，而成为愤怒的战场。意大利“铅色年代”的真正教训是，民主社会依赖于领导人和公民捍卫游戏规则，即使这些规则有利于政治对手。民主不会在人们愤怒时死亡；它会在人们不再相信失败是合法的时死亡。

费德里科·福尔尼

伦敦

《太热了，教授们受不了》（9月26日）提出了一个有趣的问题：为什么芬太尼致死案例在意大利如此罕见？然而，关于意大利黑手党已达成协议将其拒之门外的说法，超出了所提供证据的范围。你引用的宪兵指挥官说，贩毒者似乎避开芬太尼。这并不能证明教父之间存在协议，也无法解释贩毒者为何回避这种药物。意大利在2024年记录了2例与芬太尼相关的死亡，2025年为5例。但低数字并非意大利独有。一项在法兰西岛大区进行的研究在2017年至2021年间检查的12例死亡中检测到了芬太尼或其类似物。德国报告2024年有95例芬太尼相关死亡。西班牙在2023年检测到60名吸毒后死亡者体内含有芬太尼。这些数据不能直接比较，检测到芬太尼也不一定意味着它导致了死亡。然而，没有任何数据表明存在美国规模的那种疫情。如果意大利黑手党的协议是主要解释，为什么在其他欧洲国家芬太尼也相对稀少？

美国的历史提供了另一种解释。从20世纪90年代起，医生大规模开具阿片类止痛药，催生了大量使用阿片类药物的人群。一些人转而使用海洛因。大约从2013年起，非法制造的芬太尼通过非法市场蔓延，取代海洛因或与之混合。欧洲没有经历同样的阿片类药物处方激增。海洛因在欧洲大部分地区仍然可得，芬太尼并未在整个大陆大规模取代它。到目前为止，没有出现美国式疫情是欧洲的一种普遍模式，而不是意大利黑手党保护消费者的证据。永远不要相信教父。

费德里科·瓦雷泽

巴黎

英国工党内正在形成一种叙事，认为玛格丽特·撒切尔之前存在一个黄金时代（《巴杰特专栏》，10月3日）。这忽视了20世纪70年代是一个糟糕透顶的十年。通胀率超过25%，加之低增长，形成了滞胀。英国被称为“欧洲病夫”。我的抵押贷款利率是18%。每年都有罢工行动。邮政工人的罢工促使伦敦大公司创建了文件交换所，一种通过私人信使系统投递邮件的服务。码头工人、电工、电力工人：一场又一场大罢工。矿工罢工导致全国实行每周三天工作制。作为伦敦金融城一家小公司的合伙人，当工会切断电力时，我发现自己只能靠烛光工作，没有打字或通讯系统。工会领袖常与当时的首相在唐宁街共进午餐。大选来了又去：哈罗德·威尔逊、爱德华·希思、詹姆斯·卡拉汉。工资管制、物价和收入委员会、不满之冬、垃圾工甚至掘墓人的罢工，应有尽有。1979年撒切尔当选正是这一切的结果。她的政策至今仍极具争议。但有一点是清楚的：在她之前并没有黄金时代。

克里斯托弗·博丁顿

伦敦

作为一名设计“睡向未来”等项目的睡眠神经科学家，我看了巴特比关于如何像专业人士一样睡觉的备忘录后笑了（9月19日）。但最发人深省的发现并不是玩笑。当高级管理者在凌晨3点发送信息时，初级同事会早起回复，整个公司都睡得更差。我在无数组织中见过这种连锁反应。这就是为什么这类项目仍然急需，也是为什么许多项目令人失望。它们发放眼罩和追踪器，把睡眠当作每个员工的私人问题。更大的因素是领导行为。在我为一家咨询公司开展的睡眠项目中，管理层几乎没有以身作则，员工到周五就积累了七小时的睡眠债务。而领导完全以身作则的公司，员工几乎没有债务。公司应该对此慎重考虑。它应该从那些在凌晨3点发邮件的人开始。

埃尔斯·范德赫尔姆

睡眠神经科学家

瑞士卢塞恩

《经济学人》将新加坡描述为“一尘不染的城市国家”，并承认最近一篇学术论文发现某些公务员存在异常房产购买模式，其结论“其实并没有那么严重”（《公民不服从》，10月3日）。尽管如此，政府严肃对待这些所谓的“统计模式”，并正在调查是否存在任何实际不当行为。两位新加坡学者主动要求将自己的名字从论文的致谢中删除。《经济学人》声称这暗示新加坡学术文化存在“某种腐败”。但最新的QS世界大学排名将新加坡国立大学排在全球第10位，南洋理工大学排在第12位。这与《经济学人》的笼统描述难以相符。

吴志贤

新加坡驻伦敦最高专员

你们建议美国和中国的实验室披露安全事件，并让智能体逃出其沙箱的实验室承担经济责任（《人工智能军备竞赛能停止吗？》，9月19日）。医学试图两者兼得，但发现行不通。我在放射实验室工作了八年，检查AI在MRI扫描上绘制的肾脏。一个能完美勾画健康肾脏的模型，可能会悄悄漏掉一个布满囊肿的肿胀肾脏的边缘，而且错误不会自我标记。我们能发现这些失败，是因为学生可以不先问这是谁的错就指出一个看起来奇怪的体积。前沿实验室也不例外。工程师注意到智能体在试探其沙箱时，只有在不会给雇主带来代价的情况下才会报告。对危害外溢保持责任追究，但保护未发生事故的接近失误报告。否则事件会继续发生。我们只是不再听说它们。

赫里迪·德夫

纽约

丹·西蒙斯1989年出色的科幻小说《海伯利安》以人类在整个银河系的流散为背景。人类离开地球是因为一个被称为“大错误”的事件。剧透警告。那是人工智能。

丹尼斯·梅里特

马萨诸塞州谢尔本福尔斯

By Invitation

item.content:encoded:
美国国会如何防范AI灾难

邀稿｜直面终结者 2026年10月15日 多年来，人工智能科学家一直在警告：他们正在开发的技术，是他们不知道如何控制的技术。这些担忧在美国国会基本上被忽视。2024年，加利福尼亚州国会议员代表团采取了非同寻常的举措，请求州长加文·纽森否决当时一项待审的州级AI安全法案。他们说，这些风险是“假设性的”，终结者只是科幻小说。但今年夏天，一个OpenAI模型入侵了AI开发平台Hugging Face，这开始改变华盛顿的态度，也让公众感到恐惧。“事实是，”众议员罗·卡纳发推文说，“长期以来，我们中太多人没有充分重视AI安全倡导者的警告……我就是那许多人中的一员，我错了。”卡纳现在加入了来自两党的多位议员行列，共同提出了《前沿法案》，这是一项对前沿模型的雄心勃勃的监管法案，并旨在先发制人地取代各州的监管。参议员伯尼·桑德斯则提出了更为激进的限制AI发展的方案。这些提案都是好的开端。但它们既太多，又太少。现在就让各州的监管机构沉默还为时过早，而仅仅关注最强大模型带来的风险也不够。相反，我们需要一种方法，在总体上推进AI安全，同时避免AI科学家最担心的发展。国会的四项变革就能做到这一点，并为后续极其复杂的问题争取时间。

第一，国会应明确允许竞争者在安全技术改进期间达成放缓发展的协议。这类协议通常会引发反垄断风险。领先的AI实验室已将这一风险列为明确达成协议的障碍。只要这些讨论没有违反反垄断法的宗旨，就没有理由让不确定的反垄断责任迫使竞争对手陷入一场威胁人类的竞赛。第二，国会应禁止企业开发能够自行设计新AI模型的模型——“递归自我改进”技术——除非一个类似美国食品药品监督管理局的机构首先认证其安全性。至少在具有一定能力的模型上，我们不应冒险让自我改进的智能迅速超出我们的控制能力。第三，国会应确认科技公司对其技术造成的损害所面临的赔偿责任，并强制它们购买保险以覆盖潜在损害的代价。强制性保险将让市场来监督安全，当技术风险较低时，保险费也会更低。最后，国会应为AI实验室的吹哨人提供保护，使他们能够向监管机构或安全机构报告安全问题。吹哨人保护通常涵盖犯罪行为；而在AI安全上马虎行事不算犯罪。要了解正在发展的风险，唯一方法是保护那些愿意站出来的人。

反对监管的人会警告说，这只会帮助中国。这种观点反映了对中国AI发展现状的深刻无知。中国对AI技术的监管比美国正在考虑的任何措施都要严格得多。此外，中国的算力只是美国的一小部分。现在采取我们提议的步骤，将为双方就AI安全展开更认真的对话打开大门。这也可以推动美国的AI发展借鉴中国的重点方向，将技术更广泛地推广到制造业和开发中。那是一场关键的AI竞赛，而中国正在赢得这场竞赛。

让共和党人支持这四项变革应该是可能的。共和党参议员查尔斯·格拉斯利长期以来一直是吹哨人保护的领导者。同样，总统科技顾问委员会联合主席大卫·萨克斯已邀请领先实验室自行放缓发展，并坚持认为它们不会面临任何重大的反垄断责任。如果真是这样，那就没有理由不把他认为法律已经允许的事情明确化。

挑战在于中间两项变革。今天只有最强大的模型才有可能实现递归自我改进。但这是AI安全专家长期以来一直警告的“卢比孔河”——除非我们确信知道如何控制它，否则不能跨越。为什么要拿人类的命运去打赌我们不需要控制呢？至于保险，毫无疑问，仅靠私人市场无法提供覆盖AI风险所需的保单。但正如政府建立保险机制以促成核能发展一样，它也可以促成AI保险市场的形成。这将让开发者清楚地选择他们希望技术带来的风险。市场压力将推动一些开发者选择风险较低的替代方案。

所有这些必要的风险管理工作都不应由美国独自完成。在模型可能变得危险之前，测试、探查和理解模型行为的能力，是全世界共同承担的责任。英国、欧盟、加拿大、日本、韩国以及其他许多国家都已经建立了开展这项工作的机构，并开始相互分享方法和发现。美国应该处于这一网络的核心，而不是在国内重复做同样的工作。

美国需要愿意倾听那些最了解这些风险的人：开发这些技术的科学家，以及拥有所需专业知识的独立研究者。它需要超越党派分歧，认识到这一威胁是真实而全新的。当最接近技术的人士提出人类有10%的可能性终结时，我们必须倾听并采取行动。在那些AI科学家再次被证明正确之前。■

劳伦斯·莱西格是哈佛法学院的教授。约书亚·本吉奥是蒙特利尔大学的教授，也是LawZero的联合主席兼科学总监。

item.content:encoded:
唐纳德·特朗普或许能拯救加拿大

简报 | 新篇章 2026年10月15日

“我不是分离主义者，”布拉德·奥萨德丘克说。“但我厌倦了加拿大东部把我们当成受气包。”奥萨德丘克是阿尔伯塔省西部詹纳干旱草原上的一位牧场主。10月19日，这个以人均GDP衡量全国最富有的石油资源大省将举行公投。争议焦点在于省政府是否应启动一个最终可能让阿尔伯塔成为独立国家的进程。奥萨德丘克计划投赞成票。民调显示他属于少数派。民调普遍发现，至少三分之二的阿尔伯塔人不愿走上这条路。即使民调机构判断失误，独立也不会立即实现：还必须进行第二次具有约束力的公投，并可能与联邦政府进行长达数年的谈判。所有这些都提供了充足的退出通道。

然而，这次投票加剧了一个在更快乐的时光里偶尔被称为“无聊”的国家所面临的困境。微弱的失败可能助长独立运动，并鼓励法语区魁北克的分离主义者——他们在10月5日十多年来首次重新在该省掌权。加拿大受欢迎的总理马克·卡尼正忙于与美国的贸易战，其成本可能迅速升级。而背景则是加拿大经济多年停滞不前的表现。经通胀和汇率变动调整后，截至2025年的十年间，加拿大的人均GDP仅增长约4%，而美国为23%，经合组织（一个主要由富裕国家组成的俱乐部）平均为15%（见图表1）。最近一项研究得出结论，加拿大人已变得比阿拉巴马州人更穷，引起一片哗然。“我们并不是因为特朗普而经历了糟糕的几年，”右倾智库麦克唐纳-劳里尔研究所的菲利普·克罗斯说。“我们已经经历了糟糕的十年。” 罪魁祸首是生产率增长的长期低迷。在20世纪80年代，加拿大工人每小时产出约为美国同行的90%。到2022年，这一比例降至71%。根据经合组织的数据，2015年至2023年间，私营部门每小时工作的生产率每年仅增长0.8%。这同样低于富裕国家平均水平，也远低于美国（见图表2）。企业削减了投资，尤其是自2014年油价暴跌以来。克罗斯指出，2014年至2025年间，美国投资飙升51%，而加拿大仅微增4.2%。加拿大企业仅将GDP的约1%用于研发，仅为富裕国家典型水平的一半。低效企业受到省政府培育的层层监管的保护，免受竞争影响。这些监管推高了成本，并使受监管行业的从业者更难在首次获得执照的省份之外工作。1月份，国际货币基金组织得出结论，由于这些内部壁垒，加拿大实际上是在对自己征收9%的关税。

另一个可能拖累生产率的因素是近期大量相对低技能的工人涌入。疫情过后，贾斯廷·特鲁多领导的当时政府大幅增加移民，以帮助抱怨劳动力短缺的企业。2022年和2023年，人口以自20世纪50年代以来最快的速度增长，两年均激增超过100万人。如今人口已达4200万，比2020年高出10%，比十年前高出16%。劳动力储备的突然扩大，使得加拿大企业投资于长期能提高生产率的机器和培训的激励减弱。

人口激增也推高了本已高昂的住房成本。另一家右倾智库弗雷泽研究所发现，2021-24年的住房开工量与20世纪70年代大致相当，尽管年人口增长率是当时的三倍。高昂的住房成本减少了消费者支出，也让聪明的年轻才俊更有理由去国外碰运气，其中许多人去了美国。房价上涨可能也使资本从企业转移，因为砖瓦看起来是更好的投资。

加拿大的各分离运动各有其原因，但国家经济几乎未能提供任何慰藉。阿尔伯塔省的挫败感已积压数十年。该省拥有加拿大12%的人口，但去年贡献了约四分之一的经济增长和出口。许多阿尔伯塔人感到，开发其自然资源的机会（例如通过新建管道）被加拿大东部更国际化大都市的人所阻挠，他们的选票在过去一个世纪中有三分之二的时间让自由党政府执掌联邦。这种感觉加剧了关于金钱的不满：阿尔伯塔省居民向联邦预算缴纳的比他们获得的公共服务更多。尤其令人恼火的是，其中一些资金用于支持那些出于环境担忧（以及其他焦虑）而强烈反对在加拿大西部钻探和采矿的人。

阿尔伯塔的独立团体包括一些铁杆的MAGA风格组织。8月份，《经济学人》参加了一个在悬挂着蓝色阿尔伯塔旗帜的社区中心举行的疯狂会议。演讲者抨击移民。他们称加拿大总理为“共产主义者”、“粉红分子”和“全球主义者”，然后转战当地酒吧。但独立运动也有更主流的倡导者（批评者称他们为“穿西装的分离主义者”）。9月29日，约300名农民和牧场主参加了位于阿尔伯塔省首府埃德蒙顿以东约2000人口小镇托菲尔德的一个社区大厅的活动。他们排队与来自该省最大城市卡尔加里的戴眼镜律师基思·威尔逊握手，威尔逊已成为独立运动领导人之一。威尔逊否认投票支持分离会严重损害阿尔伯塔的经济。他说，公司不能只是拿起该省的自然资源然后离开。

这就是唐纳德·特朗普与加拿大的贸易战在18个多月前爆发时的背景。出口约占加拿大GDP的三分之一。2025年，超过70%的出口商品销往美国。在西方主要经济体中，加拿大的出口多元化程度最低。几十年来，加拿大政界人士一直对这种依赖感到担忧，但在减少依赖方面进展甚微。特朗普对加拿大商品征收的关税（以及他关于吞并加拿大的闲谈）时涨时落。但在8月份，他对约200亿美元商品（约占加拿大对美出口的5%）征收50%关税时，关税急剧上升。进一步的增加迫在眉睫：特朗普承诺，如果加拿大未能做出未具体说明的让步，将在1月1日将对加拿大汽车行业的关税从25%提高到50%。

这些攻击正在伤害加拿大经济，但并非致命。由于特朗普本人于2018年签署的《美墨加协定》，大多数双边贸易仍然自由。根据耶鲁预算实验室的数据，加拿大出口的平均关税接近8%。专业服务公司毕马威的分析师认为，平均关税每提高一个百分点，加拿大的增长率就会降低0.15至0.2个百分点。加拿大央行预计2026年GDP增长0.7%，明年增长1.8%。这对受影响最严重的行业（如钢铁和汽车制造）或受灾最严重的省份来说，几乎算不上什么安慰。魁北克商品的实际有效关税可能是全国平均水平的两倍。有理由担心争端进一步升级。一个严峻但遥远的设想涉及整个《美墨加协定》的中止。与此同时，持续的不确定性是加拿大急需的投资面临的全新障碍。

尽管特朗普试图从加拿大拿走一切，但他的嘲讽和攻击也给了加拿大一些回报：一种广泛的、汹涌的愤怒，如果明智地加以利用，可能使许多问题更容易解决。特朗普第二次就职后不久，加拿大国旗的销量开始飙升。（通常情况下，“在加拿大，没人想在二月买国旗，因为挂旗时会冻掉手指，”经营一家国旗制作公司的马特·斯基普说。）关税来袭时，加拿大人放弃了美国酒；超市开始在产品上贴上醒目的“加拿大制造”标签。

也许没有谁比卡尼先生从这种民族情绪中受益更多。2025年初，在特朗普就职前几天，特鲁多因民调数字糟糕而面临压力，宣布将辞去总理和自由党领袖职务。他的继任者的任期似乎注定短暂：选举即将举行，反对党保守党支持率高涨。民调机构前一年曾表示，几乎没有什么加拿大人能认出卡尼的照片。但他不仅赢得了党魁职位，还在随后的大选中获胜，得益于一波反特朗普、团结在国旗周围的义愤。前魁北克省省长、现任总理顾问让·沙雷说：“我在2025年初告诉他，‘你是加拿大政坛最幸运的家伙。’”即使现在，保守党仍处于困境：多名议员倒戈加入自由党。最近一项民调得出结论，70%的加拿大人支持卡尼政府。这为他提供了巨大机会，推动改革，这些改革可能在特朗普离任后长期惠及加拿大。

总理的首要任务是捍卫加拿大的利益，同时不让与特朗普的争吵失控。加拿大是为数不多的对美国采取报复性关税的国家之一。但它也做出了让步。去年，它废除了本会让美国科技公司付出代价的数字服务税。它在一场关于底特律和安大略省之间一座桥梁的离奇争执中受辱，特朗普政府拒绝开放该桥，直到加拿大同意追溯性地放弃其部分通行费收入。

特朗普反复无常的恶意使卡尼的主要经济计划更加紧迫：让加拿大增长更快。在他执政的头几个月，他取消了消费者碳税，取消了将最高资本利得税率提高到67%的计划，并削减了最低所得税率。他试图削减政府的日常开支，为投资腾出更多资金。到2029年，他希望联邦公务员队伍比2024年峰值时减少10%。他加倍推进早先减少移民的计划，并承诺在未来十年将住房开工量翻倍，达到每年50万套。

9月，在一次外国投资者聚会上，卡尼宣布了一项“生产率超级扣除”政策，允许企业立即注销新设备支出。这是建立在去年推出的“超级扣除”基础上的。新规则将大幅降低有效企业税率。与此同时，《建设加拿大法案》加快了对政府认为“符合国家利益”的大型项目的审批。10月1日，卡尼在阿尔伯塔石油矿区一辆巨大的矿用卡车旁摆姿势宣布，一条向加拿大西海岸输送石油的新管道成为首批获得这一认定的项目之一。他说建设应在不到一年内开始。这可谓一石二鸟：通过向亚洲出口更多能源来提振经济，同时安抚不满的阿尔伯塔人。

卡尼还在寻求减少加拿大对美国的依赖，提升其在世界上的地位。他的政府希望到2035年将对其他国家的出口翻倍，达到每年6000亿加元（4200亿美元）。8月，卡尼声称他的政府在五大洲达成了20多项贸易和安全协议（尽管有些非常模糊）。1月，他访问了中国——这是近十年来加拿大总理首次访华——在那里他为加拿大菜籽油等商品争取到了关税降低。3月，他在德里重置与印度的关系，该关系于2023年在加拿大指控印度特工在温哥华附近杀害一名锡克教活动人士后破裂。加拿大表示，目标是到2030年将两国贸易额翻倍至约500亿美元。最新的亲密关系是与欧盟——加拿大第二大贸易伙伴（尽管仅占加拿大商品出口的约6%）。9月，卡尼在斯特拉斯堡欧洲议会发表了一篇雄辩的演讲。欧盟委员会主席乌尔苏拉·冯德莱恩暗示，加拿大有朝一日可能成为欧盟的“准成员”，尽管这似乎更多是一种修辞手法而非计划。本月晚些时候的欧盟-加拿大峰会上无疑将讨论更直接的机会。这些机会包括加快关键矿产投资和更紧密的防务合作。2月，加拿大成为唯一加入欧盟1500亿欧元（1680亿美元）SAFE计划的非欧洲国家，该计划向寻求增强军事实力的志同道合政府提供低息贷款。

整饬军队是提升加拿大世界地位的重要部分。（卡尼承诺，这也将为加拿大企业提供大量机会。）2024年，军费开支约为GDP的1.3%，是北约最低水平之一。今年，在加拿大历史上最大的年度国防开支增长之一之后，军费跃升至2%。现在计划是到2030年尽快再次翻倍，达到4%。加拿大将领们很高兴：在多年精打细算之后，他们现在的主要问题是在挥霍开支时确保物有所值。政府还希望减少武装部队对美国装备的依赖。

这一切意味着什么？多伦多大学的约瑟夫·斯坦伯格表示，企业“超级扣除”对投资者来说意义重大。他担心经济计划的其他部分不过是“公告，或创建旨在最终加快事情进展的新机构”。加快重大项目的努力值得欢迎，但并未改变政治家“挑选赢家”而非为所有人改善商业环境的习惯。卡尼的好斗言论深受普通加拿大民众和厌倦特朗普的外国人的欢迎。但商界人士和政策专家认为，激怒美国那位脸皮薄的总统风险很高，却几乎没什么好处。MLI的克罗斯说，企业不会“仅仅因为有人发表了漂亮的演讲”就投入数十亿美元的投资。加拿大的报复性关税也让经济学家产生分歧。许多人认为，这增加了加拿大人的苦难，却对改变特朗普的想法无济于事。在对抗特朗普方面，其他中等强国也不倾向于效仿卡尼。

卡尼仍然容易受到有关生活成本的抱怨的影响，这是加拿大人一贯将其列为头号担忧的问题。他被指责专横，例如只是偶尔出现在议会。原住民领导人抱怨说，关于经济发展的协商不够充分。然而，退一步看，毫无疑问，在许多方面，卡尼正在取得进展，这在两年前似乎是想都不敢想的。尽管他的大部分计划与反对党的政策相似，但他广泛的支持使他能够比反对党可能敢于尝试的走得更远、更快。前魁北克省长沙雷相信，加拿大人有朝一日可能会感谢美国总统把他们从沉睡中震醒。“加拿大的惯性力量已经变得势不可挡，”他说。“特朗普现在告诉我们，我们别无选择，只能改变。”■

item.content:encoded:
亚洲各国政府能否防止粮食冲击？

亚洲 | 中暑 2026年10月15日 今年五月，约两吨死鱼漂浮在柬埔寨一个湖泊的水面上。上个月，在印度尼西亚，另一个湖泊水位下降，露出了长期被淹没的村庄Somang的废墟。在菲律宾，官员们警告首都马尼拉的居民，他们的供水可能很快减少。这些事件——均由更炎热、更干燥的天气引起——看似孤立，但综合起来，它们指向了厄尔尼诺可能给亚洲带来的浩劫。这种气候模式是一种自然循环现象。每隔几年，东太平洋上空的风向转变就会导致南亚和东南亚大部分地区出现更炎热、更干燥的天气。今年的这次事件始于五月，预计下月达到峰值，来势异常凶猛。根据一项每日指标，太平洋海面温度异常已超过有记录以来所有以往事件的峰值（见图表1）。世界气象组织预计此次厄尔尼诺将持续到明年二月。 影响将是全球性的，但亚洲尤为脆弱：数亿人口以农场为生，且各国政府仍在应对伊朗战争带来的能源冲击。在该地区许多地方，厄尔尼诺已经造成损害。印度季风（提供全年近70%的降雨量）结束时的降雨量比正常水平低了约13%——为十年来最干燥。卫星数据显示，印度尼西亚正经历11年来最严重的火灾季节（见图表2）。菲律宾官员表示，已有七个省份遭遇干旱，且到明年初整个国家可能陷入干旱。最直接的影响将体现在粮食上。依赖降雨的农民将受到最严重的冲击，尤其是在印度尼西亚，那里的主要水稻作物在10月至12月间种植，恰逢厄尔尼诺高峰期。但灌溉农田也未能幸免，因为缺乏降雨正在耗尽水库。在泰国中部，这促使政府要求农民今年不要种植第二季水稻。 这一切都叠加在伊朗战争对燃料和化肥供应的扰乱之上。世界银行预计今年化肥价格将比去年平均上涨38%。更高的投入成本和极端天气正在挤压农民收入，同时也助长了食品通胀（见图表3）。印度的年度食品通胀率从1月的2.1%升至8月的6%；斯里兰卡在9月达到了7%。然而更大的担忧是供应。泰国银行开泰银行估计，从现在到明年年中，泰国大米产量可能下降18%。泰国有充足的储备，但其他国家几乎没有可依赖的缓冲。根据美国农业部的数据，孟加拉国的大米库存仅为其年消费量的不到4%。为了评估哪个国家最脆弱，《经济学人》为亚洲11个新兴经济体构建了一个“脆弱性指数”。它结合了两组衡量标准：厄尔尼诺可能对其经济造成多大伤害（基于农业对其的重要性），以及政府能在多大程度上缓冲冲击（基于财政空间指标和福利体系的覆盖范围）。斯里兰卡、孟加拉国和柬埔寨表现最差（饱受战争蹂躏的缅甸数据不完整，否则它很可能位居榜首）。不出所料，较富裕的国家——泰国和马来西亚——表现最好。痛苦的形式各不相同。在印度，风险主要落在农民身上；在菲律宾和孟加拉国，则落在消费者身上。 厄尔尼诺将产生超出粮食和农业的影响。亚洲开发银行（ADB）警告称，它可能加剧能源冲击：河流干涸减少了水电产出，而高温又提高了空调需求，推动各国燃烧更多煤炭。公共卫生也面临风险。印度尼西亚火灾产生的烟雾笼罩了东南亚部分地区；10月12日，新加坡的空气质量被评为全球最差，甚至比德里还差。经济损失可能巨大，尤其是因为各国政府缺乏吸收冲击的能力。一项对1997年厄尔尼诺的研究发现，它在接下来五年内给全球经济造成了近6万亿美元的损失——亚洲承担了其中很大一部分。联合国估计，如果今年的粮食和能源价格冲击完全转嫁给家庭（即，如果取消补贴和其他救助措施），全球将新增约1.32亿人陷入贫困，其中9100万在亚洲。随着政府债务膨胀，避免这一情景将变得更加困难。好消息是政府能看到危机的到来。亚洲开发银行的Roshen Fernando表示，更好的数据和预测意味着政策制定者比以往厄尔尼诺事件时准备更充分。除了建立大米缓冲库存，政府还在尝试直接帮助农民。印度正在引导干旱地区的种植者转向种植豆类和其他作物；与此同时，菲律宾正在分发抗旱种子。 资金也需要提前安排。灾害基金往往只在灾害发生后才会发放。Fernando先生表示，政府应该专门为厄尔尼诺预留资金。这可以通过在高峰期到来前协商紧急信贷额度和灾害保险来实现。尤其有价值的是“预期行动”，即在预测突破预定阈值（如水库水位）时释放现金或其他援助。联合国认为，以这种方式每花费1美元，可以节省高达7美元的损失和后续援助。这类计划已在非洲和中美洲试行。但在亚洲，其覆盖范围有限——部分原因是缺乏资金。今年6月，联合国世界粮食计划署及其粮食及农业组织寻求2.02亿美元，以保护包括阿富汗、巴基斯坦和菲律宾在内的22个国家的880万人。迄今仅筹集到4000万美元。随着富裕国家捐助者收紧钱袋子，预防措施成为最先被削减的项目之一。一个多世纪前，一场特别强烈的厄尔尼诺引发了饥荒，导致印度、中国和其他地方数千万人死亡。那主要是因为没有人预见到它的到来，也不知道该怎么做。如今，一个远更富裕的亚洲知道即将发生什么。但预测只有在政府和捐助者据此采取行动时才有用。■ 如需独家报道亚洲政治、经济和安全内容，请订阅我们的每周订阅者专属通讯《亚洲简报》。

item.title: India’s government fails to crush Gen Z protests
item.description:
Asia

Asia | A vote protest Oct 15th 2026 MICROPHONES SHOVED in their faces, the youngsters raced to say their soundbites on democratic rights. Then the police van sped off with them still in mid-sentence. “That’s the only way to protest now—we just go get detained,” shrugged one. On October 10th in D...
item.content:encoded:
India’s government fails to crush Gen Z protests

Asia | A vote protest

Oct 15th 2026

MICROPHONES SHOVED in their faces, the youngsters raced to say their soundbites on democratic rights. Then the police van sped off with them still in mid-sentence. “That’s the only way to protest now—we just go get detained,” shrugged one. On October 10th in Delhi, drones filled the skies and tens of thousands of security men and women patrolled the strangely silent city below. India’s capital witnessed its most sweeping crackdown on peaceful protest for many years.

After 12 years in power, Narendra Modi, India’s prime minister, faces a challenge from Gen-Z protesters. In July the newly formed Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth movement, staged mass protests against a corrupt exam system and poor job prospects, and eventually forced the education minister to resign. This time, the CJP is riding a wave of public anger against the voting system, which it says is rigged. The authorities are also better prepared. As soon as the CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, and his two lieutenants touched down at Delhi airport to lead the crowds at a planned rally, police arrived to snatch them away. While most of the roughly 5,000 detainees got out by nightfall, the Cockroach trio was held for 24 hours.

Central Delhi felt like a city under siege: borders sealed, internet jammed, 45 metro stations locked and loudspeakers blasting out warnings. Police bruised opposition leaders and briefly nabbed journalists and lawyers. Scattered protests emerged like flash mobs, only for baton-wielding officers to disperse them.

Though the Cockroaches were squashed over the weekend, India’s opposition alliance, led by the Congress party’s Rahul Gandhi, gathered tens of thousands for a march on October 12th. They, too, demanded that Gyanesh Kumar, the chief of India’s Election Commission, resign; that the voter-verification drive he has managed must be scrapped; and that the law which, in effect, let Mr Modi hand-pick him should go. Over the past year, a “special intensive revision” of voter lists has deleted more than 130m names, many rightly, since they were duplicates or dead people. But very many wrongfully.

The government, like the commission, denies the allegations. Kiren Rijiju, a BJP minister, calls the protests—which were refused police permission—a gimmick by those who keep losing elections. Batting away comparisons to the Emergency of the 1970s, when Indira Gandhi suspended democracy, he says: “This is not an emergency, this is normal law and order.”

For India’s long moribund opposition, the rallies against vote chori (theft) are about saving democracy and the republic. But the marches also express a more diffuse anger at years of perceived governmental missteps. Rally-goers raise shoddy schooling, jobless growth, women’s safety, minority rights and unease at India’s turn towards Hindu nationalism.

The upstart Cockroaches and India’s established opposition have both vowed to protest until the election chief resigns. But Mr Kumar is virtually unsackable, because the prime minister stands by him, for now. And the authorities are doubling down. On October 14th Mr Dipke’s two lieutenants were sentenced to five days in jail on trespassing charges. To Mr Dipke, the original Cockroach, the spectacle of the crackdown suggests the government has something to hide. “Narendra Modi and Amit Shah [the home minister] are waging a war on their countrymen just to save one Gyanesh Kumar,” he says.

The opposition’s bigger ambition concerns the national election of 2029. “People finally understand how the BJP is stealing elections,” argues a close adviser to Rahul Gandhi. ■

item.title: Two Japanese towns offer lessons for shrinking countries
item.description:
Asia

Asia | Demographic doubts Oct 15th 2026 LESS THAN 40km separates the towns of Nanporo and Yubari, on Japan’s northernmost island of Hokkaido, but their fates could hardly have diverged further. Nanporo, a tranquil commuter town east of Sapporo, the regional capital, is growing its native populat...
item.content:encoded:
Two Japanese towns offer lessons for shrinking countries

Asia | Demographic doubts

Oct 15th 2026

LESS THAN 40km separates the towns of Nanporo and Yubari, on Japan’s northernmost island of Hokkaido, but their fates could hardly have diverged further. Nanporo, a tranquil commuter town east of Sapporo, the regional capital, is growing its native population at one of the fastest rates in the country. Yubari, a former coal-mining hub that went bankrupt in 2007, has seen its population decline by 95% from its peak. Their contrasting trajectories offer lessons for local life in an era of demographic shrinkage.

Start in Nanporo. The town’s population fell from around 10,000 in 1998 to fewer than 7,400 over the next quarter-century. But in recent years the trend has reversed: by last year, the population had ticked back up to 8,400. Nanporo was one of only nine out of 179 municipalities in Hokkaido to see population growth in 2020-25. It was the only one of those nine to do so without substantial foreign immigration. Meanwhile, Japan as a whole lost some 3m people over the same period.

A sense of optimism is palpable at the Hareppa indoor playground in the town’s central park. Sunlight streams through the new building’s floor-to-ceiling windows, lighting up a gaggle of children clambering up a wooden playhouse under a vaulted ceiling. In the adjoining café and library, a mum and young son peruse a shelf of children’s books: “The Very Hungry Caterpillar”, “Library Lion” and a popular Japanese series called “The Encyclopedia of Big Crises”.

A combination of structural advantages and targeted policy initiatives has helped Nanporo solve its own big crisis. While offering the peaceful capaciousness of the countryside, the town sits comfortably within the economic orbit of Sapporo, less than an hour’s drive away. Local leaders recognised that could appeal to young families, and implemented several incentives to attract them.

Many municipalities elsewhere in Japan have tried such measures, but Nanporo’s have been effective because its efforts were sustained and unique, reckons Saito Takashi, an official. Couples where both partners are under 40 years old, or with children of middle school age or younger, can receive up to ¥2m ($12,500) towards home construction; unused plots of land held in a prefectural land bank are sold at a steep discount. Parents also get 10kg of rice every year, a meaningful treat when rice prices have caused national anxiety.

The Tatsuki family are among the new arrivals. Aoi and Yamato moved to Nanporo with their young son last year, drawn by the combination of proximity to Sapporo and support for young families. They built a home and opened a café on its ground floor, where they do brisk business serving lunch sets of grilled fish and freshly-baked desserts. “It would have been super-expensive to do the same in Sapporo,” Mr Tatsuki says. After seeing the conditions, Mr Tatsuki’s older sister decided to move to Nanporo as well.

Yet Nanporo’s growth has come from migrants moving in, rather than a baby boom. Last year the town still saw twice as many deaths as births. With the national population shrinking, one municipality’s gain is another’s loss. There is a “competitive dynamic”, Mr Saito acknowledges. Not everywhere can be Nanporo.

Many places will be more like Yubari. Its population peaked in 1960 at some 117,000. (Though the size of a town now, it still carries the city designation as a relic of its past glory.) After the last coal mine closed in 1990, Yubari tried to reinvent itself as a tourist destination; mismanagement left it bankrupt. As part of a nationally administered restructuring plan, officials closed schools, halted bus routes and shut the local museum. Cutting services only speeded the decline, laments Yubari’s current mayor, Atsuya Tsukasa.

Since 2022, when Nanporo’s tide began to turn, Yubari has seen its population shrink from around 7,000 to just 5,600. More than half the remaining residents are over 65. “Almost no one is moving in, everyone is leaving,” says Noda Masaru, an entrepreneur. “And when you know the population is going down, you aren’t going to start a business, you’re going to close it.”

Yubari’s case is extreme, but hardly unique. The Population Strategy Council, a group of business and civic leaders, reported in 2024 that some 40% of Japan’s municipalities risk disappearing, given the outflow of young people. “I don’t see any prospect for reversing the trend—it’s not just Yubari, look at small towns across Japan,” Mr Atsuya says. “The question is how to survive in that context.”

While Nanporo, thanks to its favourable location near a regional hub, can realistically pursue revitalisation, for Yubari the task is to manage an inevitable further decline, for instance by becoming more compact. “We need to live in a more connected way,” Mr Atsuya says. In an era of population shrinkage, growth can no longer be the only measure of success. ■

item.title: Myanmar’s dictator tries diplomacy
item.description:
Asia

Asia | Charmless offensive Oct 15th 2026 MIN AUNG HLAING is keen to get into the world’s good books. The dictator, who seized power in Myanmar in 2021, underwent a makeover earlier this year. He quit the army and made himself president following a rigged election. Now he has gone on a diplomatic...
item.content:encoded:
Myanmar’s dictator tries diplomacy

Asia | Charmless offensive

Oct 15th 2026

MIN AUNG HLAING is keen to get into the world’s good books. The dictator, who seized power in Myanmar in 2021, underwent a makeover earlier this year. He quit the army and made himself president following a rigged election. Now he has gone on a diplomatic blitz within Asia and is talking to America. Calls to end military atrocities have gone unheeded; but the despot has some cards to play.

One is taking back those who have fled Myanmar’s war and economic collapse. This won Mr Min Aung Hlaing a visit on October 7th-8th to Malaysia, formerly his biggest critic in the region. Anwar Ibrahim, Malaysia’s prime minister, received him in return for a deal on repatriating thousands of Myanmar nationals, a bid to fend off local anger about the migrants.

Mr Anwar pleaded pragmatism, but the dictator’s red-carpet welcome was a step towards his rehabilitation among leaders of the Association of South-East Asian Nations (ASEAN). The Malaysia visit followed ones in the past four months to Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and Vietnam.

Other cards include fighting online scams and selling rare earths. These have helped lure America into talks with the regime. Michael Vance, the State Department’s intelligence chief, met Mr Min Aung Hlaing in September. Mr Vance’s visit was ostensibly to secure the release from prison of Adam Castillo, a businessman. But the budding dialogue is focused on scam centres and extracting minerals.

A rapprochement would be key to lessening Myanmar’s reliance on China, which has propped up the regime amid its heavy losses to rebels. That help has come with high-handed orders to close scam centres targeting Chinese citizens. It is unlikely that America will have any more luck than China in getting them closed. Scam profits have allowed the centres to buy off regime officials, allegedly including the former head of its anti-scams committee.

Myanmar’s rare-earth deposits, meanwhile, are largely beyond the regime’s reach, in areas controlled by ethnic armed groups, and are locked into Chinese supply chains. American officials may simply be using the minerals to get noticed by Donald Trump. “Everyone knows the White House and president are fixated on rare earths,” says a former Washington-based official with Myanmar experience. “That’s what everyone, including me, would throw out in meetings to get attention.”

Mr Min Aung Hlaing is also holding his strongest card in reserve. The trading of Mr Castillo shows an appetite for hostage diplomacy—and there is one prisoner who far outranks the rest. Aung San Suu Kyi, who led Myanmar between 2016 and 2021, has been detained since the coup. If freed, odds are that she would be barred from politics. But her release might provide the symbolic win that ASEAN and others need to wash their hands of Myanmar’s atrocious human-rights record and get back to business as usual. ■

item.title: The limits of India’s diaspora power
item.description:
Asia

Asia | Ashoka Oct 15th 2026 THE INDIAN diaspora, which numbers around 37m, is the world’s biggest. It may also be the most successful. It has a compelling case to make, especially in America, home to more than 3m people born in India. The median Indian-American household earns $151,000 annually,...
item.content:encoded:
The limits of India’s diaspora power

Asia | Ashoka

Oct 15th 2026

THE INDIAN diaspora, which numbers around 37m, is the world’s biggest. It may also be the most successful. It has a compelling case to make, especially in America, home to more than 3m people born in India. The median Indian-American household earns $151,000 annually, around 75% more than the figure for America as a whole. And many Indian-Americans occupy top jobs in business, technology and politics—think of Sundar Pichai, Satya Nadella, Zohran Mamdani and Kash Patel.

Such achievements are celebrated back in India, not just by relatives but also by a proud nation. Newspaper reports and WhatsApp forwards diligently catalogue the accomplishments of anyone with an Indian connection, however remote. Recent examples include Navi Pillay, the South African judge awarded this year’s Nobel peace prize, whose ancestors left India in the 19th century, and Anil Menon, the world’s first Malayali astronaut, a reference to his parents’ origins in the south of India.

The state encourages such enthusiasm. For years after independence, India tended to look down on its diaspora, disparaging emigrants for deserting the homeland and contributing to a brain drain. But as their numbers grew and the economy boomed, the relationship changed. In the 2000s, during the Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP) first term in power nationally, the party sought stronger ties with Indians abroad as a way of advancing India’s interests and boosting its own coffers (overseas Indians are believed to be enthusiastic donors to the party). Under Narendra Modi, those efforts have become more intense. The prime minister’s foreign trips often include rallies in stadiums packed with adoring non-resident Indians (NRIs).

To the BJP and indeed to many Indians, the success of NRIs is yet another indicator of India’s inevitable rise. But, viewed differently, it is also an indictment of the country’s inability to hold on to its talent. A study in 2023 found that of the 1,000 highest scorers in the 2010 entrance exam for the Indian Institutes of Technology, the country’s top engineering colleges, 36% were living abroad eight years later. Among the top 100, the share was 62%.

Similarly, the accomplishments of Indian-origin bosses abroad reveal dysfunction at home. Given the size of India’s economy, its businesses punch well below their weight. Of the world’s 500 biggest firms by market capitalisation, India is home to only eight. China has 41, America 234. One reason is that many Indian companies, whether small or large, are run as “lala” operations, family fiefs lacking professional management. Another is that the state has failed to create the conditions—from infrastructure to regulation—needed for them to flourish.

Emigration makes up for some of these failures. Remittances amount to 4% of India’s GDP (compared with 0.2% in China) and support millions of households. During crises, including the recent shock from the Iran war, diaspora cash has been particularly helpful. Migration has served as a social safety-valve, easing pressure on the labour market by giving educated Indians a chance of outward mobility.

It may now be shutting. The Trump administration has clamped down on migration. On October 8th it suspended tech firms, including several Indian ones, from sponsoring workers for permanent residency, accusing them of immigration fraud. Australia and Canada are restricting student visas. And it is not just potential migrants who are being targeted. Racism and resentment are fuelling hate campaigns on social media, especially in America.

The diaspora can do little to stem the hate, let alone advance India’s interests. In America it has failed to persuade the Trump administration to adopt policies favourable to India. Indeed just last month Congress in Washington passed legislation allowing 100% tariffs on India for buying Russian oil. The diaspora may be large and even influential, but it is no diplomatic corps.

Mr Modi has hailed his overseas audience as rashtradoot, or emissaries of India. But for all their attachment to India, few in the diaspora want to return to a country where decent jobs are scarce and cities unliveable. Those are the same factors contributing to frustrations among youngsters in India who are increasingly expressing their anger on the streets. Celebrating success abroad may feel good, but a real reason for national pride would be for Indians to flourish at home. ■

item.content:encoded:
中国正在大规模变废为宝

中国 | 回收超级大国 2026年10月15日 欧盟担心中国大量出口廉价电动汽车。10月12日，欧盟表示将于12月起对中国混合动力汽车进口实施每年35万辆的配额限制。预计这将使其市场份额保持在10%以下。但欧盟也对中国在制造这些汽车所需关键矿物上的主导地位感到担忧。越来越多的电动汽车将很快被报废和替换。粉碎其电池可得到“黑粉”，从中可以回收并再利用锂、钴、镍等有价值金属。从下个月起，欧盟将加大这种废料出口的难度。其目的是鼓励在欧洲本土附近进行更多黑粉加工（目前大部分黑粉被运往亚洲）。8月，已禁止中国电动汽车但仍进口大量中国电池的美国，也全面禁止了黑粉出口。然而，中国不太可能受损。据预测机构国际能源署称，到2050年，黑粉可能满足全球电池金属需求的20-30%。因此，中国正在大力提升其回收产业，不仅是为了保障电池金属的供应，也是为了保障稀土及其他多种材料的供应。其目标是让中国经济减少“线性”模式（原材料制成产品后被丢弃），而更多转向“循环”模式（关闭循环，使回收废料替代原材料）。曾经，回收利用是出于对污染的担忧。如今，在全球争相获取建设高科技经济所需材料的背景下，安全已成为主要动机。中国在垃圾处理方面积累了来之不易的经验。它的垃圾产量超过世界任何地方：约占全球城市垃圾的15%（从家庭垃圾桶里的东西到街道清扫物），以及全球工业废料（如拆迁碎料、工厂废水、废金属、矿渣和灰烬）的四分之一以上。20世纪80年代，中国开始进口废料，接手富裕国家不要的硬件、纸张和塑料。一个庞大的非正规回收行业应运而生，主要由在垃圾堆中翻捡的拾荒者主导。许多废料最终被填埋或露天焚烧，浸出有毒化学品并产生有毒烟雾。2011年，一部中国纪录片发现，北京周边垃圾场的有机废物被转化为油并出售给餐馆。2013年，出于对日益增长的公众愤怒的警惕，中国宣布“向污染宣战”，并发布了首个创建循环经济的全面国家计划。电子产品被引导至新的“城市矿山”区域进行安全拆解；生活垃圾被送往专门工厂焚烧发电；垃圾填埋比例开始下降。2017年，中国启动“国门利剑”行动，停止大部分塑料进口（2021年全面禁止固体废物进口）。官方媒体宣称中国“不再是垃圾场”。过去五年，中国大多数城市已推出生活垃圾强制分类。在垃圾管理方面，中国仍远远落后于干净整洁的欧洲国家（尽管很难说落后多少，因为它不公布详细的全国回收数据）。其较贫困的农村地区仍常常垃圾遍地。但官员们至少让中国大城市变得更干净、更宜居。现在，他们的重心正转向为了安全而进行回收利用。7月，中国发布了一份到2030年的循环经济发展规划。该规划指出：“资源安全的重要性日益凸显，而地缘政治动态……日趋复杂严峻。”这一判断基于两点考虑。第一，中国希望在从机器人到风力涡轮机等高科技制造领域占据主导地位。第二，要实现这一目标，必须确保原材料供应、铺设更多电力线路并建设更多数据中心。这需要大量铝、铜、电池金属和稀土。虽然中国控制着这些材料的大部分全球精炼产能，但其大部分矿石依赖进口。与此同时，许多西方国家希望减少对中国工厂的依赖。官员们担心它们可能会试图扼制中国的供应。去年，一家国有研究机构的研究人员曾表示，如果不进行回收利用，中国将“在未来不断面临被卡脖子的问题”。 中国希望通过回收利用，到2030年每年供应5.1亿吨工业材料，比目前水平高出约三分之一。较容易的部分是扩大钢铁、铜和铝的回收利用：这类工作已是成熟产业。回收更多塑料稍显棘手，但值得去做，以帮助中国减少石油进口。最困难的部分将是管理日益汹涌的电子垃圾浪潮。到2030年，中国预计每年将产生50万吨风力涡轮机废料、100万吨电动汽车电池废料和150-200万吨太阳能电池板废料——占全球总量的很大份额。中国已经大量生产这些产品，这一事实应使回收变得更为简单。工厂可以调整设计，使产品日后更易拆解。许多电池生产技术（如使用酸和热来分离贵重金属）也用于电池回收。以全球最大电池制造商宁德时代为例。这家中国公司的大部分销售在国内，最终将由宁德时代的子公司邦普处理，邦普是全球最大的电池回收商。这样的安排帮助中国建成了全球85%的电池回收产能。然而，重大挑战依然存在。中国的许多回收产能未被利用，因为太多电池最终落入了非正规废品商贩手中（他们浪费了电池内部大量可用物质），或者干脆被丢弃。近年来，已有多个团伙因经营非法电池收集网络而被捣毁。太阳能电池板和风力涡轮机通常用于中国偏远地区，这构成了更大的收集难题。它们所含的贵重材料（太阳能电池板中的银，风力涡轮机中的稀土钕）含量很少，使得提取更加困难。一如既往，中国希望其依靠科技的政府能够克服这些困难。2024年，中国成立了一家名为中国资源循环集团的新国有企业，以协调和整合回收工作，重点关注清洁技术产品。回收工厂已开始使用人工智能更高效地对废料进行分类。4月，电池和电动汽车制造商被要求为其产品配备数字身份证，以便在官方平台上跟踪其整个生命周期。它们还被依法要求对生产的电池进行回收。中国表示，回收利用已占其稀土供应的10%。它正努力提高这一过程的效率。目前，回收的成本远高于从原材料中提取。不过，科罗拉多矿业学院的科尔比·安德森指出，中国的稀土企业几乎全部为国有企业，“并非在所有情况下都依赖经济可行性”。为了确保回收工厂有原料供应，中国还在悄然重拾其在废料贸易中的旧角色。它正在有选择地放宽对某些外国废料的限制。2024年，中国放宽了对部分废铜和废铝进口的限制。去年，它开始允许进口黑粉。今年1月，它将对黑粉的关税从6.5%降至3%。官员们已承诺在未来五年内继续增加“高质量”回收材料的进口。如今美国和欧洲想留住自己宝贵的废料，它们会削弱中国在回收领域的主导地位吗？深圳上市的大型电池回收商格林美的副总经理张宇平认为不会。“从国家安全的角度来看，他们可能有些理由，”他说。但在中国以外进行回收的成本会很高，而且难以扩大规模。至少欧洲“消化不了”这样的挑战，张先生认为。“它们将付出沉重代价。” ■ 订阅者可以注册我们的新周刊《鼓楼》，以了解世界如何看待中国——以及中国如何看待世界。

item.title: China has captured the market for hobbyist 3D printers
item.description:
China

China | Manufacturing mould Oct 15th 2026 The fastest-growing industrial product in China today is not the electric vehicle, lithium-ion battery or even humanoid robot. It is the humble 3D printer for hobbyists. Once geeky curios, 3D printers have quietly become one of China’s most successful co...
item.content:encoded:
China has captured the market for hobbyist 3D printers

China | Manufacturing mould

Oct 15th 2026

The fastest-growing industrial product in China today is not the electric vehicle, lithium-ion battery or even humanoid robot. It is the humble 3D printer for hobbyists. Once geeky curios, 3D printers have quietly become one of China’s most successful consumer electronics. Exports of the machines grew by 90% in the first half of this year. In the past decade China’s global market share has risen from 19% to 96%, ending the dominance of Western firms.

The personal 3D-printing market is now split among the “four little dragons of Shenzhen”, says Chris Connery of Context, a London-based market-intelligence firm. Creality, Anycubic, Elegoo and the industry’s leader, Bambu Lab, reign supreme globally (see chart). Their success shows, yet again, how fierce competition in China combined with generous government support can help improve quality and drive down export prices, making Chinese products hard to beat.

The printers work by building objects layer by layer, usually by extruding molten plastic. Invented by Chuck Hull, an American, in 1983, they long remained expensive, unreliable and difficult to use. Today they routinely sell for a little more than $500 and have the sleek aluminium finish of an Apple computer. Comparable entry-level printers from Western firms start at more than double the price. Artificial intelligence allows users to create print designs for such things as tools, parts or toys by describing them in natural language rather than using complicated design-software. Just as Chinese factories helped to turn drones into recreational devices (as well as game-changers in warfare) by achieving large-scale production at low cost, so they are now doing with 3D printers.

Price wars have eaten into the printer dragons’ profits even as sales boom. But the firms still excite investors. Bambu Lab was founded in 2020 by alumni of another Chinese company, DJI, the world’s leading dronemaker. The printer-maker is reported to have a private valuation of about $10bn. Last year DJI itself invested in Elegoo, a Bambu rival. Creality listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in May. It boasts a market capitalisation of HK$12bn ($1.5bn).

The government cherishes 3D-printing firms. The business featured in its “Made in China 2025” industrial plan, which was launched in 2015 to ensure domestic strength and self-reliance in high-tech manufacturing (much to the West’s concern). Officials see 3D printers as a way to produce components of aerospace, health care and military equipment, for which China often relies on Western suppliers. Policymakers have directed research institutes and state-run firms to buy them.

Some competitors say Chinese firms have profited from Western open-source printing software. Last month an American court ruled that Bambu Lab had infringed on four patents held by an American company, and ordered it to pay $27.6m in damages. Although Chinese firms have captured the consumer market, they have struggled to do so for industrial 3D printers. Firms are wary of relying on Chinese products if it involves feeding them with sensitive designs (though Britain’s defence ministry has been using Bambu printers, its government admits). Outside China, top-of-the-range machines are still mostly supplied by American and European outfits. They can sell for millions of dollars.

Undeterred, Chinese suppliers are creating a new form of manufacturing at home and abroad. They are pioneering “3D-printing farms”—facilities with as many as 5,000 desktop 3D printers that operate like factories. Several have been built in China this year. Printing farms can mass-produce trinkets for zany consumer trends in short order, replacing expensive and slow injection-moulding techniques. Like the printers themselves, their output will be higher quality and cheaper than what came before. ■

Subscribers can sign up to Drum Tower, our new weekly newsletter, to understand what the world makes of China—and what China makes of the world.

item.title: China is channelling much more money to poor countries
item.description:
China

China | Up in alms Oct 15th 2026 Chinese diplomats often talk about the threat of a “Thucydides trap”, named after the Greek historian who described how an incumbent power, Sparta, fought to resist the rise of an upstart, Athens. In the realm of foreign aid, however, such fierce rivalry has been...
item.content:encoded:
China is channelling much more money to poor countries

China | Up in alms

Oct 15th 2026

Chinese diplomats often talk about the threat of a “Thucydides trap”, named after the Greek historian who described how an incumbent power, Sparta, fought to resist the rise of an upstart, Athens. In the realm of foreign aid, however, such fierce rivalry has been sadly absent in recent years. Another trap, identified by Charles Kindleberger, an economic historian, looks dangerous, too. He described what happens when a stabilising superpower cedes its global role before the emerging power is ready or willing to assume it. America was slow to fill Britain’s shoes in the interwar years of the 20th century. And there is now a similar gap in the realm of multilateral giving.

America has tired of the international institutions it helped create. Last year the aid it channelled through multilateral organisations like the World Bank and the UN fell by half. It has withdrawn from the UN’s World Health Organisation—and it still owes the WHO money.

China could have rushed boldly into this void. And it has indeed stumped up more cash. But its approach lacks Athenian assertiveness. “China is not currently either willing or able to fill the financial gap that would be left behind by US withdrawal,” points out Beata Cichocka of the Centre for Global Development, a think-tank in Washington.

With her colleague Ian Mitchell she has tried to add up China’s contributions to multilateral aid, channelled through development banks, UN agencies and 26 “vertical” funds that collect money for specific problems such as climate change. China itself founded some of these institutions, including the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, based in Beijing, and the New Development Bank in Shanghai.

China’s giving to these bodies has increased steeply over the past decade, from about $1bn in 2014 to more than $3bn in 2024 (see chart 1). China has, for example, become the largest donor to the WHO among its member states, promising an extra $500m over five years. It has backed Song Li, a Chinese health official, to become the organisation’s boss when the position opens up next year.

China has also pledged more money to the International Development Association, a World Bank outfit that provides aid and cheap loans to 78 of the world’s poorest countries. China was itself once one of those hard-up countries, receiving almost $10bn in soft loans from 1981 until it ceased to be eligible in 1999. China’s “transformation from major borrower to significant donor represents one of the most remarkable trajectories in multilateral development finance”, as the report points out.

This transformation is all the more welcome given the remarkable retreat of other donors. But much of China’s extra multilateral giving is mandatory, not voluntary: it must pay more dues because of its economic growth. Even the $500m pledged to the WHO mostly reflects an increase in membership dues, judging by the patchy information available. China is doing its bit. But it is not going far beyond its duty.

Perhaps this should not be a surprise. China’s GDP per person is still middling by world standards. It has only just reached the income threshold at which countries typically “step up their contributions”, points out Mr Mitchell. And China’s increased giving has not been matched by a comparable increase in voting power or voice within the institutions it finances. China’s government is “seized [by] this feeling that they pay and therefore they should have [a] say,” says Courtney Fung of Macquarie University. Its voting share in the World Bank remains at less than 6%. According to formulas the bank has used in the past, it should be more than 12%.

China’s share of UN staff is also tiny: 1.4%, ranking only 20th (see chart 2). It is trying to change that by funding more junior professionals and other entrants. China contributed 773 interns in 2022-23 compared with America’s 532. But the country’s civil servants still struggle with language barriers and unfamiliar work habits.

Some obstacles are self-imposed. China, for example, screens its candidates for patriotism (which includes political loyalty). And civil servants who have spent too long abroad worry that their home networks are “going stale”, says Ms Fung. Perhaps the Athenians felt the same way.■

Subscribers can sign up to Drum Tower, our new weekly newsletter, to understand what the world makes of China—and what China makes of the world.

item.content:encoded:
中国隐藏的税费正变得更加显性

中国 | 茶馆 2026年10月15日

在逃税者中，从阿尔·卡彭到克里斯蒂亚诺·罗纳尔多，吴华涛并不显眼。尽管如此，这位小 salesman 的胆大妄为仍值得关注。据上海市税务局称，吴先生每年收入约55万元人民币（8.2万美元），但只申报了9000元。他还声称自己是远洋海员从而享受免税，而实际上他从未出过海。当税务官员打电话给他时，他屏蔽了他们的号码。当局最终抓住了他。在税务部门对他进行了他们贴心描述的“面对面教育”之后，他承认了自己的不当行为并补缴了税款和罚款。这只是中国打击逃税的众多类似案件之一。一个重要的截止日期即将到来——10月22日，届时中国富人必须遵守针对离岸信托的新税规，否则将面临滞纳金处罚。

对税收征收的热情高涨自然引发了经济层面的疑问。这是否反映出国家财政紧张？很可能。需要额外收入来填补巨大的预算缺口。这些规则是否会吓到中国投资者？有可能。但许多投资者被困在国内市场。谁受益最大？答案很简单：税务顾问。然而，还有另一个更易燃的角度值得考虑：共产党在税收上用力过猛是否会面临政治风险。目前还没有人把绿茶倒进宁波港。但中国的纳税人，和其他任何地方一样，希望知道政府没有浪费。而对预算问责的要求，对于一个厌恶民众代表的政权来说，令人不安。

因此，中国官员的诀窍在于确保资金流入国库，同时又不让人们过多思考他们作为纳税人应有的权利。中国的财政体系长期以来正是为此而设计的。个人所得税约占GDP的1%，而富裕国家的平均水平为8%。起征点如此之高，以至于只有6500万人——占劳动力的十分之一——需要纳税。中国部分通过间接税来弥补这一缺口，尤其是包含在消费者价格中的增值税。此外还有非税收入，主要来自土地出售。总的来说，这些手段让中国以非常隐蔽的方式汲取资源，人们几乎感觉不到压力。北京大学的张长东曾指出，绝大多数人不知道自己缴纳了多少税——对党而言，这是一种无知之福。

然而，这套体系存在缺陷。当过度依赖消费税时，穷人受到沉重打击，因为低收入者将更大比例的收入用于消费。富人在理论上面对更高的所得税，但有许多漏洞可以减少税负——包括直到不久前仍可使用的离岸信托。对政府而言更紧迫的是，税收结构已无法筹集足够收入。曾长期依赖土地出让作为主要收入来源的地方政府，如今在房地产持续低迷中面临日益扩大的预算赤字。这正是新一轮征税行动如此重要之所在。过去，官员们会针对个别名人，如演员范冰冰——她在2018年被责令支付高达8.83亿元的罚金——以表明富人并非法外之人。如今，中国的征税行动范围要广泛得多。几乎所有交易都已数字化，当局也磨砺了分析数据的技术——即所谓的“金税四期”系统。他们仔细审查银行对账单以及支付宝和微信（中国主要的数字钱包）上的交易记录。所有这些监控还得到了许多其他国家税务机构的合作支持。过去一年里，拥有海外账户的人在其个税应用程序中收到了提醒，警告他们遵守法律。

超级富豪可能欠下巨额税款，足以搅动金融市场。火锅连锁店海底捞的联合创始人舒萍于9月出售了近5%的股份，价值约27.5亿港元（3.5亿美元）。公司给出的理由是个人资金需求；分析人士怀疑是补缴税款。海底捞股价下跌超过10%。其他老板——尤其是那些海外上市、财富在境外的人——也可能面临巨额补税。一位私募基金经理最近向茶馆抱怨说，他的税单让他措手不及。政府对离岸信托的新规并未豁免已有安排；而是追溯适用了税收。但他不得不接受现实，老老实实补缴。

政府指望的是几件事。富人其实无处可逃，除非改变国籍并放弃在中国的企业和资产。而大多数民众不会受到波及，甚至可能乐于看到更富有的同胞掏钱。然而，那位倒霉的逃税销售员吴先生提醒人们，法网并不止于大亨。任何有副业收入或海外经纪账户的人，如今都在税务部门的视野之内。这涵盖了众多中国中产阶级——正是那些可能质疑自己得到了什么回报的人。在21世纪初，官方媒体偶尔会赞许地提及“纳税人意识”——即纳税者应当对公共预算有所监督。随着国家对媒体控制的加强，这类讨论已销声匿迹。侧重点不再是纳税人的权利，而是他们的义务。北京税务局最近将管理公众情绪列为新改革的关键部分——这是在批评萌芽阶段就将其扼杀的委婉说法。

从财政角度看，转向更直接的税收对中国是正确的，有望建立一个更公平、更可持续的体系。从政治角度看，这是一场精心计算的赌局。中国正在让税务人员在日常生活中变得更加庞大、更具侵入性。缴税更多的人，往往会要求更多。■

item.title: America’s election officials are ready for trouble
item.description:
United States

United States | On guard Oct 15th 2026 On a fine day in Florence, a city near Phoenix, staff at the local voting centre are doing a tabletop exercise, the euphemism to describe training for election hell. The point is to imagine calamities—fire, power cuts, bomb threats—then have a Plan B, C and...
item.content:encoded:
America’s election officials are ready for trouble

United States | On guard

Oct 15th 2026

On a fine day in Florence, a city near Phoenix, staff at the local voting centre are doing a tabletop exercise, the euphemism to describe training for election hell. The point is to imagine calamities—fire, power cuts, bomb threats—then have a Plan B, C and D. Officials have always made some doomsday preparations, but this year’s exercise is more thorough, and the range of threats broader. What, for example, should they do if federal law-enforcement agents show up at the polls?

The staff run through the protocols. Monitors from the Department of Justice (DoJ) can stay if they have an official letter, and indeed the government has said 1,000 will be dispatched across the country. Any other agents must leave unless they are themselves voting; Arizona law mandates a perimeter of 75 feet (25 metres) around precincts. “If they refuse to leave, that’s when the scenario becomes a scenario,” says an election worker in the recorder’s office in Pinal county, of which Florence is the seat. In other words: call the sheriff.

Pinal is a Republican county. A portion of it lies in Arizona’s 6th congressional district, one of several dozen competitive House races in the midterm elections on November 3rd. Our forecast suggests Democrats will flip the House and possibly the Senate, too. The nagging concern is that Donald Trump may try to subvert the election’s legitimate results.

His effort to overturn his loss in 2020 alerted everyone to the many pressure points in America’s decentralised election system, and the lengths he might go to squeeze them. So far, his many attempted interventions this year have amounted to little, with Congress and the Supreme Court blocking his efforts to rewrite voting procedures. States, not the federal government, run elections, and their rules are mostly unchanged from past cycles. However, the executive branch has shifted from being a force to support electoral integrity to one undermining it, and in November the system will be tested once more.

Some changes represent not active interference, but the removal of help. Last year the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) stopped covering localities’ costs to join a service for sharing cyber threats. Membership in the programme is down by around two-thirds. The upshot is that cyberattacks are more likely to proliferate, reckons Geoff Hale, formerly of CISA. “If a jurisdiction faces one and gets compromised or repels it, but if they’re not sharing information about that attack, then other election jurisdictions remain equally vulnerable.” Similarly, the FBI is said to have no plans to activate its election command centre, which in past years monitored threats and co-ordinated with local officials.

However, election administrators increasingly view the federal government as a threat, too, says Jonathan Miller of Public Rights Project (PRP), a litigation group that represents local governments. Earlier this year the DoJ said it would prosecute officials who let non-citizens vote. Such voter fraud is extremely rare, but the spectre of voting by non-citizens propels the myth of election theft. It is the reason that MAGA activists want immigration enforcement at the polls.

Their presence would be illegal: federal law prohibits government officials from sending armed agents to precincts. On behalf of the city of Denver, PRP has sued the Department of Homeland Security, seeking to pre-empt anything like that on election day. The Trump administration says it has no intention of patrolling precincts, but that it may take targeted action, such as serving warrants against anyone suspected of being an illegal immigrant. Democrats fear that even the threat of agents near polling places will dampen turnout by minorities, who tend to vote Democratic. In a survey by UC San Diego, a third of Hispanics said they anticipate being questioned at the polls despite being citizens. Nearly half say they expect some form of intimidation.

Election experts’ nightmare is that Mr Trump might try to seize voting equipment or ballots. That would break the “chain of custody”, the controls that set out who can handle ballots and where they go, ensuring all are accounted for. Losing custody would make it hard to know whether ballots had been manipulated. “I would feel very uncomfortable about validating those ballots,” says Stephen Richer, a former recorder in Arizona’s Maricopa County. “Then you start going down the dark road of, like, do you have to call a new election?”

Two incidents concerning past elections have primed Democrats to the possibility of meddling. In January the FBI raided an election office in Fulton county, Georgia, and carted away material from 2020. Then in March, Chad Bianco, a Republican sheriff in Riverside, California, seized ballots that had been cast in a statewide referendum last year. Both the FBI and Mr Bianco cited misinformation in their requests for warrants.

Could there be a similar ruse in November’s midterms? The previous incidents occurred long after elections were over, not in the middle of one. Ed Martin, a MAGA agitator, says that the president met this month with Tina Peters, a former county clerk who had gone to prison for giving a fellow election-denier unauthorised access to voting machines in 2021, and whose sentence was then commuted by Colorado’s Democratic governor. Mr Martin, who described Ms Peters’s meeting to an interviewer, offered this cryptic assessment of the midterm elections: “The president’s going to have to do what he’s going to do.”

State and local officials are on high alert. Colorado now requires county clerks to log everything, so that they have clear records if a judge ever orders material removed from their custody. One county official in Arizona says she has made sure her voting-machine vendor has extra supplies, so they are ready if the feds seize equipment. Gabriella Cázares-Kelly, the recorder in Pima County, along the Arizona-Mexico border, says lawyers there have restraining orders drafted if immigration agents show up. “They would plug in a few things, hit print and physically run the document over to a waiting judge.”

Such scenarios remain very unlikely. Yet officials must also contend with election-denial activists, who routinely file nuisance public-records requests and challenges to voter registrations. In swing states such as Georgia, they have also managed to win positions on local boards, with some aiming for statewide office this November. As administrators prepare for “what if” scenarios, there remains the not insubstantial task of getting the basic mechanics of elections right, which can be challenging enough, says Eslir Musta of Arizona’s Coconino County. In his case, that means preparing a mule caravan to serve voters who live at the bottom of the Grand Canyon.

Just half of Americans tell pollsters they anticipate a free and fair midterms. The tighter the margin in either chamber, the more uncertainty there will be to exploit in November. Lawsuits and recounts are now standard in close races. This year control of the Senate may come down to one or two states, including some that are famously slow to count, such as Alaska. A lengthy or contested count requires patience and restraint on the part of candidates. Those are not qualities often attributed to Mr Trump.■

Stay on top of American politics with The US in brief, our daily newsletter with fast analysis of the most important political news, and Checks and Balance, a weekly note that examines the state of American democracy and the issues that matter to voters.

item.description:

item.content:encoded:
维韦克·拉马斯瓦米：过于MAGA，又不够MAGA

美国 | 漂泊不定 2026年10月15日

在一个潮湿、狂风大作的日子里，公园里一个有顶棚的野餐区很难说是政治集会的理想场所，因此很难责怪特拉华县共和党成员们兴致寥寥。10月10日在哥伦布郊区的一场活动中，约75人坐着听了一个小时的候选人和当地警方官员的演讲。这场活动的亮点是维韦克·拉马斯瓦米——一位制药业亿万富翁、前总统候选人，也是该党提名的州长候选人。他承诺将成为一个公正、独立的领导者。“你不能只告诉人们他们想听的话，”他说。而就在不到15码之外，很容易找到拉马斯瓦米的支持者们不想听的观点。在旁边的儿童游乐场上，39岁的科技工作者贾里德·赫斯勒带着年幼的儿子，解释说他不会投票给拉马斯瓦米。赫斯勒过去曾投票给共和党，但在过去两次选举中转向了民主党，并对民主党州长候选人艾米·阿克顿充满热情。“我想说，主要的驱动力就是受够了特朗普，”他说。这种情绪对拉马斯瓦米来说是个问题。俄亥俄州任期受限的共和党州长迈克·德瓦恩在2022年赢得了62%的选票，而唐纳德·特朗普已连续三届总统选举在该州胜出。如今大多数民调显示阿克顿博士略微领先。拉马斯瓦米正在证明自己：对俄亥俄州的温和派来说太MAGA，而对许多共和党人来说又不够MAGA。

特拉华县是俄亥俄州最富有、教育程度最高的县。不久之前，它还是该州共和主义的中心，2004年居民以32个百分点的优势支持乔治·W·布什。但随着该地区不断开发、人口日益多元化，它转向了民主党。到2024年，特朗普的优势已不足7个百分点。

拉马斯瓦米有一些特点，或许会吸引那些对总统持怀疑态度的郊区共和党人。他在演讲中强调削减商业税而不是驱逐出境。作为印度移民之子，他欢迎合法来美的人，并支持移民改革。去年，他在《纽约时报》发表文章，对其所在党内的本土主义派系提出了尖锐批评。他的许多竞选工作人员曾为约翰·卡西奇工作——这位共和党温和派在2011年至2019年间担任俄亥俄州州长。然而实际上，他仍然因与一位不受欢迎的总统的联系而受到玷污——过去一个月里，他曾两次出现在该总统的集会上。

在最近一场俄亥俄州立大学橄榄球赛外围的派对上（这几乎是最接近神圣的世俗活动了），很容易找到曾经的共和党人，却很难找到拉马斯瓦米的选民。“我完全投民主党，尽管我是共和党人，”一位热情的中年车尾派对参与者黛比说。特朗普就是原因。“这届政府的疯狂真让我忍无可忍了，”她解释道。

被视为温和派的是曾领导该州应对新冠疫情的阿克顿博士。2020年，德瓦恩称她为“英雄”。特朗普则试图将她重新塑造为“激进左翼疯子”。

拉马斯瓦米在右翼还有另一个问题。在初选中，他的对手凯西·普奇手持步枪，邀请拉马斯瓦米“玩牛仔对战印第安人”。他还攻击他是“一个印度教徒！”拉马斯瓦米轻松击败了他，但普奇仍然赢得了18%的选票。拥有忠实追随者的白人至上主义者播客主持人尼克·富恩特斯去年表示，他2026年的主要目标是“让维韦克·拉马斯瓦米无法赢得州长职位”。本月，他反而支持了阿克顿博士，称拉马斯瓦米是“锚婴儿”。

受到两边的挤压，拉马斯瓦米正在诉诸一场极其丑陋的竞选。他的广告和支持他的超级政治行动委员会的广告几乎完全聚焦于阿克顿博士。有些广告声称她是个酒鬼和吸毒者（依据是一份关于她与丈夫激烈争吵的警方报告）。另一些则指责她对新冠疫情期间一名老年妇女的死亡负责（事实上，这名妇女住在肯塔基州并在那里去世）。

如果拉马斯瓦米真的成为州长，他可能会再次竞选总统。但对于一个寻求领导本党的人来说，他看起来在自己党内越来越迷失。■

通过我们的每日通讯《美国简报》——对最重要政治新闻的快速分析，以及每周专栏《制衡》——审视美国民主状况和选民关心的问题，随时了解美国政治动态。

item.title: The impact of data-centre discontent
item.description:
United States

United States | The backlash Oct 15th 2026 To spot the site of a new data centre, look for the cranes. About a dozen soar over the fields of Saline township, Michigan, visible for miles around. Another hint is the convoy of cement-mixers trundling down the road, loudly and constantly. When the O...
item.content:encoded:
The impact of data-centre discontent

United States | The backlash

Oct 15th 2026

To spot the site of a new data centre, look for the cranes. About a dozen soar over the fields of Saline township, Michigan, visible for miles around. Another hint is the convoy of cement-mixers trundling down the road, loudly and constantly. When the OpenAI and Oracle project in Saline, “The Barn”, is finished, it will consume more power than a midsize city.

Beside it is the Rustic Glen Golf Club, where a few locals are enthusiastic about the project. “They’ve been talking to us, and they’re going to do a lot of nice things for us,” says a cashier. The data-centre developers have bought the club and have promised to inject cash. Fred, a farmer standing atop a tractor across the road, offers a more typical reaction: “There’s nothing good I can say about it…that was a beautiful piece of farmland, and they destroyed it.” Drinkers at a nearby brewery say the same, a little more politely, and grouse that the golfers were paid off.

Across America, data centres are popping up at startling speed. Since last November more money has been spent building data centres—not including the expensive chips inside them—than new offices (see chart 1). President Donald Trump has warned that places opposed to data centres risk becoming “backwards and poor”, but Republican candidates are trying to be more attuned to voters like Fred. In Michigan Mike Rogers, a Republican Senate candidate, supports a pause on building. Such moves may be too late. Our analysis of polling data suggests that, as anxiety over data centres grows, the projects seem to be pushing voters towards Democrats.

We matched almost 150,000 respondents from the Economist/YouGov weekly survey with their nearest data centre, using Compute Atlas, an open-source repository of such sites. Voters across the country are shifting towards Democrats, but for those living within 2km of a data centre the veer has been even sharper. Americans who live near a data-centre site are around six percentage points more likely to support the Democrats than those who live further away (see chart 2). Six months ago there was no such difference.

For Brandon, who is circulating a petition against data centres in Ohio, the issue has turned him from a Republican into a swing voter. Local Republicans refused to help his cause, he says, but “the Democrats have been amazing.” Michigan and Ohio are already home to more local moratoriums than any other states.

Why have data centres caught fire politically? Throughout dozens of conversations, voters seldom brought up AI-related concerns directly. The most common fears were practical ones, about water pollution, higher electricity bills or a hit to house prices. Neither politicians’ promises that the projects will pay their own way nor developers’ efforts to bat away concerns with cash seem to have done much good. Whatever the truth is, practical assurances count for little when voters so deeply distrust both government and big businesses: confidence in each is near 50-year lows.

The real-world effect of all that opposition has, so far, been limited. Maya Barkin of SemiAnalysis, a research firm, finds that only 2.3 gigawatts’ worth of projects are likely to be delayed by moratoriums (see chart 3). But with discontent growing, the political impact is more assured. ■

Stay on top of American politics with The US in brief, our daily newsletter with fast analysis of the most important political news, and Checks and Balance, a weekly note that examines the state of American democracy and the issues that matter to voters.

item.content:encoded:
职业相扑登陆美国

美国 | 一项宏大的美丽运动 2026年10月15日

最近一个夜晚，在佐治亚州桃树市，凯蒂·哈德曼正在训练她的“黑龙男孩们”。两个小时内，她让那些有抱负的相扑选手——大多是中年男性——进行了一场艰苦的训练。然后她邀请本刊记者试一下，给她系上相扑兜裆布（mawashi），并指导她低头冲向一名男子的胸膛，手掌瞄准“胸部和腋窝”。“这有一种触电般的感觉，”身为退伍军人的哈德曼女士说。“我们正努力消除我国那种负面印象，即相扑只是穿着尿布的胖男人互相推搡。”

10月10日，相扑冠军联赛在得克萨斯州奥斯汀举行了首场比赛。该联赛是太平洋这一侧的首个此类联赛。十六名选手参赛，最终三号种子、一位21岁的佛罗里达人夺得金牌。斯图尔特·斯奈德是这项赛事的娱乐策划大师，曾任世界摔跤娱乐公司（World Wrestling Entertainment）首席运营官，该公司数十年来一直在上演假摔跤比赛。当他看到“玉米洞”（cornhole，成年人将豆袋扔进带孔的木板）在网上爆红后，他认定小众运动正当时——下一个就是相扑。手握500万美元，他打赌自己能让美国人迷上这项源自亚洲传统的消遣。

该联赛许多冉冉升起的新星都是刚开始接触相扑。乔尼森·“吉瓦”·皮尔格里姆（Jonithan “Jiva” Pilgrim）在YouTube上发现相扑时，还住在一个哈瑞·奎师那公社。他意识到自己“天生就是个战士”，于是加入了一个俱乐部，并通过摄入乳清蛋白奶昔、豆腐和酥油来增加体重。他的俱乐部同伴多米纳斯·“多米兹拉”·戴维斯-威廉姆斯（Dominus “Domzilla” Davis-Williams）是联赛最重的选手，体重450磅（204公斤），曾是美式足球运动员。他说，相扑“感觉很熟悉”，对他的“身体积极”观大有裨益。

为了帮助相扑发展，一些习俗可能会调整。在奥斯汀，一些选手“传统”出场，只穿相扑兜裆布，露出臀部。另一些则在里面偷偷穿了短裤。皮尔格里姆先生认为，美国人会为相扑而倾倒，但他们可能还没准备好接受“那么多裸露的男性身体”。■

通过我们的每日通讯《美国简报》和每周通讯《制衡》，随时了解美国政治动态：前者快速分析最重要的政治新闻，后者审视美国民主状况以及对选民重要的问题。
