Britain | Under the radar Oct 8th 2026 Dinghies crossing the channel, laden with asylum-seekers, have turned Britain’s maritime border into a national obsession. But with all eyes on the coast, who is watching the skies? A new study from RUSI, a defence think-tank, argues that “criminals are exp...
item.content:encoded:
Are small planes Britain’s next small boats?

Britain | Under the radar

Oct 8th 2026

Dinghies crossing the channel, laden with asylum-seekers, have turned Britain’s maritime border into a national obsession. But with all eyes on the coast, who is watching the skies?

A new study from RUSI, a defence think-tank, argues that “criminals are exploiting a border-security blind spot” in general aviation—a category that covers everything from hot-air balloons to helicopters. Small planes and private jets are a trafficker’s dream. In Britain, their comings and goings are difficult to monitor, according to Cathy Haenlein, the report’s author.

Such aircraft have to submit a General Aviation Report (GAR) declaring passenger information and other details. With over 77,000 arrivals each year, the vast majority legitimate, good data are vital for identifying suspicious flights. But pilots can put in a GAR as little as two hours before departure, leaving little time to assess it. Unless the GAR contains obvious red flags, traffickers could easily encounter no customs officials when they land.

The Home Office says all high-risk flights are targeted for checks. But in 2024 London City Airport—much better resourced than most small airfields—was found to be failing to meet this goal. Britain has 538 airfields able to receive international flights, some in remote areas. Scrambling a team to meet a suspicious flight can therefore be a challenge. Worse, pilots can amend flight plans after take-off.

In 2018 some 500kg of cocaine, worth £41m ($55m), was found on a private jet arriving in Hampshire. Europol warned 15 years ago that light aircraft were being used to move diamonds across Europe. Police are assessing whether Jeffrey Epstein used private jets to traffic women to and from Britain.  Yet Britain lacks figures on such crimes. Border Force does not reveal how many flights it labels as high-risk, or subjects to extra checks. As one official says: “We’re not seeing it because we’re not looking for it.” Advances in drone technology promise further challenges.

David White, of the Light Aircraft Association, is more sanguine. Project Pegasus, set up by law enforcement, allows airfield users to report suspicious activity. Mr White says they are keen to use it, lest a few bad apples encourage overbearing regulation. “You might get away with it once,” he says, but questionable trips will quickly draw attention. “We’re nosey like that.” ■

item.title: American bombers have abandoned a British base
item.description:
Britain

Britain | Wheels up Oct 8th 2026 Uppermost in the minds of American commanders who ordered around a dozen B-1 bombers to leave their temporary base at RAF Fairford on October 4th was the fear of an Iranian plot to attack them with drones. J.D. Vance, America’s vice-president, said the decision s...
item.content:encoded:
American bombers have abandoned a British base

Britain | Wheels up

Oct 8th 2026

Uppermost in the minds of American commanders who ordered around a dozen B-1 bombers to leave their temporary base at RAF Fairford on October 4th was the fear of an Iranian plot to attack them with drones. J.D. Vance, America’s vice-president, said the decision sprang from an “abundance of caution”. It came after President Donald Trump claimed to have had intelligence of a specific threat. “They didn’t fly out by accident,” he said.

Britain gave the Americans permission, soon after the Iran war began in February, to fly “defensive” missions from Fairford and other bases against targets such as Iranian missile launchers. In July Iran threatened that “any base used to launch attacks on Iranian territory is a legitimate target for our forces”—a threat the British took seriously, and for good reason. Their intelligence services reckon Iran has been behind a growing number of attempted “hybrid” attacks in Britain.

Ukraine’s extraordinary Operation Spiderweb, in June 2025, showed how quite vulnerable airbases can be. The Ukrainians smuggled more than 100 quadcopter drones deep inside Russia, then used them to destroy as many as 14 irreplaceable bombers and reconnaissance aircraft. Ever since, air forces everywhere have feared copycat attacks. In August an attempted drone attack on Ukrainian transport aircraft at Leipzig airport, attributed to Russia, very nearly succeeded.

The sudden departure of the B-1s from Fairford, in the Cotswolds, came after armed police arrested five British men in their 20s on September 28th. They had been tipped off by a local farmer that the men had driven three vans near to the perimeter of the base. The five were arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act using explosives—though the police search revealed only cans of petrol.

All five were released on bail some 24 hours later; the police say they are under a “hugely complex” investigation “interrogating multiple lines of inquiry”. On September 30th Andy Burnham, the prime minister, confirmed “strong indications” that Iran was behind the incident but declined to say more. To many American eyes, British officials appear reticent and somewhat bumbling. A day later a sixth man, a dual British-Iranian national, was arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act but was also later released on bail. On October 6th a seventh arrest followed.

Much remains opaque. Presumably something serious prompted the B-1s’ sudden flight. But it is hard to see how that fits with the seemingly amateurish shenanigans of the “Fairford five”. Conceivably, the Iranians were planning a sophisticated operation of the kind required to send explosive-laden drones into the base. But if so, why would they give the game away with what looks, at best, like a dummy run to test Fairford’s security?

The petrol containers pose another riddle. They could have been used to start a fire close to the base’s fence, but that could not have done much damage. Some have speculated that the aim was to cause a diversion, facilitating a more serious attack elsewhere along Fairford’s 13.5-mile (22km) perimeter, which was cancelled when the men were apprehended. But there have been no reports of others having been spotted. Nor has any tell-tale gear, such as the antenna planted in a tree near Leipzig to act as a signal booster, been found.

Moreover, it is highly questionable whether Iran’s operatives in Britain would have been able to orchestrate a Spiderweb-style drone attack with any chance of success. They are often recruited via social media and lack anything like the necessary know-how. Even the simpler Leipzig attack, which was thwarted when the explosive device on a hovering drone failed to detonate, required a great deal of technical sophistication and training.

For now, the best explanation for the B-1s’ departure from Fairford is Mr Vance’s “abundance of caution”. Unlike RAF Lakenheath, a big American base in East Anglia, it does not have hardened shelters. The planes, which each cost more than $300m, have been parked out in the open. But Fairford is one of only two bases in Europe that America’s strategic bombers can use, owing to its two-mile runway. This made it valuable in the early stages of Mr Trump’s war on Iran. Hence another possible reason that the bombers have gone home: because the war has reached a desultory stage in which they are less needed.

It would therefore be wrong to read their departure as an implied criticism of other American airbases in Britain, which perform an important role for NATO. Equally, it should not be taken as an indication of future withdrawals of American forces from Europe. There is some puzzlement in Mr Trump’s administration over Fairford suspects having been let out on bail. But American officials stress that they are working well with the British, and that the B-1s—like the B-52s that left earlier—were never more than temporary residents.

And perhaps the curious incident of the five men and three vans in the night of September 28th will turn out to be the extent of Iran’s ambition. “Tehran must be mystified that a low-cost operation by recruited British nationals was followed within a week by the departure of Europe’s only forward-based US heavy bombers,” says Charlie Edwards of the International Institute for Strategic Studies, a think-tank. The lesson, he adds, for Iran, Russia and others is that Europeans hosting American assets can be made to pay a domestic price for relatively little effort on their part. ■

item.title: 养老金领取者共产主义的即将衰落
item.description:
Britain

英国 | 巴杰特 2026年10月8日 弗拉基米尔·列宁将一切政治归结为两个问题：“谁？对谁？”谁将主导，他们又将主导谁？自2010年以来，英国政府给出了简单的答案。谁？养老金领取者。对谁？其他所有人。以保守党为先锋，养老金领取者使国家屈从于他们的意志。服务于劳动年龄人口的部门受到挤压，而与老年人相关的部分则受到保护。养老金领取者关注的事务，如脱离欧盟，无论造成多大损害都得以推进。免费电视执照之类的施舍如雨点般落下。一条古老的马克思主义口号被赋予了新的含义：各尽所能，按年龄分配。 然而，对于一个岌岌可危的体系，变化可能来得很快，无论它看起来多么坚不可摧。人类学家阿列克谢·尤尔查克曾将苏联解体...
item.content:encoded:
养老金领取者共产主义的即将衰落

英国 | 巴杰特 2026年10月8日

弗拉基米尔·列宁将一切政治归结为两个问题：“谁？对谁？”谁将主导，他们又将主导谁？自2010年以来，英国政府给出了简单的答案。谁？养老金领取者。对谁？其他所有人。以保守党为先锋，养老金领取者使国家屈从于他们的意志。服务于劳动年龄人口的部门受到挤压，而与老年人相关的部分则受到保护。养老金领取者关注的事务，如脱离欧盟，无论造成多大损害都得以推进。免费电视执照之类的施舍如雨点般落下。一条古老的马克思主义口号被赋予了新的含义：各尽所能，按年龄分配。

然而，对于一个岌岌可危的体系，变化可能来得很快，无论它看起来多么坚不可摧。人类学家阿列克谢·尤尔查克曾将苏联解体的记述命名为：“一切皆为永恒，直至不复存在”。21世纪的养老金领取者共产主义——这一共产主义的老龄表亲——亦是如此。人口结构变化、经济困境和内在矛盾将终结这一曾看似不可战胜的政治安排。养老金领取者共产主义的终结即将来临。

当未来的历史学家讲述其衰亡的故事时，他们会从2026年9月在利物浦的一次演讲开始。演讲者此行的目的不是摧毁养老金领取者共产主义，而是拯救它。安迪·伯纳姆更像是试图支撑摇摇欲坠大厦的米哈伊尔·戈尔巴乔夫，而非带来混乱新生事物的鲍里斯·叶利钦。这位英国较新的首相承诺改革三重锁——这一迄今不可触碰的政策每年根据通胀率、工资增长率或2.5%中的最高值提高国家养老金。工党官员们的反应如同苏联代表大会上的代表。伯纳姆先生缓和了语气，称2030年之前——即下次选举之后——不会做出任何改变。他的党内忠实支持者既为保留三重锁而鼓掌，也为废除它而鼓掌。

戈尔巴乔夫启动了“改革”，那是一揽子旨在撼动整个经济的改革措施。伯纳姆先生则是在为老年人调配资金。节省下来的资金（到2040年每年可能达到200亿英镑，合260亿美元）将用于建立新的国民照护服务体系，确保老年人不必为养老照护支付那么多费用。不妨将其视为面向养老金领取者的“改革”。然而，正如戈尔巴乔夫所发现的那样，试图改变一个体系可能会使其崩塌。

仅仅几周前，三重锁还是英国政治中一个不可避免、无法逃避的事实：太阳东升西落，英国国家养老金每年按通胀率、工资增长率或2.5%中的最高值上涨。这是一个不可能兑现的承诺，却又是一个永远不能动用的承诺。如今不再如此。“尽管体系的崩溃在开始之前不可想象，但当它发生时却显得并不意外，”尤尔查克先生写道。养老金领取者共产主义也是如此。即便其政策并非不可能，也是不公正的。

既然年龄斗争已取代阶级斗争，税率往往取决于出生日期。在百安居工作的养老金领取者面临着20%的边际税率。他们刚毕业的同事——担心人工智能正忙着吞噬自己的职业前景——则要损失37%的工资用于扣除。无论通过增税还是削减开支，英国都面临财政巩固。一代人之前，养老金领取者是社会上最贫困的群体之一。1990年玛格丽特·撒切尔离任时，40%的养老金领取者处于贫困状态。如今，养老金领取者家庭的收入往往高于劳动年龄家庭。“各尽所能，按年龄分配”在这种背景下无法存续。所有年龄段的人都必须分担痛苦。

当年龄胜过阶级时，人口结构决定选举结果。婴儿潮一代这样的大规模世代在投票箱前欺凌政府。当他们退休后，英国变成了养老金领取者的独裁国。然后，在2020年，千禧一代成为最大的群体。因此，2024年大选是第一个如果按同代人主流投票就会落败的1950年代出生者的选举。精算表与任何民意调查一样有用。

当人们不再真正相信体系时，体系就会消亡。晚期养老金领取者共产主义充斥着虚伪。伯纳姆先生演讲之后，私下痛斥三重锁的保守党政客们却热切地为它辩护。但就像苏联官员回家后用非法获得的索尼随身听听披头士乐队一样，他们知道这个体系注定要灭亡。盲目的信念同样致命。对一个已经摇摇欲坠的政权，人们提出了离谱的要求。为什么国家养老金不能与最低工资持平？工党贵族普雷姆·西卡问道。即便这意味着养老金预算将相当于国家在教育、国防、交通、警察、法院、监狱和债务利息上的总支出，那也无所谓。对养老金领取者怎么好都不过分！

“我从未想过苏联会发生任何改变。更别说它会消失，”俄罗斯歌手安德烈·马卡列维奇说。“人们完全觉得一切都是永恒的。”当永恒终结时会发生什么？当一个霸权思想崩溃时，真空只能由其他思想填补。伯纳姆先生提出了很多建议。重新加入欧盟曾是一个疯狂的梦想。如果首相的话可信，这可能在十年内发生。同样还有沉闷但影响深远的选举改革问题。这不仅是自由派的机会。关于种族主义的禁忌同样可能迅速瓦解。“谁？对谁？”可能会有一个阴暗的答案。

英国政治似乎陷入永恒的当下，对这个国家曾经是什么几乎没有真正的记忆，也不知道它能成为什么。其规范是不可避免的、不可撼动的，直到它们被撼动。“谁？对谁？”的答案永远无法改变，尽管它最终总会改变。养老金领取者共产主义正在走向终结。一切皆为永恒，直至不复存在。■

item.title: Nagging people to eat healthily does not work
item.description:
International

International | Governments v sugar, salt and fat Oct 8th 2026 Sunday afternoons in Simón Bolívar park are an orgy of calories. Many stalls in this green corner of Colombia’s capital, Bogotá, sell obleas: sandwiches of wafers stuffed with layers of fattening fillings, including syrups, jams, car...
item.content:encoded:
Nagging people to eat healthily does not work

International | Governments v sugar, salt and fat

Oct 8th 2026

Sunday afternoons in Simón Bolívar park are an orgy of calories. Many stalls in this green corner of Colombia’s capital, Bogotá, sell obleas: sandwiches of wafers stuffed with layers of fattening fillings, including syrups, jams, caramel and cheese. An acid green “bubble-gum” sauce is among the enticing options. “Life’s too short not to eat the food that you love”, reads a sign above one of the stalls.

So Colombians evidently believe. A quarter of them are obese, according to the UN’s World Health Organisation, a share that has risen fivefold since 1980. Diabetes, high blood pressure and kidney disease—all chronic conditions associated with obesity—are rife. The health-care system, already severely underfunded and then stretched almost to breaking point by covid-19, has struggled to cope.

In 2022 the previous government decided radical action was needed. It required all processed food with high levels of sugar, salt or the unhealthiest forms of fat to be labelled as such, with big black warning signs. More important, it imposed a 10% tax on such products, which rose to 15% in 2024 and 20% last year.

Colombia is not the only place that is meddling in the food business to counter obesity. On September 29th Gavin Newsom, the governor of California, who is likely to run for president in 2028, signed a bill requiring grocery chains to place healthy foods in “high-traffic areas” within stores. A law came into effect in Scotland on October 1st barring big businesses from displaying unhealthy foods prominently in shops and from offering promotions that encourage bulk purchases of them, such as buy-one-get-one-free deals. In India on October 6th a public consultation ended on a proposal to prohibit sales of junk food to children within 50 metres of a school. The state of Maharashtra already has such a law, barring sales of junk food to anyone near a school.

Heavy-handed policies like these used to be a rarity. Between 1992 and 2020 Britain adopted no fewer than 14 official government plans to curb rising obesity (not counting the initiatives of devolved governments in Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales). Those plans involved 689 individual policies. The majority aimed to make consumers more aware of the health risks of junk food and to provide better access to healthy alternatives, especially in schools. None banned any forms of junk food, only 3% restricted access to it and only two policies (or 0.3% of the total) created any financial disincentive to consume it, such as higher taxes.

This cajoling approach has failed. England’s obesity rate has doubled since the early 1990s. About a fifth of 11-year-olds are now obese. In both rich countries and poorer ones, obesity rates have been rising steadily (see chart). In America 72% of adults are obese or overweight. In Mexico 74% are. All this costs the countries in the OECD, a club mostly of rich countries, an average of 3% of GDP a year in health-care spending and lost productivity.

Although GLP-1 drugs, the weight-loss treatments that have become commonplace in the rich world in recent years, hold out the hope of dramatically reducing obesity, they are pricey, especially considering patients must remain on them indefinitely. Poorer countries, in particular, will struggle to provide them to a big proportion of the population.

Politicians are instead turning to a bewildering array of policies intended not to persuade people to change their habits, but rather to alter the “food environment” around them. Many of the new rules concern labels. About ten years ago health officials in Britain, France and elsewhere created simple symbols in traffic-light colours to rank foods from best to worst, either for ingredients of concern (such as fat, sugar and salt) or overall, based on a formula that takes into account healthy ingredients, too. Many countries have since adopted such easily digestible scoring systems—but most remain voluntary.

That is changing fast. A bill to make France’s labels mandatory has been introduced in parliament. Singapore will soon oblige manufacturers to label foods that score poorly under its system. The most sweeping rules, however, involve warning labels like Colombia’s, akin to the frightening messages many countries require on cigarette packets. Since 2016, for instance, Chile has obliged manufacturers to place as many as four black, stop-sign-shaped alerts on the front of unhealthy products, depending on how many ingredients exceed the regulatory threshold. Canada adopted similar rules earlier this year.

Such rules have an impact, both by deterring buyers and by prompting chastened manufacturers to alter recipes to avoid being branded unhealthy. A recent analysis of Mexico’s labelling law, which came into effect in 2020, concluded that it had led to a 15% drop in calories sold, a 25% drop in added sugar and 12% drop in saturated fats, even as overall sales volumes remained stable. About 90% of the reduction in calories was the result of products being reformulated, rather than of people changing which products they bought.

Restrictions on marketing unhealthy foods are also proliferating. About a dozen countries ban television ads for junk food when children are likely to be watching or bar ads and packaging from appealing to children using cartoon characters and the like. In January Britain went a step further, banning ads for unhealthy foods online and on social media, following a similar move by Portugal in 2019. Local governments can be especially zealous. In 2022 New York banned junk-food ads on all city property, as have several places in Australia and Britain. Amsterdam and London ban them on public transport.

Then there are restrictions on where unhealthy foods can be sold. Britain’s planning law was amended in 2024 to allow local authorities to ban new fast-food joints within walking distance of a secondary school—although so many such outlets already exist that the new rules may have little effect. Maharashtra’s law is much more restrictive, but enforcement is patchy.

The difficulty of enforcement is one of the many drawbacks of complex rules around junk food. They can place heavy burdens on businesses, which also often find creative ways around them. Since 2022, for example, Britain has banned supermarkets from displaying unhealthy packaged foods near checkouts, shop entrances and the ends of aisles, to curb impulse purchases. The share of the affected foods in overall sales fell by 7% the year after the ban. But sugary, greasy pastries swiftly took their place near the entrances of shops, since freshly baked items are exempt from the ban.

Such experiences have prompted authorities in Britain to consider an alternative approach. Instead of umpteen rules about what can be sold where and to whom, they are pondering targets for the healthiness of supermarket chains’ total sales, based on the nutrition scores already in use for Britain’s restrictions on junk-food advertising. It would be, in effect, a minimum spinach-to-sweets ratio. But the chains would be free to decide whether to promote spinach more, or sweets less, or to persuade junk-food manufacturers to put more spinach in their sweets.

Supermarkets wield lots of influence over shoppers. Sainsbury’s, a big British chain, saw sales of fruit quadruple when it offered collectible Disney-themed cards with each sale. Supermarkets would probably press suppliers to make their products healthier, says Hugo Harper of Nesta, a think-tank in London. A frozen pizza, for instance, might end up with a few more vegetables on top and a bit less salt in the sauce. Nesta estimates that marginal changes to a quarter of items in the typical British shopping basket could lead to a sustained 8.5% reduction in calories in an average consumer’s diet. Such a reduction, in turn, could halve obesity.

Retailers, naturally, do not want to be responsible for getting people to eat more healthily, even if governments give them some leeway about how they do it. A simpler alternative is to curb consumption of junk food by taxing it. More than 100 countries impose special taxes on sugary drinks—with great effect. The year after Mexico imposed such a tax in 2014, sales of the products affected fell by around 6%. Many manufacturers also changed their recipes to make drinks less sugary. Mexico’s government is so fond of the tax it raised it from 1.64 pesos ($0.09) a litre to 3.08 earlier this year.

Any talk of raising taxes is awkward at a time of high inflation and widespread resentment at the rising cost of living. Public opinion does appear to be warming to more forceful regulation, however. In a poll last year 51% of Americans said they were in favour of restrictions on the sale of junk food in grocery stores and 44% approved of higher taxes on it. Nearly 70% of Britons say they would support an extension of Britain’s tax on sugary drinks to other unhealthy foods if the proceeds were used to promote better diets.

Moreover, many governments already tax food both heavily and inconsistently. In some countries it should be possible to penalise junk food by adjusting rates for different products without raising taxes overall. A study published last year in Nature found that ten European countries charge higher rates of value-added tax on fruits and vegetables than on meat and dairy. Reversing this, the researchers argued, would bring about big health benefits at almost no cost to consumers. VAT reforms along these lines are being discussed in Denmark, Germany and the Netherlands.

Junk food is popular for many reasons. It is convenient. It is often cheaper, calorie for calorie, than healthier food. Sugar, salt and fat are hard to resist. Food companies and supermarkets make more money from it than from healthy stuff, because they both sell more of it and earn higher margins on it. Against these daunting advantages, however, governments have found a formidable array of counter-measures. ■

item.title: Vladimir Putin and the pariah problem
item.description:
International

International | The Telegram Oct 8th 2026 VLADIMIR PUTIN is about to subject Ukraine and Europe to a winter of horror. Each week Russia’s president plumbs new depths of cruelty and recklessness, enraged by his failure to break Ukraine in the four-and-a-half years since he began his full-scale in...
item.content:encoded:
Vladimir Putin and the pariah problem

International | The Telegram

Oct 8th 2026

VLADIMIR PUTIN is about to subject Ukraine and Europe to a winter of horror. Each week Russia’s president plumbs new depths of cruelty and recklessness, enraged by his failure to break Ukraine in the four-and-a-half years since he began his full-scale invasion. His missiles and jet-engined drones are turning Ukrainian cities into places of sleepless misery. Russian strikes are battering ports whose grain shipments once fed hundreds of millions. Beyond Ukraine, Russia is stepping up acts of sabotage across Europe and making ever-wilder nuclear threats towards the West.

These are the actions of a rogue state. Increasingly, Russia’s near neighbours are saying as much. Last month German government ministers formally blamed Russia for a narrowly thwarted drone attack on a cargo airport in Leipzig. For good measure, the ministers pledged to defend their country against “adversaries” bent on harm. Such language would have been unthinkable before the invasion of Ukraine, when successive German governments tiptoed around Russia as a supposedly indispensable energy supplier and European great power. On October 5th the head of Germany’s foreign-intelligence agency told the Bundestag that Russia is waging a dangerous “shadow war” to test Germany’s resolve. He added a warning that this winter Ukrainians will suffer “Russian attacks of a severity and brutality that we have not yet seen”.

Across northern Europe, especially in Nordic and Baltic countries close to Russia, politicians of the centre-left and -right condemn Mr Putin as impossible to trust. For four years the theory of victory has been that “Russia must not win and Ukraine must not lose”, for the sake of the international order but also for Europe’s future security. Allied governments agreed to send money and arms to keep Ukraine in the fight and maintain harsh sanctions on Russia until domestic opposition and economic pain change Mr Putin’s calculus or end his rule. Of late, though, such big players as Britain, France and Germany wonder whether the slogan should change to offer more hope to Russians outside the regime.

There are practical reasons for Ukraine’s allies to condemn Russia’s worst actions in loud terms. Mr Putin is growing more dangerous. Though he is beyond shame, naming his crimes might help deter him from further escalation. After sharing classified details of Russian shadow attacks with opposition leaders last month, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, explained their intended effect: to intimidate France into abandoning Ukraine. “The consequence will be the opposite,” he insisted. Mr Macron added a deterrent threat of his own. With a menacing nod to France’s formidable spies and cyber-warriors, he said that Russian hybrid attacks would “not go unanswered”. There are sound political reasons, too, for centrists to sound tough and to frame the war in Ukraine as a moral crusade against a rogue Russia. In France and across Europe, their rivals in populist parties are hoping to gain from voter fatigue with the war.

Then there is the detail that Mr Putin really is a pariah. Alas, calling Russia’s leader a rogue may also be a trap. The Ukraine war is deadlocked and the allies’ theory of victory may never work. If Mr Putin’s will to fight is not broken by economic pain and domestic discontent, then Ukraine and allies will have to reach terms of coexistence with him, for this war to end or even pause.

Though drenched in the blood of Ukrainian civilians and soldiers (and of over a million Russian troops, chewed up in his war of attrition), Mr Putin has friends in high places. President Donald Trump does not consider him a pariah. He has invited the Russian to a summit of leaders of G20 countries, to be held in December at Trump National Doral, a golf resort he owns in Florida. Though European leaders in Doral may detect a spectral cloud of death around Mr Putin, he can expect a warm welcome from the leaders of China and India, and respectful greetings from many others.

That failure to isolate Mr Putin weighed on the Helsinki Security Forum, a gathering of political leaders, diplomats, soldiers, spies and scholars from some of Ukraine’s staunchest backers, held in Finland this month. A Nordic head of state saw grounds for cautious optimism in Mr Putin’s G20 invitation, if it leads to direct talks in Doral between Mr Trump, the Russian leader and Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky. Other participants worried, though, that Europe is setting itself up to fail if it continues to emphasise Mr Putin’s wickedness.

Allies talk of securing a just and lasting peace, said a former American official, just back from meetings with senior Russians in Moscow. “But all of us know, deep down, that peace is not going to be just,” he told the forum, predicting that Russia will end up keeping some Ukrainian territory and Mr Putin will never face trial in The Hague for war crimes. Other well-connected participants reported that Russian elites have no intention of paying reparations for war damages to Ukraine. It was noted that dozens of military veterans from Ukraine were recently elected to Russia’s parliament, so that the political classes may include war criminals for years to come.

Ukraine has more right than any country to condemn Russia as a pariah. Its people have courageously resisted Mr Putin’s aggression and show no signs of giving up the fight. But Ukraine also has to survive. If Ukrainians are ever ready for peace on imperfect terms, Europeans cannot be purer than Ukraine. Europe will have grounds for alarm, especially if a ceasefire leaves an emboldened Russia free to regroup and prepare for further aggression. But they can hardly tell Ukrainians to keep fighting on for their sake. All Europe can do is make Ukraine as strong as possible. Denying Mr Putin a full-throated victory may well be the only punishment he faces for his aggression. In a wicked world, it may have to do. ■

item.content:encoded:
印度制造业的辉煌时刻或许终于到来

商业 | 印度制造 2026年10月8日

印度纺织品制造商Raghuvir Exim的最新工厂令人叹为观止。这家工厂生产出口床品，占地约200英亩（80公顷），位于西部古吉拉特邦艾哈迈达巴德郊区。Raghuvir Exim修建了宿舍，以容纳工厂满负荷运转时所需的5000名工人。印度女性就业率很低，而这家工厂积极招募了女性员工。工厂使用的是优质的欧洲机器，而非更便宜的中国机器。而且大部分能源来自太阳能。然而，自去年8月开业以来，这家工厂起步艰难。据家族企业第三代成员哈迪克·阿加瓦尔（Hardik Agarwal）介绍，工厂最初产能利用率仅15%左右。几乎在同一时间，美国对印度出口商品征收50%的关税，严重打击了销售。

印度制造业的近代史充满了这样的失望。2014年，总理纳伦德拉·莫迪（Narendra Modi）推出了一项放松管制和基础设施投资的计划，名为“印度制造”（Make in India），并宣称到2022年，制造业将占国民收入的四分之一。而截至去年，这一比例仅为16%，过去十年几乎未有任何增长。

然而，现在或许正是印度的时刻。8月份（可获得的最新数据）制造业产出同比增长9%，尤其得益于汽车和电子产品的产量激增。这部分反映了海湾战争的影响：印度通常用美元购买石油，油价飙升导致卢比暴跌，进口商品变得更加昂贵，出口商品则更加便宜。央行于10月7日宣布三年来首次加息，但未能扭转卢比的跌势。但印度制造业产出上升也反映了其作为制造基地日益增长的吸引力。按美元计算，印度8月份电子产品出口同比增长90%，其中运往美国的iPhone占据了很大一部分。

事实上，在印度的部分地区，一场转型正在如火如荼地进行（见图）。起点是古吉拉特邦，这里是石化和制药等行业的中心；向东南延伸至马哈拉施特拉邦，这里有汽车制造中心普纳，也是印度金融之都孟买所在地；再向南进入卡纳塔克邦，那里有围绕科技中心班加罗尔的航空航天和国防公司集群；然后进入南部的泰米尔纳德邦，那里各类制造业如今蓬勃发展。

这一组邦——不妨称之为“工业邦”（Industrial Pradesh）——居住着约3.5亿人，约占印度人口的四分之一，但每年创造约2400亿美元的制造业增加值，占印度总量的一半。其经验为整个国家提供了许多启示。首先是积极争取投资（包括外资）的必要性。早在2003年，时任古吉拉特邦首席部长的莫迪就创办了两年一度的“活力古吉拉特”（Vibrant Gujarat）博览会，为该邦的政治和商业领袖提供了吸引外国投资者的机会。马哈拉施特拉邦工业发展公司负责收购土地、建设工业园区，并帮助企业接通电力和水源，以吸引工厂入驻。投资促进机构Guidance Tamil Nadu通过确定潜在生产地点并清除官僚障碍来吸引企业。“在泰米尔纳德邦这样的地方，如果你想获得许可证，可能需要花点钱，但你能拿到许可证，”一家制造商的高管表示。而在印度其他地区，贿赂之后往往是索要更多贿赂——而且许可证依然遥遥无期。

在“工业邦”各地涌现的各种产业集群，往往围绕锚定企业（anchor businesses）而建——这是给整个印度的第二条经验。在古吉拉特邦的萨南德镇，塔塔汽车的一家工厂于2010年开业，以取代西孟加拉邦的一个饱受反资本主义抗议困扰的厂址。（莫迪在说服这家企业集团将生产迁至其邦的过程中发挥了核心作用。）此后，一个汽车零部件供应商网络在周边如雨后春笋般涌现，各自建立了自己的工厂。“在印度每一个成功的产业集群中，都有一个锚定参与者，”咨询公司波士顿咨询（BCG）的拉胡尔·贾因（Rahul Jain）表示。

许多锚定企业最初是从进口零部件组装成品起步，然后随着本地供应商获得必要的专业知识和规模，逐渐转向本地供应商。这种模式最初出现在汽车制造领域，如今已成为其他行业的典范。如今，大约四分之一的苹果iPhone在印度组装，工厂位于卡纳塔克邦和泰米尔纳德邦，由台湾公司富士康以及塔塔集团旗下的塔塔电子运营。最初，合约制造商只是简单地组装进口部件，这让一些人抱怨莫迪在2020年推出的被称为“生产挂钩激励”的制造业补贴，不过是在为中国制造的零部件进口买单。然而近年来，手机零部件制造商也开始在印度设立本地工厂。一项行业估算显示，印度智能手机制造的增加值已从2021年的45亿美元上升至去年的173亿美元。

印度渴望在清洁能源和半导体领域复制这一成功。根据倡导组织Ember的数据，自2022年以来，印度从中国进口的成品太阳能电池板数量大幅下降。用于电池板的太阳能电池以及用于电池的硅片的进口最初上升，但随后随着印度在供应链上向上攀升而缩减。印度太阳能产业中心古吉拉特邦如今能够以有竞争力的价格和良好的品质生产所需的一切，Vishakha Group的吉吉什·多希（Jigish Doshi）表示。该公司为太阳能电池板生产铝边框以及各种其他部件（一座玻璃熔炉正在建设中）。在唐纳德·特朗普于2月对其征收高额关税之前，印度对美国的太阳能出口一直在激增。

电池超级工厂也在纷纷涌现。同样总部位于“工业邦”的另外两家企业集团——信实工业和阿达尼集团——正与中国最大的电池制造商宁德时代（CATL）就本地生产合作进行洽谈。印度的半导体生态系统也开始成形。今年印度已新开设五家芯片制造厂，其中四家位于“工业邦”。这些工厂主要组装和测试用于汽车、冰箱等产品的基础芯片，预计未来几年印度人对这类芯片的需求量将非常巨大。但印度政府也在试图鼓励生产更先进的芯片。在上月的一次行业会议上，芯片制造供应链中的美国和日本公司承诺建立工厂，生产半导体所需的高纯度气体和精密工程部件。

印度制造业仍有很长的路要走。“工业邦”远非全球制造业重镇。其制造业产出大约与土耳其相当，但人口却是土耳其的四倍。即使与同为贫穷但快速增长的亚洲国家越南相比，其人均制造业产出也低三分之一。这部分反映了跨国公司对与印度政府打交道的持续不安——这是给印度的第三条经验。其令人困惑且严格执行的税收制度尤其令人头疼。法国酒业公司保乐力加（Pernod Ricard）目前面临3.14亿美元的追溯性税收索赔。德国汽车制造商大众（Volkswagen）因被指控错误分类其进口零部件以支付较低进口关税而面临一场大规模法律诉讼。与此同时，苹果正在与印度反垄断机构就其应用商店相关的反竞争行为指控作斗争。（三家公司均否认有不当行为。）

即便如此，许多印度实业家仍心情乐观。尽管床品工厂仍低于满负荷运转，阿加瓦尔对其业务前景感到乐观。他在欧洲和南美发现了新市场，在等待美国取消对印度关税期间，这些市场将产生大量销售。而且他可以从这样一个事实中获得安慰：目前大型本地竞争对手仍然寥寥无几。但这种情况可能不会持续太久。■

item.title: 中国想进入你的大脑
item.description:
Business

商业 | 心智游戏 2026年10月8日 BrainCo是一家总部位于杭州的“神经科技”初创公司，其展厅展示了其可穿戴设备的强大能力。在一处展台，一名截肢者弹奏着钢琴，随后轻松地取下了无需手术即可安装的仿生手臂。在另一处，一名佩戴假腿的截肢者来回踱步，挑战围观者猜猜哪条肢体是机械的。BrainCo的设备不仅适用于严重事故的受害者。在另一个展台，本刊记者被要求躺下，戴上一个面具，该面具向前额叶输送低振幅微电流，据称可以诱导放松。 过去十年中，“脑机接口”（BCI）——能够向人脑发送信号并接收信号的机器——一直与Neuralink紧密相关。Neuralink是埃隆·马斯克于2016年创立的美国初...
item.content:encoded:
中国想进入你的大脑

商业 | 心智游戏 2026年10月8日

BrainCo是一家总部位于杭州的“神经科技”初创公司，其展厅展示了其可穿戴设备的强大能力。在一处展台，一名截肢者弹奏着钢琴，随后轻松地取下了无需手术即可安装的仿生手臂。在另一处，一名佩戴假腿的截肢者来回踱步，挑战围观者猜猜哪条肢体是机械的。BrainCo的设备不仅适用于严重事故的受害者。在另一个展台，本刊记者被要求躺下，戴上一个面具，该面具向前额叶输送低振幅微电流，据称可以诱导放松。

过去十年中，“脑机接口”（BCI）——能够向人脑发送信号并接收信号的机器——一直与Neuralink紧密相关。Neuralink是埃隆·马斯克于2016年创立的美国初创公司。该公司是首家进行无线大脑植入物试验的公司，该植入物使严重残疾人士能够仅凭思想长时间控制计算机，无需额外硬件。

然而，中国急于迎头赶上。今年早些时候发布的中央政府最新五年计划将神经科技列为中国寻求主导的未来产业之一，与量子计算、机器人和聚变能并列。国家此前已向企业、大学和监管机构调配资源，以努力缩小与美国的差距。2024年，科技部制定了脑机接口研究的伦理指南。2025年，医院引入了国家标准收费和计费代码，以便该技术更容易被用于医疗目的。今年秋天，首批脑机接口技术本科生将在天津大学开课，这是全球首个提供该课程的项目。

数百家中国初创公司和数千家供应商目前正在研发脑机接口产品。在Neuralink的主要中国挑战者中，有脑虎科技（NeuroXess），它是首家完成全无线大脑植入物临床试验的本地公司；阶梯医疗（StairMed），由中囯科技巨头阿里巴巴支持；以及脑机接口公司NeuCyber，它得到了国家支持。地方政府正在吸引投资；内陆省份安徽的官员已设定目标，到2028年批准三项植入电极临床试验。

侵入性较小的脑机接口技术在中国也引起了广泛关注。半侵入式方法是在大脑表面植入设备，而非穿透该器官。上海初创公司脑睿图（Neuracle）设计的一款旨在帮助手部运动功能的产品于3月获批，成为全球首款商业化的半侵入式脑机接口植入物。获批两天内，中国医疗管理机构为其分配了医疗保险代码，为销售铺平了道路。

此外还有非侵入式可穿戴设备，例如BrainCo生产的产品。目前约有20家公司在销售脑机接口可穿戴设备，从助眠设备到脑控游戏小工具，种类繁多。这些设备通常戴在头上，要么读取脑电波，要么泵入电流。行业高管们谈论着一个巨大的尚未开发的可穿戴神经科技市场。BrainCo的Nyx He表示，科学已不再是创造设备的制约因素。她表示，相反，重点正转向开发日常生活中实用的产品。中国的神经科技老板们将希望消费者保持开放的心态。■

item.title: 为什么你的零食比以前更块大、更有嚼劲

Business

item.content:encoded:
为什么你的零食比以前更块大、更有嚼劲

商业 | 口感运动 2026年10月8日

看看人们在超市里伸手去拿的新零食，你可能会注意到一种趋势。食品巨头亿滋国际推出了一款夹着酥脆Lotus Biscoff饼干的Dairy Milk巧克力棒。竞争对手玛氏则推出了Skittles Gummy Crystals，在耐嚼的糖果中加入了微小的脆粒，以及其广受欢迎的Cheez-It饼干的“超脆”版本。口感，似乎成了新的味道。

长期以来，大型食品公司对零食的每一个方面都进行了精心设计，使其令人欲罢不能，从包装的鲜艳色彩到撕开包装时散发的香气。但对口感的高度重视是新鲜事物。它包括产品食用时的声音，以及业内所称的“口感”。研究公司Mintel估计，声称具有口感特点的零食占比从2023年的31%上升至去年的41%。其中，“酥脆”是最流行的描述，尽管“耐嚼”和“绵软”也在迅速增长。

口感可能难以调配。亿滋国际研发主管Norberto Chaclin指出，混合酥脆和柔软的成分很棘手。水分会从湿润处迁移到干燥处，使脆的东西变软。以Dairy Milk Biscoff为例。它经过精心设计，用一层牛奶巧克力外壳防潮，并在饼干碎旁边加了一层基于脂肪的Biscoff酱以保持其酥脆。这款巧克力棒经过了长时间测试，以确保其口感在整个保质期内保持不变。

这样的复杂性或许可以解释为什么食品制造商难以跟上公众的兴趣。通过追踪社交媒体上的讨论，Mintel估计，截至今年4月的两年里，美国对“口感放纵型”零食的需求增长了28%。而供应量（以零食销量衡量）仅增长了8%。

是什么推动了对口感的渴求？一种解释是GLP-1减肥药的兴起，这类药物抑制了患者的食欲。这意味着当他们伸手去拿零食时，首先会问：“值得吗？”研究公司MMR的Andrew Wardlaw指出。更大的感官冲击——包含声音、感觉和风味——增加了“产品戏剧性”，使吃零食更具吸引力。另一个因素是社交媒体。年轻消费者沉迷于短视频，视频中网红们开着最大音量咀嚼食物。品牌已经注意到这一点，制作出旨在诱发ASMR（自主性感觉经络反应）的广告——这种内容会让一些人产生刺痛般的放松感。去年，带有“crunchtok”标签的帖子累计观看量超过15亿次。

食品行业本身则将口感视为最后一种差异化形式。Wardlaw先生认为，零食的口味已达到“顶峰”，几乎没有新奇的 flavours 可供探索（除非进入令人倒胃口的领域）。大多数消费者已经尝试过各种形式的巧克力，从整块（大块和迷你）到分享装和单人装零食袋。对许多人来说，吃零食已变得越来越无意识，因为他们一边刷社交媒体或狂刷剧集。亿滋国际的营养师Rimi Obra-Ratwatte将人们对口感丰富零食的需求比作观看3D电影的愿望。“一切都变成了放大体验，”她解释道。大型食品公司希望消费者不会很快厌倦这种体验。否则，他们可能面临另一种“关键时刻”。■

item.title: 唱片公司因AI音乐而手忙脚乱
item.description:
Business

商业 | 新一集Napster篇章 2026年10月8日 音乐行业对技术剧变并不陌生。从黑胶唱片到卡带到CD再到流媒体，音乐的录制和销售一直处于不断革命的状态。向流媒体的转变给行业带来了沉重打击。在Napster时代非法文件共享兴起、最终让位于合法流媒体之后，收入花了20多年才恢复，即使按名义价值计算，也只回到1990年代的水平（见图表1）。生成式人工智能开启了一个新的颠覆时代。它有可能改变音乐创作本身的整个过程。 AI制作的音乐已经让人感受到它的存在，既以“垃圾内容”的形式出现在时代精神中，也出现在排行榜上。糟粕比以往任何时候都多。总部位于巴黎的Deezer的老板亚历克西斯·兰特尔涅表示...
item.content:encoded:
唱片公司因AI音乐而手忙脚乱

商业 | 新一集Napster篇章 2026年10月8日 音乐行业对技术剧变并不陌生。从黑胶唱片到卡带到CD再到流媒体，音乐的录制和销售一直处于不断革命的状态。向流媒体的转变给行业带来了沉重打击。在Napster时代非法文件共享兴起、最终让位于合法流媒体之后，收入花了20多年才恢复，即使按名义价值计算，也只回到1990年代的水平（见图表1）。生成式人工智能开启了一个新的颠覆时代。它有可能改变音乐创作本身的整个过程。 AI制作的音乐已经让人感受到它的存在，既以“垃圾内容”的形式出现在时代精神中，也出现在排行榜上。糟粕比以往任何时候都多。总部位于巴黎的Deezer的老板亚历克西斯·兰特尔涅表示，每天约有9万首完全由机器生成的曲目上传到他的音乐流媒体服务——占总上传量的一半。最大的流媒体平台Spotify表示，过去一年已下架了7500万首“垃圾曲目”。其中许多垃圾内容是机器农场非法上传的，目的是骗取欺诈性版税。但许多人类艺术家也合法地使用AI来增强他们的创造力。“就像奥泽皮克，”兰特尔涅先生说。“每个人都在用，但没人愿意承认。”一个更大的问题是AI制作音乐的合法性。一些唱片公司指控AI音乐实验室盗版并提起诉讼。一些公司已经和解，希望从授权中比从诉讼中赚更多的钱。令人困惑的是，有的公司两者都做。正如咨询公司MIDiA Research的马克·穆里根所说，当用AI创作音乐的能力降低了进入门槛时，所有公司都在努力解决如何保持对行业控制权的问题。许多音乐行业高管在Napster时代磨练了技能（并签下了他们的第一批唱片合约）。他们不想再被打个措手不及。股市表明投资者感到担忧。两家最大的上市唱片公司——环球音乐集团（UMG）和华纳音乐集团（WMG）——的股价在过去几年里落后于整体市场（见图表2）。（第三大唱片公司索尼音乐未单独上市。）值得关注的关系是大型唱片公司与Suno之间的关系。Suno是一家备受争议的美国AI音乐公司，成立四年，最近估值54亿美元（超过WMG 147亿美元市值的三分之一）。这提供了一个自然实验：UMG和索尼音乐已起诉Suno，并在9月提起的案件中加倍下注；WMG曾是原诉讼的一部分，但已达成和解。 在新案件中，UMG、索尼音乐等公司指控Suno盗用了超过6万首受版权保护的录音，涉及从艾薇儿·拉维尼到贾斯汀·汀布莱克等艺术家，并将其输入其模型。根据美国版权法，每件作品的赔偿金最高可达15万美元，这可能表明原告正在推动巨额赔偿（或施压以达成丰厚的授权协议）。Suno承认，用于训练其模型的数千万条录音中包含受版权保护的材料。但它辩称，学习音乐风格并生成新的原创音乐在法律上属于“合理使用”。此事尚无定论：美国创意产业对AI实验室（包括Anthropic和OpenAI）提起了100多起诉讼，其中许多案件的关键在于合理使用是否适用。在Suno案件审理期间，WMG的和解也引起了关注。该唱片公司告诉投资者，其AI合作关系的收入将在本财年开始流入。这将是娱乐行业首批真正带来真金白银的AI交易之一。WMG的老板罗伯特·金克尔表示，与Suno和解的决定是基于权宜之计：法院可能需数年才能就合理使用作出裁决。“如果我能让合作伙伴放弃合理使用的论点并开始付钱给我们，我为什么要等？”他说。和解本身也可能预示着重大变化。例如，9月Suno推出了v6，据称这是其首个完全使用WMG等公司授权音乐训练的模型系列。选择加入的艺术家和词曲作者在其作品被使用时，将根据Suno的订阅收入与Suno分享收益。金克尔先生预计这将为艺术家带来新的收入来源，因为粉丝们会根据其曲目的混音或 mashup 创作并发布AI音乐。他举例说，可以在 Fleetwood Mac 的《Dreams》上叠加艾瑞莎·弗兰克林的嗓音。UMG对粉丝混音也有自己的雄心。今年，它宣布与Spotify和AI音频初创公司ElevenLabs达成授权协议，使UMG的材料能够被“超级粉丝”改编。Spotify营销主管萨姆·杜博夫表示，需求是存在的。他估计，在某些平台上，未经授权的混音和翻唱每月有10亿次播放；Spotify希望将市场规范化。UMG的迈克尔·纳什表示，公司估计20-30%的流媒体用户愿意为获得AI驱动的超级粉丝产品支付高达目前订阅费两倍的费用。超级粉丝希望成为音乐的共同创作者而不仅仅是听众的想法尚未经过验证。音乐高管指出，创意产业的其他领域，粉丝们会为了乐趣而修改他们喜欢的材料，从同人小说到“modding”（修改）电子游戏。他们希望AI能激发观众对音乐的类似参与。一些人还提到了中国，在腾讯音乐娱乐等音乐流媒体平台上，修改正在日益流行。不过，中国的趋势并不总能传到西方。很多取决于有多少顶尖艺人选择加入。纳什先生希望有1000位UMG艺人加入。但到目前为止，UMG、WMG、Spotify和Suno都没有公布任何已签约的大牌明星，这表明对艺术完整性的疑虑仍然很高。而在顶级名字同意参与之前，很难知道他们的粉丝会有多热情。MIDiA的穆里根先生表示，唱片公司与AI音乐制造商之间的合作关系具有防御性质：行业巨头，无论是唱片公司还是流媒体平台，都希望巩固现状。“他们想控制AI，而不是让AI控制他们，”他说。但他们可能仍会被绕过。他认为，新技术将使新艺术家更容易在没有唱片合约的情况下崭露头角，并使新的流媒体平台得以出现。“最终你会看到一个更加碎片化的音乐世界。”UMG和Spotify的高管不同意。他们押注稀缺性——超级巨星时代的标志——将占上风。UMG的纳什先生（其签约艺人中包括泰勒·斯威夫特）表示，进入门槛降低的主要受益者不是新艺术家，而是“地毯式轰炸[流媒体]服务的欺诈者”。稀缺性来自巧妙的营销和受众培养。如果AI也学会了如何做到这一点，那么该行业将陷入深深的困境。■ 编者注（2026年10月5日）：本文已作修改，删除了Suno表示过早讨论的内容。

item.title: 捷豹的新车是其生存的最后机会
item.description:
Business

item.content:encoded:
捷豹的新车是其生存的最后机会

商业 | 拯救“大猫” 2026年10月8日

“你以前见过这样的车吗？”捷豹新款Type 01的设计师之一在10月6日于纽约揭幕这款1000马力电动轿车时问道。“捷豹故事的新篇章”长而低矮，气势恢宏。尽管声称“与过去的伟大捷豹一脉相承”，但该品牌的传统在很大程度上被淡化了。它被重塑为一个比以往版本更高端的全电动品牌，这既是对过去的告别，也是对昔日辉煌的回溯。这场大胆的转型是捷豹生存的最后机会。如果它所寻求的新客户不为之倾倒，那么“独一无二”的说法可能真的会成真。

多年来，如何处理捷豹一直让汽车高管们愁眉不展。自2023年简称为JLR的捷豹路虎，一直更依赖其另一部分业务，包括高端揽胜，其旗舰SUV起售价现已远超10万英镑（13.2万美元）。捷豹品牌可能从未为塔塔汽车赚过钱，塔塔汽车是印度企业集团旗下的汽车制造部门，于2008年以23亿美元从福特手中收购了JLR。尽管拥有运动型车型的传统——如20世纪60年代推出的E-Type——但捷豹的轿车长期以来一直是该品牌最畅销的产品。然而，随着时间的推移，它们获得了抽着烟斗的银行经理和高尔夫俱乐部停车场的老气形象。

塔塔为重塑捷豹产品线以挑战德国高端汽车制造商投入巨资，但这一努力并未奏效。尽管它成功地将车辆打造到类似的设计标准和制造质量，但大多数驾驶者仍然忠于他们的德国机器。2018年，捷豹达到顶峰，销量约为18万辆，而宝马和奔驰各自销量均超过200万辆。此后几年销量急剧下滑（见图表）。

最新一次重塑始于2021年，是一场更大的赌博。JLR已至少花费22.5亿英镑将捷豹重新打造为一个纯电动品牌。2024年，它停止了现有车型系列的生产。同年11月，它开展了一场营销活动，发布了一则颇具争议的广告， featuring 性别模糊的模特穿着色彩鲜艳的未来主义服装，却没有展示汽车，这激怒了汽车爱好者，甚至引发唐纳德·特朗普的评论（他的评价是“严重觉醒”）。该活动的两款概念车（亮粉色和淡蓝色）被评论家描绘为要么大胆要么疯狂。传统主义者（其中很少有人真正拥有过捷豹）对新圆体字形和去掉咆哮猫标志感到不满。该广告背后的代理商被更换，JLR强势的设计总监格里·麦戈文在不明原因的情况下离开了公司。

现在的问题是，焕然一新的捷豹能否说服足够多的年轻客户——该品牌正是瞄准他们——为Type 01支付至少13万英镑，这大约是2024年停产时最便宜捷豹价格的四倍。行业分析师费利佩·穆尼奥斯认为，在这个价位上，这款车将“非常小众”。不利因素还包括高端电动汽车需求不确定——保时捷Taycan销量不佳是德国品牌近期困境的原因之一——以及来自竞争对手的日益激烈的竞争。想要购买昂贵电动车的驾驶者可能更喜欢新款梅赛德斯AMG GT或宾利首款电动车Torcal。有些人甚至可能选择特斯拉翻新的Roadster，它计划于10月15日亮相，据称配备了火箭推进器。

新款捷豹的定位也凸显了JLR一个长期存在的问题：品牌之间的重叠，以及寻找新细分市场以拓宽其盈利业务的需求。揽胜正在扩大其电动SUV系列，价格与Type 01大致相当，甚至计划推出一款纯电动轿车，将直接与新捷豹竞争。

在JLR面临压力之际，押注捷豹可能会消耗资源并分散注意力。一年前的一次网络攻击导致公司生产中断数周。截至2026年3月的一年中，税前利润骤降至仅1400万英镑，而前一年为25亿英镑。中国销量暴跌，关税损害了美国业务，美国是公司最大的市场，占其销量近30%。作为回应，JLR在9月宣布将通过裁减4000个工作岗位来削减成本，这约占其员工总数的十分之一。

捷豹老板罗登·格洛弗表示，“成功将以每年数万辆的销量来衡量。”有传言称，计划将新车的电动平台用于SUV和双门轿跑车。然而，如果Type 01未能找到足够多的买家，它可能会成为捷豹故事的终章。■

item.description:
Business

商业 | 代币总额 2026年10月8日 记账单位是个有用的东西。甚至在货币普及之前，人们就试图想出标准化的方式来记录事物。在《伊利亚特》中，用青铜或黄金制作的盔甲价值以牛的数量来表示（青铜九头牛，黄金一百头牛）。毛皮、巨石和成堆的盐都曾用作计量标准。人工智能的宇宙由它自己的单位支配：代币（token）。这些是文本片段，通常为四个字符，AI模型读取或回复时使用。然而，代币的问题在于，它们不像牛或毛皮那样运作得那么整齐。首先，事先不清楚一项给定任务会消耗多少代币。模型制造商收取的价格也相差悬殊：中国初创公司DeepSeek提供的一个流行模型，每个代币的价格大约是顶级美国实验室Anthropic...
item.content:encoded:
模型市场的崛起

商业 | 代币总额 2026年10月8日

记账单位是个有用的东西。甚至在货币普及之前，人们就试图想出标准化的方式来记录事物。在《伊利亚特》中，用青铜或黄金制作的盔甲价值以牛的数量来表示（青铜九头牛，黄金一百头牛）。毛皮、巨石和成堆的盐都曾用作计量标准。人工智能的宇宙由它自己的单位支配：代币（token）。这些是文本片段，通常为四个字符，AI模型读取或回复时使用。然而，代币的问题在于，它们不像牛或毛皮那样运作得那么整齐。首先，事先不清楚一项给定任务会消耗多少代币。模型制造商收取的价格也相差悬殊：中国初创公司DeepSeek提供的一个流行模型，每个代币的价格大约是顶级美国实验室Anthropic生产的尖端模型的四十分之一。对于使用AI的公司来说，这让人非常头疼。一个简单的任务，比如让模型处理发票，可能会累积出巨额账单。为了防范这种情况，一些企业限制员工可以消耗的代币数量。但这可能会阻碍生产力。

这种混乱催生了一种新的业务：模型市场。其中最著名的是OpenRouter，由Alex Atallah于2023年联合创立。ChatGPT发布后，Atallah开始思考未来会是什么样。“我当时最大的问题是：这会不会变成一个OpenAI主导的赢家通吃市场，”他说。他怀疑这样的结果，从而得出结论：市场将在AI行业中发挥核心作用。OpenRouter让客户可以轻松地在不同模型之间切换。如果Anthropic的Claude宕机了，他们可以使用OpenAI的模型。或者当某个实验室在代币上打折时，他们可能会切换过去。OpenRouter对通过其平台路由的使用收取少量费用。业务如此之好，以至于8月份支付巨头Stripe同意收购这个市场。据报道，它将为一家成立仅三年的公司支付75亿美元。

OpenRouter并不是唯一的模型市场。大型云计算提供商也运营类似的服务。亚马逊通过Bedrock提供一系列模型，通过现有云服务协议计费；谷歌通过其Vertex AI服务提供同样的服务。但许多客户对这些产品持怀疑态度：云巨头们自己构建模型，并投资于前沿实验室，很难保持中立。

OpenRouter最初在开发者中获得了追随者，因为它提供了一种尝试多种模型的方式，以及一种快速判断哪个模型表现最佳的手段。ChatGPT发布后，许多AI实验室开始“基准冲刺”——制造能轻松通过某些测试（如SAT）但在更有用的任务上表现不佳的模型。在OpenRouter的市场上，客户用真金白银投票，创造了一个更公平的排名系统。

最近，公司开始将OpenRouter作为控制成本的工具。值得注意的是，DeepSeek和另外两家中国模型制造商Z.ai和小米提供的廉价系统主导了该平台上的代币消耗（尽管OpenAI的一个模型目前也表现不错）。即便如此，Atallah认为许多企业在使用代币方面仍然不够精细。他向企业客户建议，根据任务的开放性程度，将任务分为低、中、高“熵”。廉价模型通常足以处理低熵任务，比如决定哪个模型应该审查一些代码，也能处理大量中熵任务，比如实际审查那段代码。前沿模型可以保留给高熵任务，比如从头编写代码。“我看到很多公司犯的错误是，他们根本不去分解这些事情。对他们来说都是一样的，”Atallah说。“那真是巨大的浪费。” ■

item.description:
Business

商业 | 熊彼特 2026年10月8日 英国的问题，安迪·伯纳姆上个月对他的工党支持者说，在于“股东从不亏损，公众从不获胜”。然而如今伯纳姆自己却陷入了麻烦，因为他钟爱的股东亏损太多。上周，英格兰足球超级联赛裁定，在其阿联酋老板的掌管下，顶级足球俱乐部曼城通过“虚假”交易严重低报了财务亏损，从而使该俱乐部得以在支出上超越其竞争对手。 大多数从企业丑闻演变为政治事件的问题，都是以轰然巨响的方式爆发的。石油泄漏或银行挤兑既出人意料又令人震惊。但曼城事件却几乎没有让任何人感到意外。（不出所料，该俱乐部否认有不当行为。）联赛方面的指控源于2018年泄露的文件，涉及2008年阿联酋副总统谢赫·曼苏尔收...
item.content:encoded:
奖杯与资产

商业 | 熊彼特 2026年10月8日

英国的问题，安迪·伯纳姆上个月对他的工党支持者说，在于“股东从不亏损，公众从不获胜”。然而如今伯纳姆自己却陷入了麻烦，因为他钟爱的股东亏损太多。上周，英格兰足球超级联赛裁定，在其阿联酋老板的掌管下，顶级足球俱乐部曼城通过“虚假”交易严重低报了财务亏损，从而使该俱乐部得以在支出上超越其竞争对手。

大多数从企业丑闻演变为政治事件的问题，都是以轰然巨响的方式爆发的。石油泄漏或银行挤兑既出人意料又令人震惊。但曼城事件却几乎没有让任何人感到意外。（不出所料，该俱乐部否认有不当行为。）联赛方面的指控源于2018年泄露的文件，涉及2008年阿联酋副总统谢赫·曼苏尔收购该俱乐部后不久达成的交易。这些交易此前已成为欧洲足球管理机构在2020年结案的一起案件的主题。

与其说曼城事件引发了愤怒，不如说它引发了更糟糕的东西——对足球以及对英国的麻木。“这大概不是我的问题，而是他们的问题，”曼城前主教练罗伯托·曼奇尼谈到他与阿布扎比一家俱乐部的第二份合同时如此表示，据称这份合同增加了他的收入却没有影响曼城的账目。“嗯，那当然。”这就是英国公众的反应——他们已经习惯了破碎的体制，对掌权者的期望也早已大打折扣。令人震惊的不是这个国家商业和文化生活的很大一部分建立在欺骗之上，而是一个有一定权威的机构竟然会将其揭露出来。

至于伯纳姆本人，他现在发现自己与他曾认为是好人的投资者产生了分歧：据报道，当他担任市长时，阿联酋人向曼彻斯特投入了大量资金，而当他担任首相时，他们却计划停止向米尔顿凯恩斯提供资金。这场丑闻的设计简直不能再巧妙，它让英国对自己擅长的事情感到痛心。英超联赛是世界上最富有、最具观赏性的足球联赛。这起争议正在伦敦解决，而伦敦仍然是全球企业纠纷的首要场所；处理曼城案件的律师们收取的大概是天文数字般的费用，他们几乎是英国经济中唯一能与美国比肩的领域。比赛日当天，人们挂起了横幅，向代表足球俱乐部的律师们致敬。“你就是那个扮演帕尼克勋爵辩护的人吗，老兄？希望司力达律师事务所能在圣诞节前解决我们的进攻问题。”

英国实际上从其海湾投资者那里得到了一笔好交易，这一点并不重要。当一个国家再也负担不起自己引以为傲的奖杯资产时，据说它就面临着一种选择：高贵的毁灭，或不光彩的外国所有权。漫步在英国国家的心脏白厅，这一选择显得更加鲜明。旧战争办公室和苏格兰场已被改造成由国际资本拥有的豪华酒店。海军部拱门如今是一家华尔道夫酒店，俯瞰着通往白金汉宫的林荫道，仿佛在说：“你是下一个！”这已经够令人沮丧的了，直到你在街道尽头看到另一种景象——那里被一系列频繁更换的、灯火通明的糖果兼纪念品兼电子烟商店所占据。英国是一个店主的国度，而这些商店是这个国家令人沮丧的象征。

英国足球拒绝了这种破败，转而拥抱来自国外的财富。曼城的主席是阿布扎比主权财富基金老板、大英帝国司令勋章获得者哈勒敦·阿尔·穆巴拉克。伯纳姆钟爱的埃弗顿曾归一位居住摩纳哥的英国伊朗裔商人所有，他因与俄罗斯金属大亨合作而声名鹊起（“太妃糖”在险些被一家此后破产的投资公司收购后，于2024年转给了现任美国老板）。上个赛季，基尔·斯塔默爵士的阿森纳在酋长球场赢得了联赛冠军。纽卡斯尔联队（显然是托尼·布莱尔爵士最喜爱的球队）在英国零售业亿万富翁迈克·阿什利手下萎靡不振，但在沙特主权财富基金旗下境况有所好转。

然而，理性并不能治愈麻木，而麻木最终总是具有破坏性的。如果联赛的裁决开始让人觉得是意料之中的结局，那些热爱比赛但对背后肮脏交易无动于衷的球迷，可能会觉得这并不比在一场结果已定的选举中投出一票更有吸引力。可能对曼城施加的制裁不会扭转这种冷漠的潮流。追溯性地将奖杯授予 rival 球队不会给他们带来任何庆祝的理由。将曼城踢出联赛会让对手的胜利变得不那么真实，直到他们回归。该俱乐部已对联赛的裁决提出上诉，这保证了更多的法律争论——以及更多的麻木。就在去年，2008年倒闭的美国银行雷曼兄弟的伦敦分支机构终于在所有索赔得到解决后完成清算。曼城丑闻会不会持续更久？

20世纪英国伟大的法官之一丹宁勋爵写道，体育争议最好由体育界自己解决，而不是由法院解决。21世纪英国伟大的电视商人之一休格勋爵则认为，自我监管已经失效：“英超联赛的老板们需要有胆量现在就施加惩罚，并立即执行。”麻木不仅是英国面临的危险。今年夏天，国际足联（全球足球管理机构）主席詹尼·因凡蒂诺试图将部分赛事业务出售给投资者，但未能成功。这确实引起了轩然大波。但因凡蒂诺也将他组织的恩惠授予了唐纳德·特朗普，而特朗普家族的企业交易（包括涉及海湾资金的交易）如今大多已被人漠然视之。在特朗普总统任期初期，与他合作的商人们容忍这些交易，认为放松管制更为重要。如今很少有人再提及它们。 ■

item.content:encoded:
全球正面临一场严峻的液化天然气危机

财经与经济 | 流动与失序 2026年10月8日 四年前，欧洲在乌克兰战争中与俄罗斯管道切断联系后，曾急于替代其40%的天然气进口。它转向了卡塔尔——当时全球最大的液化天然气（LNG）生产国。“26多年来我们一直可靠，”这个海湾国家的能源部长萨阿德·阿尔-卡比当时在他金碧辉煌的办公室里夸耀道。“我们从未错过任何一批货物。”如今，这番豪言显得空洞。今年3月，当伊朗在美国和以色列攻击后封锁霍尔木兹海峡时，卡塔尔宣布遭遇不可抗力，并告知买家无法履行合同。此后它仅发运了98批货物，比2025年同期少了536批。缺口达3900万吨，占去年全球供应量的9%，且仍在扩大。亚洲液化天然气价格约为每百万英热单位（mmBtu）25美元，比战前高出140%（见图表1）。 乐观主义者——或者在这种情形下勉强算得上乐观的人——指出，这仍远低于2022年每百万英热单位70美元的峰值，尽管全球六分之一的供应已中断。亚洲过去接收卡塔尔出口的80%以上，如今已设法从美国、澳大利亚、马来西亚、尼日利亚及其他生产国获得了几乎与通常所需相当的数量。2026年迄今亚洲液化天然气进口量为1.93亿吨，仅比去年同期低700万吨（见图表2）。政客们似乎更担心柴油而非天然气。这是自满：真正的液化天然气考验尚未到来。一些买家推迟采购，寄望价格下跌。许多其他买家则孤注一掷地押注新的液化天然气来源，以减少对海湾地区的依赖。这两种赌注都有风险。若未能奏效，可能要到为时已晚时才会明朗。 迫在眉睫的考验正在逼近。夏季通常是欧洲公用事业“为冬季囤积脂肪”的时候。这解释了为何2022年天然气价格在8月见顶。然而，今年欧洲买家却让亚洲抢走了通常流向他们的大西洋货物。一些人仍希望战争迅速结束。但大多数人指望的是厄尔尼诺带来的暖冬——这种天气模式会升高欧洲气温。预测者预计欧洲人今年将推迟开启供暖。巨大的赌注押在预测者模型的准确性上。欧洲天然气储存量仅为73%，是历年同期最低纪录，而2022-25年的平均值为90%（见图表3）。德国的储气量仅为59%。能源贸易商Six One Commodities将过去十个冬天的天气数据输入其计算机模型，以测算在现有储量基础上，到春季欧洲还能剩下多少天然气。在三个模拟年份中，储量将降至极低水平，以致提气速度可能放缓并需要采取紧急措施。 9月30日，德国政府下令一家国有进口商在12月15日前确保额外的8太瓦时天然气能力，相当于8批液化天然气货物。但欧盟委员会似乎并不急于恢复其因战争而放宽的要求——即公用事业需在11月前将储气量补充至90%（若恢复，且各国政府涌入市场抢购，他们将需要支付溢价）。同时，现货即期交付价格高于期货价格。因此大多数进口商几乎没有囤货的动力。数据公司S&P Global的Zhi Xin Chong认为，如果天气保持温暖且卡塔尔的供应在12月前恢复正常，欧洲将能挺过去，天然气价格也将下跌。而这两个都是令人不安的“如果”。分析师估计，若11月意外寒冷，欧洲将争抢货物，价格可能飙升至每百万英热单位30-40美元。若寒冷持续，与亚洲的竞争将加剧。一位新加坡前能源官员警告称，在真正严酷的冬天，“价格可能没有上限”。而电网任何其他环节的问题——水电站水库干涸、核反应堆意外停堆、俄罗斯对欧洲能源基础设施的攻击——都可能将价格推至天际。至于卡塔尔，它尚未重启其液化装置。这表明它并不认为和平即将到来。若其供应不能很快恢复，欧洲将需要额外2000万吨液化天然气以在明年冬天前补充库存。其对供应的寻找将在整个2027年推高价格。海湾危机终结了大多数液化天然气观察人士在战前所持的全球市场将在2026年转为过剩的观念。然而，支撑这一观念的许多新液化天然气项目仍在推进中。Six One Commodities的Aimie Parpia表示，反常的是，当前短缺越严重，未来潜在的供应过剩就越大。上月在曼谷举行的年度盛会Gastech上，可以窥见最终超级过剩的迹象。在为期四天的会议中，一流的出口商——开发商、能源巨头、国有巨擘——通过平板拼接屏幕和油轮模型展示了新项目。交易商在会场中穿梭，锁定未来的货物。设备制造商订单排满。进口商现在追逐新合同，同时担心日后过度采购。关键词是“多元化”。咨询公司Wood Mackenzie的Massimo Di Odoardo表示，对持续价格波动的预期，让开发商得以继续推进今年早些时候看似前景不太确定的新供应项目。仅美国一地，液化能力预计到2030年将翻近一番。加拿大的液化能力也将大幅攀升。更小型的模块化液化装置的出现，正在打开从阿根廷到塞内加尔等曾经缺乏建设液化天然气项目基础设施的国家的气田。总体而言，新项目到2030年可能使全球供应增至6.3亿吨，比去年增长近60%。与此同时，需求将低于战前预测（见图表4）。包括中国在内的一些国家已取消新建进口终端计划，担心另一场地缘政治危机可能令其陷入困境。许多国家正在重启燃煤电厂、发起雄心勃勃的可再生能源招标，并重新考虑核电。另一家咨询公司Rystad Energy预测，到本十年末，年需求将为5.74亿吨，低于战前的5.83亿吨。 如果卡塔尔全力恢复生产且所有计划项目都能实现，供应将超出需求5500万至7500万吨。届时市场平衡将意味着要么有生产商低于产能运转，要么有买家超需求购买，或者两者兼有。分析师认为，无论如何，液化天然气价格都可能跌至每百万英热单位6美元以下。这低于大多数长期合同下提取货物的成本。由于担心未来几年充满考验，买卖双方都在追逐“灵活性”。日本JERA和德国Uniper等大型公用事业公司正在吸纳交易人员、储罐和再气化装置，以便持有多余采购并在价格合适时转售。项目开发商为获取更多利润，正在去除中间商并建立自己的交易部门。石油和天然气巨头纷纷签署协议，成为小客户的一站式服务商。结果可能是成群交易商互相买卖，或向供应已十分充足的下游用户销售。一些人将持有无法售出的货物，积累亏损。资本提供者可能变得过于谨慎。天然气危机的直接后果已经够糟了。其连锁效应可能让市场在未来多年内持续失衡。■

item.title: The bond market sell-off is helping the dollar
item.description:

Finance & economics | The dollar smirk Oct 8th 2026 NO FORECAST IS ever a complete consensus in financial markets. But some get close. At the end of 2025 the idea that the dollar would weaken was one. Dollar bulls were few. Most big investment banks and asset-management firms made bearish pr...
item.content:encoded:
The bond market sell-off is helping the dollar

Finance & economics | The dollar smirk

Oct 8th 2026

NO FORECAST IS ever a complete consensus in financial markets. But some get close. At the end of 2025 the idea that the dollar would weaken was one. Dollar bulls were few. Most big investment banks and asset-management firms made bearish predictions. So did The Economist: in February we suggested that the greenback might extend last year’s miserable run, as its safe-haven status continued to fade.

So far, so wrong. The DXY index, which measures the dollar against a small basket of rich-world currencies, has risen by 4% in 2026 (see chart). It is at its highest since Donald Trump began his trade world war in April last year. Several factors, not least global enthusiasm for American stocks, have helped frustrate the dollar doomsters. But these factors will not support the greenback for ever.

The movements of other currencies are part of the explanation. Investors have soured on the euro, in particular. It has slid from $1.17 to around $1.12, owing to growing worries about political and fiscal stability in Europe’s currency union. The yield on French ten-year government bonds has risen from 3.5% to 4.9% this year amid fears of fiscal mayhem, and is now around 1.3-1.4 percentage points above the German equivalent. Investors dumping euros have only so many places to go: the dollar is an obvious choice (the euro is down against sterling and the yen, too).

Another reason for the dollar’s rally is darkly ironic: the rise in energy prices caused by America’s war with Iran. In the past high oil prices typically weakened the greenback. Oil was something that America bought from abroad, and although crude is priced in dollars, many of those it handed over to foreign sellers would eventually be converted into some other currency. Since America became a net energy exporter in the late 2010s, thanks to the shale-fracking boom, this mechanism has gone into reverse. Pricey petrol and diesel may be a political headache for Mr Trump’s Republican Party a month before midterm elections, but they are a salve for the dollar.

A deeper source of the dollar’s strength is the American economy, which continues to surprise even optimists. Late last year economists expected growth of between 1.6% and 1.9%, at an annualised rate, in each quarter this year. In fact growth hit 2.5% in the first quarter and 2.2% in the second, fuelled by household consumption and business investment in infrastructure for artificial intelligence. The third quarter may have been stronger yet: the Atlanta Fed’s “nowcast” points to 3.7%.

A hot economy may force the Federal Reserve to keep raising interest rates, which makes owning Treasury bonds and other interest-bearing American assets more lucrative. In the year to July foreign buyers bought a net $450bn or so of American corporate debt, the most in any such period in nearly 20 years even after adjusting for inflation. Foreigners are hungrier still for American equities: in the same 12 months they purchased a net $900bn-worth of American stocks and investment-fund units. That is a record for any 12-month stretch—and 80% above an earlier peak in 2021.

The problem for the dollar is that these sources of strength are narrower than in the past. Historically America’s currency rallied both when the country’s economy was going strong and when the world, even including America, was falling to pieces. Stephen Jen, a currency strategist and investor, dubbed this the “dollar smile”.

Now the smile is more of a lopsided smirk. Although the dollar’s movement against the euro shows that its appeal as a safe haven remains, this matters much less than the allure of America’s risk assets. Should those assets disappoint—if, say, the boom turns out to be a bubble and pops—return-chasing investors will dump them, and the dollar, as quickly as they snapped them up. Currency traders had better get used to bigger mood swings. ■

item.content:encoded:
为什么股票是新的砖瓦

财经版块 | 纸面百万 2026年10月8日

新生周是英国大学生活的入门仪式，往往伴随着廉价啤酒和黏糊糊的舞池。对于德国出生的苏菲·布兰克来说，这让她初次接触到了另一种英国传统：踏上房产阶梯。她说，她那群刚出校门的新同学已经在规划如何拥有自己的住房了。现年33岁的布兰克从事人工智能和内容创作工作，并在社交媒体上发布理财相关内容。她说自己在伦敦西部的诺丁山“快乐地租房”，并把积蓄投入了股票。她宣称，房产阶梯可以再等等。

在德国，人们倾向于租房居住。但在英语国家，人们只要负担得起就会买房，并且长期以来通过这种方式积累大部分财富，这得益于二战后鼓励购房政策的广泛推行。在美国和加拿大，房主比租房者更富有，而且这一差距随时间不断扩大。据贷款机构约克郡建房互助会估计，在英国，到退休年龄时，房主平均比租房者富裕近80万英镑（约合110万美元），其中房产几乎占了一半的差距。在澳大利亚，大约每七个纳税人中就有一人拥有投资性房产。

如今，房产是否还是通往财富的道路似乎不那么确定了，尤其是对年轻人而言。尽管许多国家的住房市场近期有所降温，但根据《经济学人》的最新估算，经通胀调整后房价仍接近历史高位。对许多人来说，登上房产阶梯的成本高得难以想象：在爱尔兰，18至34岁的人群中有五分之三与父母同住。但房产作为投资的吸引力也在下降。随着利率上升抑制房价，家庭财富中来自股票的比例超过了房产，逆转了二十年的趋势。据咨询公司内部的智库麦肯锡全球研究院（MGI）计算，2025年全球家庭财富增加了40万亿美元，其中57%来自股票，15%来自房产——这与之前25年形成鲜明对比，那期间房产的平均占比为52%，股票为26%（见图表）。

美国处于这一转变的极端一端。据高盛银行计算，7月份股票在家庭财富中的占比自二战以来首次超过房产。在因房价过高而买不起房的年轻人中，股票投资的激增尤为明显。摩根大通发现，2015年至2024年间，25岁人群中开设投资账户的比例增长了六倍，该银行认为这一趋势可能与高昂的住房成本有关。

资产价值的波动是主要原因。数据公司穆迪分析预测，2026年至2035年间，美国房价年均涨幅将从过去十年的大约5%放缓至2.1%。与此同时，英格兰的平均房价按实际价值计算现在比二十年前还要低。相比之下，股票正在蓬勃发展。MGI的扬·米施克表示，企业股票市值与资产净账面价值的比率已达到历史最高点，比互联网泡沫时期的峰值高出50%。

政策也发生了转变。各国政府正在取消助长房价膨胀的税收优惠和补贴。5月，英国出台了新的租房者保护措施，使他们免受竞价战、过度涨租和无过错驱逐的影响。2023年，加拿大禁止外国人购买房产，该限制将于2027年到期。投机性投资因此正在退潮。英国的购房出租房东正以创纪录的速度抛售房产，多伦多的公寓销量暴跌。在美国，翻房数量下降，利润率也大幅缩水。

远离房产的转变有其好处：抑制房地产热潮降低了发生2008年式金融危机的风险。（话虽如此，股市也可能崩盘，而且一旦崩盘往往更快。）但这也反映了一种心态的转变。从布兰克社交媒体帖子的回应来看，年轻人对“房产能保障财务安全”这一观念越来越感到幻灭。她说，尽管拥有住房对“老一辈人来说效果极佳”，但如今的年轻人“只能梦想”达到同样的房产财富水平。■

item.content:encoded:
Indian celebrations will be more expensive this year

Finance & economics | Sugar spikes

Oct 8th 2026

Mumbai’s festive season kicks off with Ganesh Chaturthi, which this year fell in September. Hindus bring idols of the elephant-headed god into their homes. He stays for up to ten days before the often-colossal statues are immersed in the Arabian Sea. Mumbaikars also feast on his favourite food: dumplings stuffed with grated coconut and jaggery (set sugar-cane juice). Then come nine nights of dancing and fasting for Navratri, celebrating nine avatars of the goddess Durga. On the eighth day young girls representing aspects of Durga are given suji ke halwe, a mix of semolina, ghee and sugar.

Next is Dussehra, marking Lord Ram’s victory over the demon king Ravana—feted across northern India with tens of millions of jalebiya, deep-fried batter coils soaked in syrup. The sugar rush peaks with Diwali, the festival of lights, as families and offices exchange elaborate gift boxes of mithaiyan, traditional sweets.

This year such treats may taste bittersweet. India’s sugar prices have spiked. A kilo of sugar now costs 53 rupees (55 cents) in Mumbai, a 15% increase from 46 rupees in June. Anyone trying to beat the festive rush was stung even more: in late August prices reached 70 rupees in several cities (see chart), a rise of more than 50% in two months. Inflation more broadly, at 4.8%, is above the Reserve Bank of India’s target of 4%, prompting the first interest-rate rise in four years on October 7th.

Some suggest nature is ultimately to blame for the sugar-price spike. Unseasonal rains last October left cane fields in Maharashtra, a big sugar-producing state, waterlogged. Across the “sugar-cane belt” of northern India, farms have been struck by red rot, a fungal disease. Production forecasts for the year have been cut by more than a tenth. Others point at the government, which allowed 800,000 tonnes to be exported even after it was clear that output would fall short. It has since banned all exports. An unpopular policy of blending ethanol with petrol is an easy target. But it cannot explain the spike: only 9% of this season’s crop is being turned into ethanol, compared with 12% in 2022-23.

Lower production led to speculation. “It was expectations-led,” says Sanjay Kumar of Delhi University. Mills reckoned that their inventories of sugar would be worth more in the future and so kept a tight hold of their stocks. The government intervened, obliging mills to sell their quotas, through which it regulates supply, every 15 days rather than monthly. It also allowed some tariff-free imports. Normally sugar imports are subject to a tariff of 100%, enough to deter foreign producers. Although little foreign sugar has arrived, this was enough to cool the market “psychologically”, says Mr Kumar.

India’s government has in the past been more worried about the risk of glut than of shortage. A fixed “fair and remunerative” price is a political sweetener for farmers: 365 rupees per 100kg for the season starting this month, a third more than in 2018. Guaranteed returns encouraged planting and left mills with huge stockpiles. The government permitted exports and then subsidised them. By 2021 India was the world’s second-largest seller of sugar, after Brazil. When the World Trade Organisation ruled against its export subsidies, the government leaned harder on ethanol blending to absorb some of the excess. Intervention begat further intervention.

A warmer world risks upsetting this constructed market. El Niño, a recurring pattern of atmospheric warming, could contribute to a weak monsoon next year as well as poor output in Brazil and Thailand. The price of sugar futures, traded in America, has risen by 24% this year. Even allowing more imports would not shield Indian consumers from these higher global prices. A government that built a system to protect sugar-cane growers now wants to shield sweet-toothed Indians from higher prices. It is a sticky situation. ■

item.content:encoded:
寻找税收阿尔法

财经与经济学 | 梧桐树 2026年10月8日 没有什么比缴税更让富人——以及就此而言，不那么富的人——恼火的了。许多人宁愿把钱亏在一匹瘸腿马上，也不愿把钱交给政府。这种缴税的痛苦曾促使美国人发起革命。如今，它依然促使纽约人迁往佛罗里达，或者促使中层银行家移居米兰。最近，这种对税收的厌恶催生了美国最热门的投资策略：税收感知型投资，或称“税收阿尔法”。

“阿尔法”通常指相对于某个基准的超额回报，而“税收阿尔法”则指对美国迷宫般复杂税法的巧妙运用。它通常意味着制造亏损，用以抵销其他地方的收益，从而减少应缴纳给美国国税局（IRS）的税款。这一策略长期以来一直是顶级投资者投资组合中的特色。近来，它变得更加复杂，也更加普及。

税收感知型投资“傻瓜版”（并非字面意思的傻瓜：关于这个，请参阅上周的梧桐树专栏）涉及选择具有税收优惠的投资工具，博客Tax Alpha Insider的布伦特·沙利文表示。投资者可能会从频繁产生应税收益的共同基金，转向策略性地安排派息时机的交易所交易基金（ETF）。做得精明的话，这能带来额外的好处。

收益集中在少数几只头寸上的投资者，常常希望在不必承担巨额税单的情况下进行分散投资。第351条转换——税收感知型投资领域的一大支柱——正是让他们做到这一点。他们的顾问可以用他们的持仓来设立一只定制ETF，然后他们可以用其他资产进行再平衡。在ETF份额卖出之前，这一切都是免税的。新设立的第351条ETF所持资产价值从2022年的8亿美元跃升至去年的79亿美元。

但创造税收阿尔法最巧妙的方式，涉及投资者通常会避免的事情：亏钱。美国税法赋予投资者决定何时实现收益和亏损的余地。如果他们在某个纳税年度通过将资金投入税收感知型账户而产生亏损，他们就可以抵销投资组合中其他地方的收益。这样一来，即使他们的投资组合整体价值在上涨，他们也能减少税单。

一种方法是“直接指数化”。希望跟踪标普500指数的投资者可能会买入一篮子能代表该指数的股票。如果某只股票贬值，他们可以卖出它，记下亏损，然后买入一只权重相似的股票。这种做法的好处往往会随时间递减。最终，你会没有亏损股票可卖。

一种更新的技巧是税收感知型多空投资（确实太新了，以至于顾问们还没想出更朗朗上口的名字）。假设一位投资者将100美元投入一个税收感知型账户。她的投资经理可以利用卖空和保证金来提供130美元的多头头寸和30美元的空头头寸。（她的净敞口仍是100美元。）随着时间推移，经理会平掉亏损头寸（在上涨市场中，主要是空头），以记下亏损。他会再投资于类似证券，以维持账户的平衡。与直接指数化一样，该账户跟踪一个选定的基准，但在此过程中会产生更大的亏损。

税收是被延迟，而不是被消除：最终，投资者也必须实现收益。但延迟可能很有价值。沙利文估计，多空账户中的资产规模已从2023年的67亿美元飙升至2026年第三季度的至少1870亿美元。这一增长很大程度上归因于那些不仅向亿万富翁、也向普通百万富翁提供该策略的基金。去年，大型投资公司嘉信理财开始允许更多顾问在其平台上管理多空账户。但它们仍然是一项精英业务：到2026年第二季度，它们仅占其收入的1%。

税务部门想要叫停这场游戏。或许是担心监管机构的愤怒，在过去一年里，嘉信理财和另一家大型投资公司富达开始拒绝大量寻求开设多空账户的客户。9月28日，美国国税局和财政部表示，将对最激进的第351条转换征税。财政部还表示将调查其他流行的税收阿尔法来源。其部长斯科特·贝森特抱怨“滥用金融工程”和“旨在利用我们联邦税法的产品”。

贝森特当然知道，这种滥用之所以大量发生，很大程度上是因为税法本身在引诱它。像许多规避手段一样，税收阿尔法是税法错综复杂的产物——而贝森特只针对其中一小部分。顾问们喜欢它，因为这意味着在多年被超低成本被动基金挤压之后，能获得更高的费用。投资者喜欢它，因为它让他们能占到国税局的便宜。出于这两个原因，无论如何，它肯定会继续存在下去。■

item.title: Governments are mishandling the affordability crisis
item.description:
Finance & economics

Finance & economics | Free Exchange Oct 8th 2026 STRIKES, BREAD riots and “socialistic agitation”: these worldwide expressions of discontent had a common cause, argued Irving Fisher, an economist at Yale University, in 1912. That shared grievance was the rising “cost of living”. The problem ...
item.content:encoded:
Governments are mishandling the affordability crisis

Finance & economics | Free Exchange

Oct 8th 2026

STRIKES, BREAD riots and “socialistic agitation”: these worldwide expressions of discontent had a common cause, argued Irving Fisher, an economist at Yale University, in 1912. That shared grievance was the rising “cost of living”. The problem was felt in places as far apart as Canada and India, France and Japan. To expect any single locality to tackle the forces at work was almost as absurd as expecting “villagers on the Bay of Fundy to attempt to prevent the rise of the tides”.

The IMF agrees with him. In its latest World Economic Outlook, the fund’s economists look at more recent increases in the cost of living. The tides reached their highest points in 2007-08, when food and oil prices rose in tandem, and in 2022, after the invasion of Ukraine. Since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz the cost of living has once again been on the rise. During these crises, global factors have accounted for about 70% of the increase in the typical rich country, the IMF’s authors calculate. But of course national politicians tend to get closer to 100% of the blame.

What counts as a cost-of-living crisis (or, to Americans, an “affordability” crisis)? For most people, the answer is obvious. They know it when they see it printed on their shopping bill or posted outside a petrol station. But Fisher was keen to distinguish a “mere rise in prices”, otherwise known as inflation, from “a rise in prices more rapid than the rise in incomes”. A trolleyful of goods can cost more money without becoming any harder to obtain, if wages are rising just as fast.

The goods in the trolley can also change. A.A. Konüs, a Russian economist, defined the cost of living in 1924 as the expenditure required to secure a given “state of want-satisfaction”. If some prices rise and others fall, canny householders will change their shopping habits in response. They will satisfy their wants by buying less of the expensive stuff and more of the cheaper, “without necessarily changing the height of [their] standard of living”.

The IMF’s economists adopt a practical definition, concentrating on unusual increases in the cost of basic necessities, such as food and energy. Alternatives to these goods are hard to find. And their prices fluctuate violently, unlike other essentials, such as health care. To distinguish between cost-of-living crises and mere inflation, they rule out cases where the rising price of food and fuel is matched by a broader increase in consumer prices or wages.

By that definition, almost 90% of the 85 countries they study have suffered a cost-of-living crisis in the past 20 years. Eleven have suffered three or more. In the typical crisis, the cost of basic necessities rises by more than 8%, relative to other prices, over 18 months, and can remain higher for several years. Pay packets fail to keep up. At the worst point, inflation-adjusted wages fall by as much as 5.9%, relative to a crisis-free scenario.

In the face of this misery, what can be done? The people of the Bay of Fundy, which lies on the east coast of Canada, may be powerless to stop the tides, which rise higher in their bay than anywhere else. But they have not simply sat on their hands in the face of nature’s might. They have built hundreds of kilometres of dykes, punctuated by sluice gates, known as aboiteaux.

Policymakers around the world have been similarly active in response to cost-of-living crises. In emerging economies, these responses are evenly split between attempts to suppress the prices faced by end-buyers and efforts to raise the incomes of those affected. In rich economies, the split is more like 40-60 in favour of raising incomes. In the poorest countries, that mix is reversed.

Price-suppression, which includes cuts to tariffs and indirect taxes as well as price controls, can reduce inflation expectations “slightly”, the IMF authors concede. But these measures have little else to recommend them. They benefit the rich more than the poor for the simple reason that the rich buy more of the stuff the policies keep cheap. The IMF authors calculate that for every euro spent suppressing the price of electricity, gas and petrol in European countries, only 20 cents reached the poor.

Price-suppression sometimes takes the form of subsidies to producers. These make downstream firms more competitive overseas, increasing their exports. The money, in other words, flows from the taxpayer to foreign customers. Even price controls, which do not require direct payments from government coffers, can impose fiscal costs in the long run. The state must often bail out utilities that cannot pass on the extra cost of their inputs.

These measures also muffle the valuable signal that market prices send. Consumers have no reason to temper their demand or satisfy their wants with an alternative bundle of goods. They have no reason to wear a sweater rather than dialling up the thermostat. They are like reckless households in the Bay of Fundy who neglect to fortify their homes near the shore, confident that old flood barriers will keep them dry.

Why then do governments keep meddling with prices? Some poor countries lack the infrastructure to provide better kinds of help, such as means-tested handouts to the poor. Price controls or duty cuts are also quicker to enact. Rather than compensating people for hardship, they seek to prevent discontent at its root. The fact that the benefits are not confined to the poorest is a fiscal drawback but a political advantage.

Price-suppression is, if anything, becoming more popular. During this year’s crisis, about 70% of policy responses by rich countries’ governments have tried to keep a lid on prices. That was up from under 40% in 2022-23, after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Between those two episodes several incumbent governments around the world were ousted at the ballot box. Politicians do not want today’s cost-of-living crisis to cost them their own living. ■

item.content:encoded:
今年的诺贝尔科学奖是现实版科幻

科学与技术 | 跳出框框的思考 2026年10月8日

当威斯康星大学麦迪逊分校的弗朗西斯·哈尔岑在今年晚些时候接受他的诺贝尔物理学奖时，他将享受到难得的独自站在聚光灯下的特权。大多数物理学奖得主必须与一位合作者或竞争对手分享舞台。哈尔岑博士将是自1992年以来第一位独享所有荣誉的人。周二公布的获奖评语表彰了他“对冰立方中微子观测站的决定性贡献”，该探测器位于南极附近，占据一立方公里的冰层，汇集了14个国家450名研究者的努力。但据乌普萨拉大学物理学家、诺贝尔物理学奖委员会秘书乌尔夫·丹尼尔森所说，“没有他的科学远见，这是不可能实现的。”

探测中微子需要极大的科学远见。中微子呈电中性（因此得名“neutr-”），且体积微小（因此得名“-ino”），实际上它们既不受电磁力影响，也不受引力影响，这使得它们能穿过大多数粒子探测器而不被察觉。它们与普通物质的相互作用主要局限于通过名副其实的弱核力进行的交互。尽管中微子如同幽灵一般，但它们在宇宙中无处不在。它们是裂变和聚变反应的副产品，这使得太阳成为一个强大的近邻来源：每秒钟约有650亿个太阳中微子穿过指甲盖大小的区域。产生中微子的太阳反应也会释放其他粒子，包括质子。然而，有时到达地球的质子的能量比来自太阳的质子高出数百万倍。这表明它们来自更遥远、更强大的源头。这些天然粒子加速器究竟是什么，以及它们如何产生如此高能的粒子，在很大程度上仍是未知数。质子带电荷，因此在到达地球的途中会被磁场偏转，使其起源点难以追溯。然而，加速这些质子的相同过程也应该产生高能中微子。

在上世纪80年代，哈尔岑博士是意识到中微子不愿与物质相互作用、因此能长距离无阻碍穿行并充当来自其他不可见物体的理想信使的人之一。但探测它们仍然是个问题。此前的探测器依赖建造巨大的全氯乙烯（一种干洗液）容器，等待中微子与液体中原子之间的罕见相互作用。虽然类似的方法也可以应用于寻找更罕见的太阳系外中微子，但需要比以往建造的探测器大得多的设备才有可能捕捉到一个。于是，冰立方的想法应运而生。建设始于2004年，于2011年完成。两年之内，它捕捉到了28个高能宇宙中微子，为宇宙打开了一扇新窗口。周二，当被问及这扇窗口可能揭示什么时，通过电话联系到的哈尔岑博士回答说：“真正的兴奋之处在于我还无法回答这个问题。”

生理学或医学奖得主在概述其研究的潜在益处时可能被允许更加乐观。斯坦福大学的卡尔·德塞罗思、柏林洪堡大学的彼得·黑格曼和维尔茨堡大学的格奥尔格·纳格尔因奠定了光遗传学的基础而获得认可。这一技术使神经科学家能够利用光瞬时激活单个脑细胞，从而有可能精确确定特定细胞在做什么。这使研究人员能够研究基础神经生物学以及疾病的神经基础。

故事始于上世纪90年代的黑格曼博士。当时他正在研究一种名为衣藻的单细胞藻类属如何对光做出反应。他发现它们的反应比人眼的同等反应更快。在人眼视网膜中，一个蛋白质分子检测到光，然后间接触发另一个称为离子通道的蛋白质产生电信号。黑格曼博士假设，在他的藻类中，这一复杂的进程被压缩了。用当时可用的工具来验证他的猜测被证明是困难的，直到蓬勃发展的基因组学科学拯救了他。一组日本研究人员绘制了衣藻的DNA图谱，表明它包含两个基因，类似于某些其他生物体中光敏感蛋白的基因。当黑格曼博士获得纳格尔博士的协助时，这一见解得到了证实。纳格尔博士将新发现的两个基因的DNA插入一些青蛙的卵中，这些卵随后产生了足够数量的目标蛋白质以供测试。正如黑格曼博士所预测的那样，它们被证明是光刺激的离子通道。

意识到他们的发现后，纳格尔博士和黑格曼博士尝试将其中一个基因（编码现在称为channelrhodopsin-2的蛋白质）插入从仓鼠和人类胚胎中提取的肾细胞中。这也成功了。换句话说，他们发现了一种使哺乳动物细胞对光敏感的方法。然而，正是德塞罗思博士构想出将channelrhodopsin-2插入以其存在意义就是传递电信号的细胞——神经元中。当这个想法得到测试时，培养的大鼠神经元不仅在被光照射时做出反应，还能将信号传递给邻近的神经元。

宣布这一发现的论文发表于2005年，但其他研究人员也在探索类似的想法。三年前，当时在纽约纪念斯隆·凯特琳癌症中心工作的格罗·米森伯克使用来自果蝇的光敏感蛋白做了类似的工作。正如一些人所指出的，米森伯克博士可能有充分的理由感到恼怒。麻省理工学院的神经科学家爱德华·博伊登——他在斯坦福读博士时曾与德塞罗思博士合作——也是另一个令人惊讶的遗漏。不过，无论优先权的细节如何，这一领域此后已经爆炸式发展。德塞罗思博士的实验室引领了潮流，首先是在活体小鼠大脑中重复了在培养的大鼠细胞中所做的事情，然后发明了使用极细光学纤维照亮并从而刺激神经元群的技术。这些技巧结合起来，使研究人员能够控制小鼠胡须的运动。

光遗传学现在已经成为数千篇论文的主题。它被用于动物研究中，以探究抑郁症、精神分裂症、失明、耳聋、痴呆、成瘾和焦虑。甚至有人尝试用它来恢复一种名为视网膜色素变性的失明患者的视力。大橡树从小橡子长成。或者，在这种情况下，从小藻类长成。

化学奖，通常如此，也从生命研究中获得灵感。许多对生物学至关重要的分子是手性的，能够以两种镜像形式存在，至少在理论上，这两种形式在宇宙中应等量存在。然而，自然是无情地选择性的。对于生物体而言，氨基酸通常是左旋的；糖是右旋的。正是为了在理解这种不对称性可能如何产生方面取得进展，巴黎萨克雷大学的亨利·卡根和东京理科大学的Soai Kenso接到了来自斯德哥尔摩的电话。

在此之前，化学家已经能够选择性地生产具有给定手性的分子。但所有这些反应都依赖于手性催化剂，这种催化剂通常由不等量的左旋和右旋分子混合而成。假设是反应产物中左右旋分子的比例将与催化剂本身的比例匹配。这带来了一个问题：如果反应只能匹配催化剂的不对称性，那么大规模的不对称性又如何能出现呢？1986年，卡根博士通过发现手性催化剂可以超越这一基准，驳斥了这一假设。从催化剂中左旋分子比右旋分子多三倍开始，他可以设计出产生六倍失衡溶液的反应。这是一个有意义的改进，但仍然太小，无法将无生命物质的近乎完全对称性转变为生命所展现的近乎完全手性。

正是Soai博士弥合了这一差距。在2003年发表的工作中，他证明，可以通过工程手段使具有微小手性分子失衡的溶液产生手性不断增加的反应产物。这种自我放大可以产生快速变化。例如，仅重复反应三次，Soai博士就能使溶液的不对称性增加63万倍。所谓的Soai反应，并不是生命手性产生的方式。首先，Soai博士使用的试剂在40亿年前不可能存在。但正如一位诺贝尔奖委员会成员所解释的那样，尽管如此，这是自数十亿年前生命诞生以来，人们第一次从非手性分子组合中创造出手性。■

item.title: Burglars could be identified from airborne DNA
item.description:
Science & technology

Science & technology | Every breath you take Oct 8th 2026 BURGLARS HAVE been steadily running out of things they can safely leave behind at a crime scene. First came footprints, then fingerprints and stray fibres. Even microscopic strands of DNA left on tools and surfaces have been used to c...
item.content:encoded:
Burglars could be identified from airborne DNA

Science & technology | Every breath you take

Oct 8th 2026

BURGLARS HAVE been steadily running out of things they can safely leave behind at a crime scene. First came footprints, then fingerprints and stray fibres. Even microscopic strands of DNA left on tools and surfaces have been used to catch the incautious. Now they have something else to worry about: fragments of genetic material in the air.

All people, criminals and non-criminals alike, shed tiny traces of themselves wherever they go. Some of this material—mainly skin cells, dandruff and saliva—ends up suspended as a personal debris cloud that can hang around after the person is gone. A new study published in Forensic Science International: Genetics, a journal, shows that volunteers who pretended to ransack houses in controlled tests could be identified from DNA pulled from the air 30 minutes after they scarpered. As with most forensic evidence, it alone is not proof of wrongdoing. But it could raise some awkward questions for someone without a good reason to be there.

Carried out by a team led by Chiara Fantinato at Oslo University Hospital, the study is an impressive application of methods to capture and analyse what is known as environmental DNA (eDNA)—the genetic traces left by an organism in its surroundings. For more than two decades ecologists have used eDNA from water, soil and atmosphere to detect creatures without needing to see or capture them. The technique has been used to track elusive Burmese pythons in the Florida Everglades and to audit the inhabitants of Loch Ness. (Fish and plenty of eels. No plesiosaurs.)

In 2022 the Oslo group showed that enough eDNA could be collected from indoor air to construct genetic profiles of its occupants. In a separate test, they analysed office air to identify workers who had recently occupied the space. That led them to wonder if the same techniques could be used for forensic purposes. Working with a group in Australia, the researchers found 22 households, split evenly between Oslo and Adelaide, who were willing to allow into their homes first a mock burglar and then a forensics team in full protective gear to run an air-sampling device in the kitchen for a couple of hours.

The intruders were people who had never previously visited the houses. They were asked to spend 15 minutes inside, opening drawers and cupboards as a burglar might. After they fled the scene, the scientists waited 30 minutes, to simulate the delay before investigators might arrive, and then turned on what Dr Fantinato says was basically a vacuum cleaner. They sifted the material collected for DNA and analysed it in the usual way. As airborne DNA falls to the ground, where it contributes to surface dust, the researchers also collected sweeps to build their forensic profiles.

The results offered better news for housebreakers in Australia than Norway. Whereas the samples collected in Oslo could be matched to intruders in 82% of cases, the success rate dropped to 36% for Adelaide. The reasons for the difference are unclear, but could be due to such factors as environmental conditions, the number of people living in the house and how well the various rooms had been cleaned.

There are other complications to note. DNA found in the air does not always have to be from a recent visit, for example: movement can stir DNA-carrying dust into the air, or DNA from people who have never set foot inside could be carried in on people’s clothes. The researchers themselves were surprised by how sensitive their technique was. Despite the efforts they put in to prevent their own DNA leaking into the crime scenes, some was vacuumed up and identified anyway.

It is unlikely, Dr Fantinato says, that air samples would ever prove reliable enough to provide the clinching evidence of someone’s guilt. “It’s an investigative tool,” she says. “Like other types of DNA evidence, it’s just part of the puzzle.” It is still too early to apply the method to real cases. That will require understanding such nuances as why different people shed different amounts of DNA, and standardising techniques between labs. But her team has spoken to police forces about one day helping them with their enquiries. ■

item.content:encoded:
OpenAI声称解决了数百个长期存在的数学难题

科学与技术 | 数字运算 2026年10月8日 2026年10月6日（星期二）可能会成为数学史上最具里程碑意义的日子之一。就在那天，美国人工智能公司OpenAI宣布，其由未发布模型驱动的AI智能体在数周内至少解决了372个长期存在的数学问题。这些发现详细记载于700多篇AI生成的论文中，代表了前所未有的研究规模和速度。这样的成果泛滥让一些人感到不安。对许多研究者而言，发现潜在新数学真理的兴奋感，伴随着对其领域未来的担忧。他们表示，若不加倍谨慎，数学的大规模生产将带来更多解答，却更少理解。

AI在数学领域的进步突飞猛进。就在上个月，OpenAI声称同一个内部模型仅用88小时便解决了纳维-斯托克斯问题——千禧年大奖难题中的标志性问题之一。如今，数百个其他重要难题也被攻克。这些问题覆盖了整个数学体系，从代数、几何到概率论和逻辑学，其中许多已困扰专家数十年。自主数学家们得出一个解答所需的平均算力，仅相当于该公司公开可用模型约三个小时的推理量。尽管其余千禧年大奖难题仍未解决，但其中一两个似乎已取得进展。其中最引人注目的是黎曼猜想，它涉及素数的分布。在这场成果洪流中，还埋葬着一项对棘手难题“三维Kakeya极大猜想”的证明声明。纽约大学库朗研究所的数学家王虹，因在2026年7月的一个密切相关问题上做出贡献而被授予菲尔兹奖——数学界的诺贝尔奖。

究竟取得了哪些突破，以及通过何种手段实现，数学家们可能需要数年时间才能厘清；许多论文篇幅超过100页。在已解决的372个问题中，仅有127个附带了保证逻辑一致性的代码（该领域的规范），而智能体的内部推理过程只公布了其中10个。这372个问题也只是OpenAI向其智能体提出的4000个问题中的一部分，不过公司尚未公布哪些问题超出了其能力范围。这样的透明度将有助于评估该技术的能力与局限。

一些人担心这种做法不利于数学的长期进步。上个月OpenAI解决纳维-斯托克斯问题后不久，28位菲尔兹奖得主发表了一封公开信，警告AI实验室对待数学的方式与该领域的目标相悖。写信者指出，将开放性数学问题作为测试新模型能力的基准，模型制造者有可能过早地关闭探索方向，却没有产生新技术、新问题，最终也没有产生新理解。此后已有超过8000名同行签署了这封信。OpenAI声称已注意到这一点。该公司表示，在筹划如何发布其新发现时，它借鉴了一个独立咨询小组的建议——该小组由九位著名数学家组成，是在纳维-斯托克斯声明发布后成立的。除了分享其模型内部推理的一些细节外，OpenAI还承诺资助一系列会议，以帮助理解这些成果。

总而言之，OpenAI此次发布的规模意味着其真正影响只能事后才能看清。瑞士洛桑联邦理工学院的马丁·海雷尔表示：“一个问题的真正重要性，最终取决于它开辟的新途径以及其证明为其他问题带来的启示。”海雷尔既是OpenAI咨询小组的成员，也是那封菲尔兹奖得主公开信的签署人之一。就目前而言，AI所揭示的数学问题更多是关乎存在性，而非数值性。■

item.title: Should you be using a tongue-scraper?
item.description:

item.content:encoded:
Should you be using a tongue-scraper?

Science & technology | Well Informed

Oct 8th 2026

People have used tongue-scrapers since at least the Roman era. Napoleon Bonaparte’s was made of silver. George Washington took his everywhere. Today “influencers” like Hailey Bieber and Gwyneth Paltrow scrape their tongues as part of their “wellness” routines. But does tongue-scraping add anything to dental hygiene that brushing and flossing can’t do alone?

The mouth, like the gut, is home to lots of microbes. A healthy oral microbiome includes around 700 species of bacteria, along with fungi, protozoa and viruses. But poor oral hygiene, smoking or bad diet can upset the balance. That results in bacterial colonies, called biofilms, in which species thrive that cause tooth cavities, gum disease and chronic bad breath (halitosis).

Biofilms are the basis of dental plaque, which forms because teeth, unlike the mouth’s other tissues, are not constantly shedding their cells, and thus any bacteria clinging to them. But tongues, which host about two-thirds of the oral microbiome, are also susceptible to biofilms—which can turn them white or yellow. The gaps between the tiny protuberances covering a tongue’s upper surface teem with bacteria and are especially hospitable to anaerobic species, the respiration of which does not require oxygen but does often generate foul-smelling sulphurous compounds.

Given all this, it might be expected that evidence for the virtues of regular tongue-cleaning would be as abundant as that for cleaning teeth. Alas there is not much.

A trial published in 2018, involving 36 people suffering from gum disease, for example, found that adding tongue scraping to a normal dental-cleaning routine did indeed reduce halitosis. Another, on 45 children, which was published in 2015, showed it significantly lowered levels of Streptococcus mutans—a principal cause of tooth decay.

This particular trial, however, cast doubt on the idea that you need to use a special instrument to keep your tongue clean, for it also found that brushing tongues with a normal toothbrush or rinsing the mouth with salt water both worked just as well as using an actual scraper. Similarly, a third trial—of 56 people with bad breath, published in 2021—found that tongue-scraping and tongue-brushing removed tongue biofilms and reduced odiferous sulphur compounds to the same degree. A fourth, of another 80 bad-breathed individuals, published earlier this year, got similar results with tongue-brushing (rather than scraping) backed up by a dose of Streptococcus salivarius, a so-called oral probiotic that crowds out hostile bacteria such as S. mutans.

Good lingual hygiene may also improve someone’s sense of taste. A review of four trials published in 2025 found that removing tongue coatings increased intensity of salt perception, with one study doing so for 60% of participants.

Together, these results suggest tongue-scrapers might indeed do the biz, but that other approaches to lingual hygiene (including using the toothbrush with which you anyway clean your teeth) can be equally effective. Nevertheless, Zoe Brookes, a professor of dentistry at the University of Plymouth, urges caution. The studies, she says, are too small to draw strong conclusions. And removing too many bacteria from a healthy tongue might equally disrupt the oral microbiome. To maintain a healthy mouth, she observes, nothing beats toothbrushing (twice daily), flossing and cutting out the sweets.■

After a free, evidence-based guide to health and wellness? Sign up to our weekly Well Informed newsletter.
