item.description:
Culture

Culture | Pods for demigods Oct 8th 2026 EACH WEEKDAY morning Jordi Hays and John Coogan, two entrepreneurs-turned-podcasters, enter a sauna in Los Angeles with copies of the Wall Street Journal. They come out with jackets, ties and hot takes on the tech news of the day. Then they go on air as h...
item.content:encoded:
Superstar podcasts are Silicon Valley’s way of talking to itself

Culture | Pods for demigods

Oct 8th 2026

EACH WEEKDAY morning Jordi Hays and John Coogan, two entrepreneurs-turned-podcasters, enter a sauna in Los Angeles with copies of the Wall Street Journal. They come out with jackets, ties and hot takes on the tech news of the day. Then they go on air as hosts of the “Technology Business Programming Network” (“TBPN”) podcast, riffing with guests, banging gongs and blowing airhorns. The president of TBPN, Dylan Abruscato, calls it a “variety show” in the vein of a late-night talk show. Silicon Valley laps it up. It is not uncommon to see “TBPN”, rather than CNBC, streaming on the TV screens in tech firms’ offices.

Podcasts are the latest example of a power law in Silicon Valley. Only a few become big hitters. Those that do attract the demigods of tech as guests, making them even more influential. “TBPN” has interviewed Sam Altman of OpenAI and Mark Zuckerberg of Meta. The “All-In” Podcast, hosted by four plutocrats who straddle tech and MAGA politics, held a summit in Los Angeles in September attended by Elon Musk and Jensen Huang. (When Donald Trump phoned Nvidia’s boss on stage during the summit, Mr Huang put the president on speakerphone.) Dwarkesh Patel, a bearded 26-year-old who acts—and looks—like a high priest of AI research, hosts tech bigwigs for hours on the “Dwarkesh Podcast”. So does Lex Fridman, a gravel-voiced computer scientist whose podcast runs longer than some marathons.

All share an in-crowd mystique bordering on incestuousness. In April OpenAI reportedly spent $100m-200m to buy then-18-month-old TBPN (though there was no mention of the affiliation during Mr Altman’s interview). The “All-In” hosts are self-described “besties” with many of their billionaire interviewees. In San Francisco Mr Patel has shared digs with Anthropic’s researchers. They are fascinated by AI, which they talk about with passionate intensity and expertise. They are also an echo chamber, with a tin ear at times to the concerns of the rest of America.

This new podcasting elite reflects a big change in Silicon Valley’s relationship with the media. During the last great investment boom, the dotcom era of the 1990s, publications like Wired were tech-industry gospels. They covered the internet like Rolling Stone wrote about rock’n’roll, says John Battelle, a founding editor of Wired: “We thought we were covering the counterculture.”

But the rise of social media and the growing power and wealth of big tech generated a rift between Silicon Valley and news outlets. Mr Battelle says that parts of the tech establishment started to view traditional media as “anti-American” for questioning the “dominance of the tech hierarchy”. For their part, old media, whose business model has been hurt by the tech giants, sometimes smell of sour grapes. Podcasters, who share their guests’ techno-optimism, provide a friendlier platform.

The watershed came during the 2024 presidential race. Led by Mr Trump, politicians saw the medium as a less filtered way of getting their message out than the press or broadcast TV. “All-In” played a role. Two of its billionaire co-hosts, David Sacks and Chamath Palihapitiya, threw a fundraiser in San Francisco for Mr Trump. Shortly afterwards he appeared on their show. That helped raise the profile of the hosts, as well as of tech podcasting in general. (For more than a year Mr Sacks was Mr Trump’s AI “czar”, even dressing the part by wearing a Russian fur hat at an “All-In” event.)

Since then such superstar shows have gone from strength to strength. They take different approaches. The hosts of “All-In” delight in being anti-woke. They abhor what they call the “lamestream media” almost as much as they lampoon effective altruism (EA), a philosophical doctrine that they argue puts too much focus on the existential risks of AI. Mr Patel, in contrast, has said EA influenced him to start the “Dwarkesh Podcast” on ai. “TBPN” is not all bells and whistles. Its hosts have a deep knowledge of venture capital (VC), which they demystify with quips; they also work closely with media outlets and give airtime to their tech scoops.

Helping them thrive is what would be called, in Silicon Valley jargon, a flywheel. Just before he hit the big time in 2024, Mr Patel tweeted his bank balance. It showed savings of $0.14. Then Mr Zuckerberg came onto the show and the advertising dollars poured in. As more prominent executives take part, not only do advertisers notice; so do potential customers, investors and jobseekers, raising the quality of the audience. “This is luxurious media with very valuable eyeballs,” says Josh Kaplan, boss of Smooth Media, which represents podcasters.

The format is particularly well-suited to Silicon Valley, where founders invent stories for a living. They are venerated like the great men of history (Silicon Valley is still mostly a great manosphere). “We’re not journalists; we are enthusiasts,” says Patrick O’Shaughnessy, whose podcast, “Invest Like the Best”, has a strong following in VC circles. Firms such as Andreessen Horowitz have piled in too, creating podcasts to tout their portfolio companies to investors and themselves to founders. These offerings may be popular, but do not expect them to invest in the costly investigative work that uncovers frauds, such as that at Theranos, a health-tech startup, exposed by the Wall Street Journal in 2015.

Instead, AI is at the centre of their discussions. Unlike many parts of America, they treat it as almost the only topic worth discussing. But this obsession has further pushed Silicon Valley into a “monoculture”, says David Senra, an influential podcaster. Recently he has been to tech dinners where conversation veers only between AI optimism and doomerism. “It sounds like they are all reading the same tweets,” he says.

Lulu Cheng Meservey, a PR consultant to tech founders, reckons nine-tenths of people in tech speak only to other people in tech. Podcasts exacerbate that. As for using the format to transmit enthusiasm about AI to the outside world, it is not working. They may be well-meaning, she says, but “when a billionaire AI salesman is telling you whether to buy AI, you are taking that from someone who is entirely unrelatable to you.”

It may get worse. Silicon Valley’s podcasters sprinkle their conversations with reverence for space missions, robots and other techno-wizardry. In an AIpocalypse, they would come out better off than most people. Mr Battelle calls it the “golden ticket on the rocket ship”. If all else fails, they can podcast from Mars. But will people still want to listen to them? ■

item.title: “The Social Reckoning” is a fatally earnest sequel to a classic
item.description:
Culture

Culture | Film Oct 8th 2026 “I’m not two years out of a dorm room anymore,” snaps Mark Zuckerberg at an adviser in “The Social Reckoning”. The last time Facebook’s boss was portrayed on the big screen, a dorm is precisely where he was. “The Social Network” (2010) dramatised the company’s birth a...
item.content:encoded:
“The Social Reckoning” is a fatally earnest sequel to a classic

Culture | Film

Oct 8th 2026

“I’m not two years out of a dorm room anymore,” snaps Mark Zuckerberg at an adviser in “The Social Reckoning”. The last time Facebook’s boss was portrayed on the big screen, a dorm is precisely where he was. “The Social Network” (2010) dramatised the company’s birth at Harvard and established Mr Zuckerberg’s reputation as a chilly, ruthless weirdo. Its epilogue noted that Facebook had 500m members and that Mr Zuckerberg was the world’s youngest billionaire. Today Facebook has 3bn users and its 42-year-old boss is worth a quarter of a trillion dollars.

“The Social Reckoning”, a much-anticipated sequel to “The Social Network”, takes place around 15 years later. It follows Jeff Horwitz, a journalist at the Wall Street Journal (played by Jeremy Allen White), as he coaxes information from Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison), a disillusioned member of Facebook’s toothless “Civic Integrity Team”. The film adopts its predecessor’s time-hopping structure, flipping between hunts for the material and publication, when all hell breaks loose.

The movies share a writer in the form of Aaron Sorkin, who won an Oscar for his “Social Network” script (which was based on a book). But there the similarities end. Mr Sorkin stood in for the original director, David Fincher. Jesse Eisenberg declined to play Mr Zuckerberg for a second time, so the role has gone to Jeremy Strong, best known for “Succession”.

The main problem with “The Social Reckoning” is not that its director or actors have changed. It is that Facebook itself has. Back in 2010 Facebook was cool. It had been available to the general public for only four years: young people were glued to it; their grandparents had not yet taken it over. Mr Zuckerberg, then 26, was Time’s person of the year. “The Social Network” was devastating because it methodically gutted the world’s hottest company and its founder (or rather, co-founder, as the film made clear).

Today’s Facebook is a mightier company but a softer target. Social networks are reviled by legislators, litigators and parents. Facebook and its rivals have paid out in multiple court cases involving harm to children. Its efforts to silence criticism—gagging a former executive who wrote a book, “Careless People”, for instance—have backfired spectacularly. Almost no one in the world is less cool than Mr Zuckerberg, whose approval rating in America is -43%, just ahead of Vladimir Putin.

The result is that “The Social Reckoning”, which styles itself as an exposé, often feels more like a sermon for the converted. Mr Strong, who is known for his extreme method-acting approach, has nailed Mr Zuckerberg’s monotone voice and stiff manner. But whereas the young Zuck of “The Social Network” was a complex character—arrogant and treacherous but tragically insecure—in the “Reckoning” he is a cartoon villain. Surrounded by computer monitors and a bulletproof sofa in his imperial headquarters, he barks at quivering underlings as they labour through their slide decks. “Fuckin’ Civic Integrity”, he scoffs, after the team meekly suggests dialling down harmful content at the expense of 1% of engagement.

His henchmen are no subtler. Facebook’s comically horrid PR man says that the social network is better than any nation. “We’re post-government around here,” he sneers, when threatened with regulation. The now-familiar notion that the company puts profit before the greater good is conveyed with a megaphone. “If engagement keeps falling…it’ll be a bad earnings report!” squeals one executive, as the company debates whether to tone down its wickedness.

The second difficulty for the movie is that its subject matter is more nuanced than Mr Sorkin would like. The film’s central question—should Facebook suppress bad content?—is not so simple. The script implies that Facebook should take down lies. But should the flawed Mr Zuckerberg therefore be elevated to a global arbiter of truth? Some dialogue is unintentionally persuasive to the contrary. “The voters aren’t children,” argues Mr Zuckerberg in one scene. “Facebook isn’t the ref…We’re the public square.” Quite.

Mr Sorkin’s earnestness was perfectly tempered by Mr Fincher’s cynicism in “The Social Network”. It was a movie with no real heroes, between the perfidious Mr Zuckerberg and those he trampled, including a flash Sean Parker (an early supporter) and the absurd Winklevoss twins (who say Mr Zuckerberg stole their idea). The “Reckoning”, by contrast, is divided neatly into goodies (diligent journalist, brave whistleblower) and baddies (scheming Zuckerberg, robotic cronies). The outcome is an unsatisfying caricature.

Film and TV schedules have lately been clogged with dramatisations of Silicon Valley. The most successful ones have tended to be those based on true stories, including what happened at Uber (“Super Pumped”), WeWork (“WeCrashed”) and Theranos (“The Dropout”). But now those corporate dramas are well-known—and helped make up people’s minds about the Valley’s recklessness.

Yet more takes are on the way. On October 8th Paramount+ will launch “Cupertino”, a series about a fictional law firm fighting big tech. A new documentary about Theranos’s Elizabeth Holmes will come out this month, too. In December “Artificial”, starring Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman, will be the first movie to tell the story of OpenAI. “The Social Network” remains the model for how to do it well. Alas, its follow-up offers a reminder of what a hard act it is to follow. ■

item.title: Malcolm Gladwell and Harel Shapira are up in arms about guns
item.description:
Culture

Culture | Under the gun Oct 8th 2026 FEW THINGS about Americans baffle foreigners more than their attachment to guns. Thirty years ago mass shootings in Australia and Scotland prompted both countries to tighten their gun laws; today, legally owning a handgun in Britain is almost impossible and g...
item.content:encoded:
Malcolm Gladwell and Harel Shapira are up in arms about guns

Culture | Under the gun

Oct 8th 2026

FEW THINGS about Americans baffle foreigners more than their attachment to guns. Thirty years ago mass shootings in Australia and Scotland prompted both countries to tighten their gun laws; today, legally owning a handgun in Britain is almost impossible and getting one in Australia requires licensing, registration and a background check. In America, meanwhile, 40% of people live in a household with a gun, and each year more than 1m Americans become first-time gun owners. What explains this form of American exceptionalism? Two new books try to answer that question in very different ways.

Malcolm Gladwell, a prolific Canadian journalist who lives in America, has written a book that follows his familiar formula: ten short chapters crammed with anecdotes wrapped around nuggets of wisdom, like social-science fortune cookies. “The American Way of Killing” emerged from a series on his popular podcast, “Revisionist History”; annoyingly, it reads like it, with whole chunks of raw transcript slapped down on the page.

But, as with most of Mr Gladwell’s books, readers will come away thinking differently about the world. For instance, one of the few gun-control measures most Americans support is a ban on assault weapons. Mr Gladwell argues it would do little; most gun deaths involve handguns, which are readily available. Many on the American left would be happy to shrink police forces; Mr Gladwell notes that European cities tend to have larger police forces than similarly sized American ones and argues that keeps them safe, because their presence helps prevent crimes.

Mr Gladwell’s usually fluid writing has a shrill, rebarbative edge. He accuses Americans of “moral recklessness”, misdiagnosing “the nature of the violence that plagues their streets” and having a “fundamentally dishonest way” of discussing guns. “Not only do Americans get things wrong, but they seem uninterested in ever getting things right,” he huffs. Those who share his views on guns may enjoy his scolding, but his tone will turn some off.

Harel Shapira, by contrast, does far more showing than telling. A sociologist at the University of Texas, Mr Shapira spent years taking firearms-training classes in Texas to better understand why and how guns appeal to ordinary Americans. The instructors are dedicated professionals, mostly conservative but not nutters “running tactical drills deep in the woods in preparation for a battle with the deep state”. Both students and instructors sincerely believe that owning and knowing how to use guns will help keep them safer.

Mr Shapira and his fellow students do not just learn to load, aim and clean their weapons. They are also taught “the ‘warrior mindset’" or “the state of mind that we ‘good guys with guns’ were meant to embrace”. The school’s founder says that there are three types of people: sheep (passive), wolves (predatory) and the type he wants them to be: sheepdogs, who protect the flock. The police are a “reactive force” who often arrive too late; a sheepdog has to always be prepared for danger.

The school’s founder encourages them to carry their guns loaded. “There are bad guys everywhere,” he warns. Many of Mr Shapira’s fellow students fear petrol stations, where they feel vulnerable when they get out of their cars to refuel. For his instructors, Mr Shapira writes, “a diverse and vibrant public sphere does not hold the promise of a fulfilling life. It holds only the potential for a violent death.”

The consequences of a mindset that encourages an armed response to ubiquitous danger quickly becomes clear. One of his instructors shot and killed a young black man who broke into his home. It turned out he was a mentally disabled resident of a nearby group home who had escaped and ran down the street, banging on front doors. When the young man, dishevelled and probably “cold, frightened, disoriented”, did not heed the instructor’s orders to leave, he shot him five times.

Was the instructor a “good guy with a gun”? Some thought so: he faced no charges. Mr Shapira is not so sure. But what makes his book so exceptional is that his personal doubts did not stop him from listening to his instructor’s story with empathy, curiosity and understanding—all of which he extends to his subjects.

In that sense, these two books are not just about guns; they present two ways of engaging in culture-war arguments. Both authors dislike guns and presumably wrote their books to persuade others of their beliefs. Mr Gladwell tries to scold his opponents into submission, which seldom works. Mr Shapira, however, listens and shows his readers a world full of complex people rather than caricatures.

Whether any author can change minds on this issue is a bleaker question. A majority of American adults has been threatened with a gun, seen someone shot or had a family member killed by a gun, according to KFF, a think-tank. Yet in recent years American gun laws have become only laxer, with states embracing “permitless carry” of firearms. America’s gun-violence problem will last until voters follow Australians and Britons—and decide they have had enough. ■

item.content:encoded:
想穿越中东一游吗？

文化 | 夹在中间的男人 2026年10月8日

据某些说法，那是史上最昂贵的派对。为纪念波斯帝国建立2500周年，伊朗末代国王穆罕默德·礼萨·巴列维邀请各国国王、王后、皇帝和总统，在波斯波利斯古城废墟间的一处奢华营地中共同庆祝。宾客们啜饮酩悦香槟和拉菲罗斯柴尔德酒庄的葡萄酒，享用来自巴黎马克西姆餐厅的美食，还对着5万只进口鸣禽目瞪口呆。（这些鸟儿最终全部死于酷热。）伊朗民众对这种奢靡感到愤怒。“我们几乎连面包和萝卜都供不起他们，”国王如此麻木不仁地回怼道。对于伊朗革命的缔造者与精神之父阿亚图拉鲁霍拉·霍梅尼而言，这场派对是“魔鬼的盛宴”。它标志着国王统治终结的开端。七年后，国王出逃国外，亲信被处决，甚至连他的马也遭到公开折磨并被枪杀。派对结束了。

英国历史学家西蒙·塞巴格·蒙蒂菲奥里在上一本书中探讨了世界历史。他的最新著作《大锅》则更加雄心勃勃：它梳理了自1900年以来中东的历史。你可能会想，这个主题还有什么新东西可说？关于阿拉伯人的厚重历史著作比比皆是。以色列人与巴勒斯坦人之间的冲突，用蒙蒂菲奥里自己的话说，已经催生了“一个名副其实的产业”的分析。无数大部头梳理了塑造该地区的外交、战争与革命。

蒙蒂菲奥里的贡献在多个方面独树一帜。他涵盖了整个中东核心地带，包括土耳其、伊朗、以色列和阿拉伯国家：这是一种出奇罕见的做法。更重要的是，他将读者带至当下，分析仍在持续展开的事件。他旨在通过“人的故事，往往是统治者的故事”来讲述这段历史，从而“为宗教、地缘政治和意识形态的沉重议题增添轻盈”。蒙蒂菲奥里还希望为西方人看待中东的方式“恢复某种平衡”。这些任务无一轻松。

然而，《大锅》的宏大视野令人叹为观止。他在该地区飞速穿梭，从1915年穆斯塔法·凯末尔·阿塔图尔克与协约国军队作战，到1932年阿卜杜勒阿齐兹·本·阿卜杜勒·拉赫曼·沙特夺取利雅得、建立沙特王国。随后，这本书继续推进，历经以色列建国、伊朗革命、苏丹内战的恐怖以及过去三年的血腥冲突。

书的广度不可避免地意味着深度的牺牲。1915-16年的亚美尼亚种族灭绝仅用不到一页篇幅处理。但蒙蒂菲奥里也成功纳入了大量细节，使宏大叙事栩栩如生（例如，伊朗是继美国之后第二个承认新以色列国的国家；或者埃及的贾迈勒·阿卜杜勒·纳赛尔对列昂尼德·勃列日涅夫说，如果他是以色列领导人：“我绝不会放弃被占领土。”）。

鉴于蒙蒂菲奥里匆匆掠过如此多的“人的故事”，他或许本可以借鉴吉莉·库珀女爵士某部作品的做法，附上人物表。那肯定会色彩斑斓。《大锅》中人物纷呈，包括被中情局昵称为“肥混蛋”的埃及国王法鲁克；“穿着睡衣的病秧子”穆罕默德·摩萨台；以及新伊朗共和国首任总统阿布哈桑·巴尼萨德尔，他有着“滑稽的小胡子、过大的眼镜和法国新浪潮电影导演式的利落西装”。

平衡则更为棘手。他首先通过该地区各成员国的视角直接书写，而非从帝国主义者或入侵者的角度切入。在美国正逐步退出其作为中东主导力量的角色、且没有哪个国家显得愿意或能够接替之际，这是一种值得的努力。

在历史仍在形成之际书写历史尤为困难。他对2023年10月7日袭击事件及以色列回应——“其历史上规模最大、时间最长、最不受约束的战争”——的分析，在许多读者看来极为合理。然而，毫无疑问，一些人会认为他的判断对以色列过于宽容，而另一些读者则认为他对巴勒斯坦人过于同情。但他真正精准之处在于他对伊朗革命重要性的强调。他将伊朗编织进中东历史之中，而非像许多其他人那样孤立地对待它，并突出其对地区乃至世界的重要性，这是本书的显著成就之一。他将伊朗革命的影响比作1789年法国大革命和1917年俄国革命，认为与它们一样，它“改变了世界”。当前中东的乱局印证了这一判断。■

item.title: 为什么你最喜欢的面包店和咖啡店现在都开始卖帆布手提袋了
item.description:
Culture

文化 | 着装密码 2026年10月8日 从郁金香和兰花到豆宝宝玩偶和宝可梦卡片，人类对狂热痴迷并不陌生。但最奇怪的现象之一，莫过于当下对美国杂货店Trader Joe's迷你手提袋的追捧。9月30日推出的限时万圣节主题手提袋——售价2.99美元，大小与iPad相当——引发了全美各地门店外的长队。一些Trader Joe's门店对每位顾客可购买的数量实施了严格限制。（人们似乎并不介意这些手提袋小到没什么实际用处。）狂热爱好者们转而涌向转售网站，售价在20美元到异想天开的5万美元之间。 周边商品——用时髦的说法叫“merch”——似乎无处不在，适用于一切事物。研究公司牛津经济研究院估计，全球每...
item.content:encoded:
为什么你最喜欢的面包店和咖啡店现在都开始卖帆布手提袋了

文化 | 着装密码 2026年10月8日

从郁金香和兰花到豆宝宝玩偶和宝可梦卡片，人类对狂热痴迷并不陌生。但最奇怪的现象之一，莫过于当下对美国杂货店Trader Joe's迷你手提袋的追捧。9月30日推出的限时万圣节主题手提袋——售价2.99美元，大小与iPad相当——引发了全美各地门店外的长队。一些Trader Joe's门店对每位顾客可购买的数量实施了严格限制。（人们似乎并不介意这些手提袋小到没什么实际用处。）狂热爱好者们转而涌向转售网站，售价在20美元到异想天开的5万美元之间。

周边商品——用时髦的说法叫“merch”——似乎无处不在，适用于一切事物。研究公司牛津经济研究院估计，全球每年在这方面花费3380亿美元。（他们相当宽泛的定义包括授权产品、服装、品牌商品和按需印刷产品。）从面包店、书店到家喻户晓的品牌和五金店，各种公司都在兜售此类商品。就连科技公司也加入了进来。Palantir在7月推出了带有其标志的白色网球服。最近OpenAI发布了其首个公开发售的服装系列。“这是在大庭广众之下被霸凌的最佳方式，”一位X用户嘲讽道。

当然，周边商品并不是什么新鲜事。长期以来，它在三个领域一直很常见。一个是儿童产品——任何不得不为一条艾莎裙或巴斯光年玩具掏钱的家长都深有体会。另一个领域是音乐。巴克莱银行预测，哈里·斯泰尔斯的粉丝们今年夏天在该歌手巡演的伦敦站每人将挥霍100英镑（约合135美元）。周边商品也是体育队的一大收入来源。纽约仍然到处是蓝橙配色的服饰，这是尼克斯队的颜色，该队是纽约市获胜的篮球队。英超球队阿森纳在2024-25赛季的球衣和周边商品收入增长了26%，达到1.3亿英镑。

然而如今，更多种类的企业正在把周边商品当作营销手段。制作这类产品既便宜又容易，这有所帮助。一个帆布手提袋批量生产可能成本不到1美元，但在其使用寿命期间可能会被成千上万人看到。对于Daunt Books或莎士比亚书店——它们的帆布手提袋深受文人喜爱——这意味着数十亿次的曝光。周边商品还能让公司展现有趣的形象。许多公司借助幽默来传达个性。6月，超市Lidl配合世界杯推出了“三只Lidl球衣”。这款恶搞的英格兰足球衣采用防液体和防异味面料：这样更能承受周围热情球迷喷洒的啤酒。它在55秒内售罄。

对消费者来说，品牌周边可以是支持心爱本地企业的一种方式，这一趋势在疫情期间得到推动。纽约大学的贾里德·沃森表示，周边商品热潮也标志着年轻人通过衣着和配饰进行“信号传递”的方式发生了变化。他说，在数字时代长大改变了他们的消费心理。服装品牌看起来千篇一律。现在，人们渴望通过自己经历过的体验或去过的地方来展示个性，这些让他们感觉自己与众不同。“地位的形式已经改变，”品牌咨询公司Tracksuit的康纳·阿奇博尔德表示：“过去你用价格标签、设计师品牌或昂贵的手表来彰显地位。现在更多是看品味和归属感。”

与直觉相反，穿周边商品来脱颖而出也是一种与社群建立联系的方式。西方近一半的公民不隶属于任何组织，无论是信仰团体、体育俱乐部还是其他公民组织。在这种社会原子化的背景下，穿一件周边商品——尤其是某个小众事物的周边——就相当于“在大池塘里当一条小鱼，还能找到其他小鱼”，沃森先生说。对一些人来说，终极目标仅仅是得到陌生人会心的赞许点头。

下一个趋势是更具个人化的周边商品。像Etsy这样的公司让消费者能够生产定制物品，如杯子、火柴和T恤，用作生日派对、单身派对和婚礼的回礼。今年，《建筑文摘》报道了人们送给房客周边商品的事，并问道：“你的家应该有自己的周边商品吗？”人们越珍视体验，纪念品就越有价值。大家都明白了这一点。■

item.content:encoded:
Cyril Hilsum invented the flat-screen displays that hold us in thrall

Obituary | The world seen anew

Oct 8th 2026

Whenever in later life a fresh idea struck him, Cyril Hilsum would leave the dinner table and wander to his lab. He didn’t have far to go. Part of it was in the garage, part in the scullery, of his house in Pinner, north-west of London. The rest was in the kitchen. One counter was his electronics bench, with an oscilloscope, a pair of waveform generators, a spectrum analyser and a tray of voltage dividers looped to each other and to a soldering station with a maze of cables. On the facing counter stood a three-roll mill for working conductive powders, a precision balance, a small vacuum chamber and many labelled jars of carbon black and nickel powder. Everything had its place here apart from kitchen stuff; but he dined, and lunched too, mostly on red wine, ready meals and chocolate. Fruit and veg he disdained. He lived very healthily on a diet of curiosity, hard work and endless ideas.

In all he had over 70 patents to his name. The last, filed when he was 97, was for ink with sensors that conducted electricity. His lasting fame, though, came from liquid-crystal displays. In the 1970s he realised that these could replace the bulky, power-hungry TVs of old, with their bulging cathode-ray tubes and curved screens, with slim flat-screen models that could be hung on a wall. He and his collaborators started small, with digital watches in 1974; but in no time flat screens were everywhere, in computer monitors, cockpit displays, departure boards and, especially, mobile phones. Sharper images took longer; but in the modern screen-bound age, he changed the world’s way of seeing.

It had been difficult work. Liquid crystals certainly behaved like liquids, because they flowed, but their molecules could keep a structure for a very brief time. It was up to him to stabilise them and induce them to work at room temperature. In two years he and two colleagues, George Gray and Peter Raynes, produced and patented a whole new controllable family of them.

His second-proudest achievement was to build in 1962 Britain’s first semiconductor laser, which involved getting gallium arsenide to behave. This was extremely hard. To make it he had to mix gallium with arsenic in a silica tube, heat it furiously, stick it in a shed and wait til morning. By then it would have burst the tube asunder, and he would have to pick out the pieces. But now he had a compound whose electrons were finely tuned to convert electrical energy efficiently into light, making a laser so compact that it could be used with ordinary batteries in everyday devices: CD players, burglar alarms, speed-detection devices, LEDs, printers and scanners.

The mini-radars proved especially useful. They could be fitted under trains to start them braking, even at 200mph, and one version, called Claribel, used the speed and trajectory of a bullet to pinpoint the position of hidden snipers in Northern Ireland. Once deployed, the sniping stopped. As for him he was stopped too, by a policeman with a speed-gun, as he roared down a motorway in his usual mode; but got away with it by saying he was its inventor, and that one was wrongly calibrated. He didn’t lose many arguments, even with the law. But then, with his nimbus of hair and his high domed forehead, he did look every inch an inventor.

At that time he was working at the Royal Signals and Radar Establishment at Malvern, where he stayed from 1964 to 1983. Strictly speaking he was a civil servant, although he never felt like one; he was a scientist and an engineer. An engineer first perhaps, who at three had taken his toys apart to see how they worked and, sometimes, succeeded in reassembling them. His bent was practical and, often, commercial. That came from being the son of struggling street traders in the East End. At weekends he worked on the stalls (chamois leather on Portobello Road, flat caps on Petticoat Lane), and in the evenings he often watched his father concealing, with gold paint, the printed price on chocolate bars, in order to sell them for more. A large part of his impetus to replace cathode-ray tubes was the fact that the British government was paying huge royalties to the Radio Corporation of America for using them. When everyone went roaring after liquid crystals, the government speedily earned £100m.

He was still frustrated, though, by officialdom’s general failure to exploit the good ideas British scientists had, and at 57 he left Malvern to lead the GEC Hirst Research Centre. Amazingly, it was the first time he had ever decided what to do in life. Previously, he had simply moved from project to project as ministers or higher-ups dictated. He went willingly, because every promotion was a step further from the East End, and because his quick mind (he beat Alan Turing at chess, once) always won him a measure of independence. At school he and his friend Jack had been allowed to sit in the back row, working at their own fast pace. At both Malvern and at GEC, and before that, he had a lab of his own.

He believed strongly, however, that scientists should be accountable for what they were doing. His consistent question was, Why? Why had his mother insisted on washing him every day, when he hardly got dirty? And why did theoretical physicists sit every day at their desks or in their labs, enjoying taxpayer funding, without trying to apply what they had learned? If they had seen an effect, it was up to them to find a use for it, as he infallibly had.

In 2006 the British Liquid Crystal Society introduced a Cyril Hilsum medal. He was pleased, but almost embarassed. He cared more about the scholarship he had set up in memory of his wife Betty, his rock, and the prize he started in memory of his daughter Karen, who died at 42. She had been a promising engineer. All through his career he had hired or promoted women equally with men. In fact, as scientists he preferred them. Men cared about learning more; women cared about using science for good. That was much more crucial, for him, than any wonders they might do in the kitchen. And anyway, they could hardly get into his. ■
